News.title: BA pilots hit by food poisoning at 30,000ft with one 'incapacitated 'and put on oxygen
News.content:
BA pilots hit by food poisoning at 30,000ft with one 'incapacitated 'and put on oxygen

The flight deck crew who had breakfast while on a stopover in India, all fell ill with food poisoning with the worst hit having to be put on oxygen during the long-haul journey to Heathrow

View 2 Images Pilots on a BA flight fell ill after contracting food poisoning (Image: Getty Images)

British airways pilots were struck with food poisoning after a stopover - with one officer ‘incapacitated’.

‌



The pilots had broken their journey to the UK in India and had breakfast together in a nearby hotel lounge in Hyderabad, as well as drinking bottled water they bought from an outside vendor.

‌



One officer was hit hard and was left ‘incapacitated’ and had to be put on oxygen at 30,000 feet on the lengthy 10 and a half hour flight to London Heathrow. The other two pilots were able to continue working during the flight, but their symptoms progressed once the plane landed in Britain.

‌



British Airways confirmed passenger safety was not affected and that the flight operated safely. But insiders at pilots’ union Balpa reportedly said officials are angered as there was a large amount of previous complains surrounding the hygiene at their £130-a-night hotel.

View 2 Images BA confirmed they had launched an urgent investigation to ensure a similar ordeal does not happen again (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The pilots filed Air Safety reports and provided samples to ensure medical staff could pinpoint the direct source. British Airways is reportedly assessing the hotel options they have within the Southern Indian city of Hyderabad.

The airline said: “The welfare of our colleagues is a top priority and we are reviewing crew accommodation in this location following some isolated reports of sickness.

“During the flight one of our pilots became unwell. In line with established procedures, the aircraft continued safely to its destination and landed normally.

Article continues below

BA confirmed they had launched an investigation, adding: “The safety of our customers and crew is always our highest priority and at no point was the safety of the flight compromised.”

News.title: Boy, 15, suddenly drops dead after kicking football machine at fairground
News.content:
Boy, 15, suddenly drops dead after kicking football machine at fairground

Alessio Colletti, from Sarono, near Milan, was on holiday at Luna Park in Spotorno in northern Italy when he died while using the calciometro machine

View 2 Images Alessio Colletti was a promising young footballer (Image: Jam Press)

A teenager has been electrocuted to death while using a fairground football machine.

‌



The incident took place as Alessio Colletti, 15, was on holiday with a friend and the pal's parents at Luna Park in the seaside town of Spotorno, northern Italy. The 15-year-old footballer approached the "calciometro" - a classic fairground machine which measures kick power.

‌



Alessio is reported to have taken off one of his shoes to play barefoot when he was hit by a massive electric shock the moment he touched the machine on July 16. It is claimed that the attraction's safety switch reportedly failed to trip.

‌



The promising young footballer collapsed to the ground and, despite resuscitation efforts that lasted more than two hours, Alessio died at St Paul's Hospital in Savona. A manslaughter investigation has now been launched to establish the circumstances of the incident.

View 2 Images A manslaughter investigation was launched following Alessio's death (Image: Jam Press)

‌



The fairground ride owner, the technician who tested the attraction and the engineer responsible for its annual safety checks are all under investigation. Investigators will look at why the life-saving differential switch, which is designed to cut power at the first sign of leak, failed to activate.

A seized cable and connectors are being examined for possible rain damage after a downpour shortly before the incident, as reported by NeedToKnow. An electrical engineering expert from Turin University will carry out forensic tests.

Alessio, from Sarono, near Milan, will be the subject of a post-mortem examination on Friday. Luna Park remains closed while checks continue on permits and safety compliance.

Article continues below

Alessio's football club, Amor Sportiva Saronno, paid tribute with a black-ribbon post, writing: "Ciao Colle, you will always be with all of us." Local rivals Virtus Cantalupo added: "There is pain that the heart cannot accept... the football stops, rivalries stop. Only the pain remains."

Friends described Alessio as a talented midfielder with a bright future in the game. His devastated family is still waiting for the green light for a funeral in Saronno once the body is released.

Spotorno sits on the Italian Riviera, about 50 miles west of Genoa – a favourite spot for families seeking sun, sea and fairground fun during the peak summer season. The case has raised questions over electrical inspections and emergency cut-outs on ageing attractions at travelling fairgrounds.

News.title: 'Anthony Taylor quitting is a huge pity - but grassroots referees will quit unless action is taken'
News.content:
'Anthony Taylor quitting is a huge pity - but grassroots referees will quit unless action is taken'

Anthony Taylor has decided to call full time on his refereeing career at 47 after serving on the Premier League for 16 years — and he had previously indicated he had been considering quitting

View 3 Images Our man, Bradley Jolly, is a football referee having taken the whistle as a young adult

Anthony Taylor's full-time whistle is such a pity — but sadly it is unexpected.

‌



Referees across the UK will have spotted subtle signs Taylor, 47, had been weighing up retirement in recent months. He hinted in interviews at the pressures of refereeing, alluding to experiences with which many grassroots officials will have found far too familiar.

‌



Is it any wonder then that Taylor — often described as the country's best referee — has hung up his whistle? I am a referee with nearly 10 years of experience and the issues Taylor has pointed out happen on park pitches and the semi-pro level. I've experienced myself, and seen my colleagues plagued by the ugly side.

‌



Players surround the public enemy, managers use him or her as their scapegoat and refs are abused. Little is done to help us. Taylor's retirement — after 16 years at the top — will resonate with the approximate 28,000 of us in the UK. A staggering 7,000 of us leave the game each year and, with Taylor often regarded as an idol, I fear many more — from exciting prospects to veteran whistleblowers — will follow in his footsteps.

Thomas Tuchel has no regrets as Argentina boss rubs salt in the wounds after beating England READ MORE :

Premier League referee Anthony Taylor retires from football and teases what's next READ MORE :

Announcing his retirement, Taylor said: "Officiating at the elite level has been an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant."

And, in October last year, Taylor, who is a former prison officer, said: "There's certainly been moments — and I won't be alone in this — there's certainly been moments where you are thinking, 'Is it worth it?... And certainly, moments where you're thinking, 'What's being said is completely unfair'."

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Taylor is pictured during the 2026 World Cup match between Portugal and Spain, which would turn out to be his final professional match (Image: EYE4images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

I, for one, was not surprised the Wythenshawe-born referee, who had been on Fifa's list of officials for 14 years, quit after overseeing Spain's 1-0 win over Portugal in the World Cup last 16 on 6 July.

I actually admired Taylor's strength for continuing after a chair and drinks were thrown in the direction of the English referee and his group as they made their way through a gathering of Roma fans at Budapest Airport. He had refereed Roma in the 2023 Europa League final, which Roma lost. The dad was ushered to a safe area by airport security, and since revealed his family had not attended big games following this incident.

‌



Don't get me wrong — I have of course not encountered anything of such nature during my tenure, way below Taylor's level. I have been attacked after a game, though, and know multiple others who have been.

View 3 Images Anthony Taylor shows a red card to Arsenal's Mikel Merino their clash against Liverpool last year (Image: Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

In his interview last year, Taylor also said: "We have this archaic psychological tactic of 'let's bombard the ref or bombard the fourth official with the hope of getting a decision out of it'."

Article continues below

And he's right. It must stop. We will continue to lose amazing top-flight referees, we will continue to lose the dedicated grassroots officials who turn up week in, week in, in the gales, rain and snow. I know I am considering giving football the red card — and who can blame me?

Thank you, Anthony Taylor. Your service to the game has been fantastic. You've refereed more than 800 matches across two decades. You've officiated every major domestic cup final. Yet, you've been treated disgracefully time and time again.

News.title: People taking GLP-1 weight loss medication urged to eat these 10 foods
News.content:
People taking GLP-1 weight loss medication urged to eat these 10 foods

Experts say nutrient-dense foods become even more important as appetite decreases on GLP-1 medications

View 3 Images Pharmacist has shared the best foods to eat when taking the common medication (stock image) (Image: Getty)

As more people begin taking GLP-1 weight-loss medications such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, healthcare professionals are warning that eating less doesn't automatically mean eating better. While the medications are highly effective at reducing appetite and supporting weight loss, experts say many patients unknowingly consume too little protein and too few essential nutrients, increasing the risk of losing lean muscle alongside fat.

‌



According to Sobia Qasim, Superintendent Pharmacist at Curely, preserving muscle during weight loss is just as important as losing body fat, with poor nutrition potentially affecting long-term health. Muscle mass naturally declines with age in a condition known as sarcopenia, and building strong nutritional habits while losing weight can help support muscle strength and mobility in later life.

‌



Sobia says the challenge isn't simply eating fewer calories. It's making every bite count. "One of the biggest misconceptions is that weight-loss medication does all the hard work. While these medicines help reduce appetite, they don't replace the need for good nutrition," she said.

‌



"When you're naturally eating much smaller portions, every meal becomes more important. The goal shouldn't just be to lose weight, it should be to lose body fat while preserving muscle, strength and overall health. Many people focus solely on the number on the scales, but without enough protein and key nutrients, you may also lose lean muscle during the process.

"That's why choosing nutrient-dense foods is so important." Rather than relying on large meals, Sobia recommends choosing foods that deliver high levels of protein, calcium, fibre and healthy fats in relatively small portions.

View 3 Images There are several foods the pharmacist recommends while taking GLP-1 medication (stock image)

‌



10 foods pharmacists recommend while taking GLP-1 medication

Edamame beans . A small bowl provides around 17g of protein, along with fibre, magnesium, and iron, making it ideal when appetite is reduced.

Sardines . Rich in protein, calcium, vitamin D and omega-3 fatty acids. One of the most nutrient-dense foods for supporting both muscle and bone health.

Skyr yoghurt . Naturally high in protein while remaining relatively low in sugar and calories, making it more filling than many standard yoghurts.

‌



Pumpkin seeds . Packed with magnesium, zinc, healthy fats and protein to support muscle function and recovery.

Calcium-set tofu . Delivers both plant protein and calcium, making it an excellent option for vegetarians and vegans.

Lentil pasta . Contains considerably more protein and fibre than traditional pasta while still being an easy swap for familiar meals.

‌



White beans . A surprisingly good source of protein, fibre and calcium that can be added to soups, stews and salads.

Chia seeds . Tiny but rich in fibre, calcium and omega-3 fatty acids. Easy to sprinkle over yoghurt or porridge.

Tinned salmon (including the soft bones). Provides high-quality protein alongside naturally occurring calcium and vitamin D.

‌



Quark . Often overlooked, quark is exceptionally high in protein while remaining low in fat, making it a useful snack or breakfast option.

Sobia says these foods can help patients meet their nutritional needs without forcing themselves to eat large meals. She said: "People often assume they need huge portions of chicken or protein shakes, but many simply don't feel hungry enough for that while taking GLP-1 medication.

"Choosing foods that pack a lot of nutrition into relatively small portions can make a real difference. Ingredients like sardines, Skyr yoghurt, edamame and pumpkin seeds provide protein and important nutrients without requiring large meals."

‌



View 3 Images The pharmacist recommends adding seeds to your diet, including chia seeds (stock image)

Simple food swaps that increase nutrition without increasing portion size

Instead of white pasta, try lentil pasta. Why? More protein and fibre to help support muscle and fullness.

Instead of flavoured yoghurt, try plain Skyr with berries. Why? Higher protein and less added sugar.

‌



Instead of crisps, try roasted edamame. Why? A protein-rich snack with added fibre.

Instead of cream cheese, try quark or cottage cheese. Why? Significantly more protein for a similar serving size.

Instead of white rice, try quinoa. Why? More protein, magnesium and fibre.

‌



Instead of butter on toast, try nut butter. Why? Adds healthy fats and a small protein boost.

Instead of sugary cereal, try overnight oats with chia seeds. Why? More fibre and longer-lasting energy.

Instead of fizzy drinks, try fortified milk or calcium-enriched soy drink. Why? Supports calcium intake while also providing protein.

Article continues below

However, Sobia says nutrition is only one part of maintaining muscle during weight loss. She said: "We also encourage patients to include resistance exercise where appropriate, whether that's weight training, resistance bands or bodyweight exercises. Muscle is incredibly important for long-term health, mobility and maintaining weight loss.

"Weight-loss medication should be viewed as part of a wider lifestyle approach rather than a standalone solution. Eating a varied, nutrient-rich diet and staying physically active will help patients get the greatest long-term benefit from treatment."

GLP-1 medications continue to become more widely available across the UK. Patients are urged to seek professional guidance throughout their treatment to ensure they continue meeting their nutritional needs while losing weight.

News.title: King Charles pestered by troublesome fly as he and Camilla begin to wind down for summer break
News.content:
King Charles pestered by troublesome fly as he and Camilla begin to wind down for summer break

The King and Queen made their traditional visit to the Sandringham Flower Show today, with the royal couple arriving on a horse-drawn carriage and being cheered by the crowds

View 5 Images King Charles and Queen Camilla at the Sandringham Flower Show today (Image: Getty Images)

The King batted away a fly and the Queen got the giggles after being given a large knitted radish as they undertook one of their final engagements before the summer break.

‌



The couple were on their traditional pilgrimage to the Sandringham Flower Show, an event that has been held on the royal estate in Norfolk for almost 150 years. This year, for the first time, it is being run by the Royal Horticultural Society, of which His Majesty is patron.

‌



It also saw the monarch collaborate on a new ‘RHS Legacy Garden’ using local Norfolk materials to celebrate his long-held passion for horticulture, as well as champion rural skills and biodiversity.

‌



Why Prince William and Kate are rewriting history and giving George the childhood his dad never had READ MORE :

View 5 Images A troublesome insect pestered the King (Image: Getty Images)

Their Majesties arrived on the horse-drawn Victoria Carriage throughout the Old Norwich Gates to the main house to cheers from the crowds.

After standing for the national anthem they immediately set about shaking the first of hundreds of hands as they were shown round by RHS President Keith Weed and director general Clare Matterson.

‌



The King, who along with his wife had enjoyed a private viewing the previous night, looked delighted to meet with garden collaborator Catherine Macdonald to view his garden, which offered a county feel.

The couple constantly stopped to meet and greeted the many thousands of members of the public who lined the route to catch a glimpse of them. "Are you all mad keen gardeners?" His Majesty asked. "I’m the same age as you," one well-wisher told him. "You are looking good!"

View 5 Images The couple arrived at the show on a horse-drawn carriage (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

‌



"It gets much harder doesn’t it?" Charles, dressed in a summer beige suit and brogues, laughed. He also beamed when another fan told him: "You look so like your mum."

Camilla, 79, sporting a pretty new £245 green Lexy London dress and a large plaster on her right thumb, asked another: "Are you enjoying yourself? There’s a lot to see."

She was given a gift of a bag of citronella-based insect repellents by The Oil Hut, which might have come in useful earlier when her husband was forced to swat away a flying pest.

‌



The sovereign was invited to present a new ‘The Kings Biodiversity Award’ to Sophie Goldber who has designed the ‘Mindful Chef’s Gathering’ inspired by a traditional orchard redesigned for a smaller garden. He also gave an award for The Best Exhibit in the Floral Marquee Award to family-run business Roaleyn Fuschias from North Wales.

View 5 Images The couple were on one of their final engagements before the summer break (Image: Getty Images)

Meanwhile Her Majesty presented The Queen’s Choice of Upcycled Containers Award to the Whissonsett & District Horticultural Society and Gardening Club, with a special award to Ingoldisthorpe Church of England Primary School for their appropriately-named ‘The Queen Bee’ design featuring a ‘majestic queen bee planter symbolising leadership’. She told them: "Very well done. It is such fun."

‌



The King also stopped to speak to a group of children from Weeting Primary School in Brandon saying: "Have you got a garden here? Have you been very busy at school? Do you grow any vegetables? Do you eat them? Have you tried any spinach - it’s the best thing on the world. Have a very nice holidays. You must be on holidays now? These poor exhausted teachers!"

Meanwhile the Queen examined a large purple knitted radish with an impish smile on her face. "Thank you very much indeed, it’s very kind," she beamed.

View 5 Images The King greets crowds of wellwishers (Image: Chris Jackson/PA Wire)

‌



She also chatted to a girl from Brighton who told her that she had been a member of the Pony Club at Plumpton , Sussex, where she herself grew up. "So was I!" she trilled. The couple departed in their horse and carriage but not before shaking several dozen more hands.

They have one more official engagement before departing for Scotland for the summer. The RHS Sandringham Flower Show is the first RHS Show to be hosted at a Royal residence and,like other RHS Shows, features expert growers and nurseries and celebrates charities and communities.

News.title: Small boats that could carry 2,000 people to UK seized in 'serious blow' to smugglers
News.content:
Small boats that could carry 2,000 people to UK seized in 'serious blow' to smugglers

A shipment of small boats and engines which could have carried 2,000 people across the Channel was seized on its way from China to Germany via a UK port, the National Crime Agency (NCA) announced

View 2 Images Small boats that could have transported 2,000 people across the Channel have been seized (Image: NCA)

A shipment of small boats and engines that could have carried 2,000 people across the Channel has been seized on its way from China.

‌



The UK's border security commander hailed the operation - which saw 25 inflatable boats and engines confiscated - as a "serious blow" to smuggling gangs. The 10 metre long boats, which could each have transported around 80 people on the perilous journey, were found inside a container at Felixstowe which was bound for Germany.

‌



It is understood to be the first time a bulk consignment of boats and engines has been seized in the UK. The NCA said the container was due to go to Hamburg in Germany - a key staging post for people traffickers.

‌



They would then have been moved to northern France or Belgium and used for dangerous Channel crossings. The government has pledged to smash the smuggling gangs responsible for small boats landing on UK shores.

Andy Burnham addresses Wes Streeting hot mic joke about prisoners being released early READ MORE :

View 2 Images The 10 metre boats were on their way to Germany from China (Image: NCA)

The NCA said it and its international partners have intercepted more than 1,500 boats and engines since 2023. The seizure was made as part of an ongoing investigation into criminal gangs.

‌



Border Security Commander Duncan Capps said: “This seizure delivers yet another serious blow to the criminal gangs facilitating dangerous and illegal Channel crossings.

“Thanks to the hard work of the NCA, Home Office intelligence teams and Border Force officers, disruptions like these to criminal networks and their supply lines are happening more than ever before."

He said those smuggling flimsy small boat equipment would face the full force of the law. NCA Branch Commander Adam Berry said: “This was a significant seizure of small boat equipment which will put a huge dent in the profits of the criminal network involved.

‌



“It will also have stopped these dangerous boats and under-powered engines being used to put lives at risk in the Channel.

“Once we identified that the shipment would pass through a UK port on its way to Germany, we were able to work quickly with our partners at Border Force to ensure it would go no further.

“Targeting the supply lines of people smuggling gangs is just one way we are trying to disrupt them. Our investigation continues.”

Article continues below

There is no suggestion that the crew or operators of the ship knew what was in the container. The Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act, passed last year, created new criminal offences making it illegal to supply or handle items used in organised immigration crime.

News.title: Friends legend claims dead mother has 'texted her' from the afterlife
News.content:
Friends legend claims dead mother has 'texted her' from the afterlife

The actress shared a baffling real-life story involving her mum, Nedra Stern — who died in 2020 — and what she suggests could be eerie messages from beyond the grave

View 3 Images Lisa captured the nation's hearts as the eccentric Phoebe Buffay (Image: Getty Images)

A beloved Friends actor has claimed that her late mother texted her "from the beyond". Lisa Kudrow captured the nation's hearts as the eccentric Phoebe Buffay in the beloved US sitcom. One example of the character's quirkiness is The One with the Cat, in which Phoebe becomes convinced a stray cat plays host to the spirit of her late mum.

‌



It seems sometimes life really does imitate art, as the actress has now shared a baffling real-life story involving her mum, Nedra Stern — who died in 2020 — and what she suggests could be messages from beyond the grave.

‌



Speaking to Mayim Bialik, who played neuroscientist Amy Farrah Fowler in The Big Bang Theory, Lisa explained how her father, a doctor, would take care of her mum, checking her urine for UTIs and "did not wanna let her go".

‌



But once she passed away, something strange occurred. Lisa said on Mayim Bialik's Breakdown podcast: "So, okay, when she passed away, my brother was up when he got the call.

"It was like 2:30, like almost 3:00 in the morning. My father was up when he got the call. My husband was up. She loved my husband. My sister and her husband, their alarm went off in their bedroom.

View 3 Images Lisa claimed that her late mother may have texted her from beyond the grave (Image: NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

‌



She continued: "Everything's on his phone. He was like, 'Breach, master bedroom. I don't see a breach', like, nothing happened. And my sister, who could be really unnerved by an alarm going off and wake her up, was fine, calm, not scared."

She added: "I woke up because my brother called me. So after she passed away, they're exchanging these stories, and everyone is a little, 'Isn't it weird, though, that I was up?

"Isn't it weird that you had that alarm?' And I'm saying it's not weird at all. She flew around and woke everybody up when she passed. I don't think that's weird at all, except she didn't wake me up."

‌



Later, Lisa assembled a slideshow for the funeral. She says at the time, she was selecting photos while texting — but wasn't speaking aloud — when she noticed something bizarre.

She said: "And then I get another text and I open it up, and it's as if I've already responded. There's some writing in the box, message box. And, like, I didn't write that.

View 3 Images Lisa also spotted a mysterious "XOXOXO" (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"It said in all caps, 'M-O-M', no cursor and no suggestion, Mommy? But I'm not noticing that. I'm just saying, 'I didn't write that'. Delete, delete, delete. And answer them because I'm busy. I've got a task to do. Don't have time for a quirky phone."

She continued: "And then another text. 'What? M-O-M all caps. I didn't write that'. Delete. Delete. Delete. And I'm answering. I'm still not connecting. And then I think it happened one more time. I went, 'Why is this? Oh, because I'm thinking about my mom'. I'm doing that, but I'm not speaking."

A couple of days later, Lisa was with her husband, Michel Stern, and a friend when Michael revealed that his phone had been "weird" of late, a sentiment that Lisa could, of course, sympathise with.

‌



Having explained the "MOM" incident, Lisa said her friend told her: "Lisa, your mom texted you", with Lisa adding "from the beyond". But that wasn't the end of the matter. In fact, her mum seemingly messaged her "another time".

She said this time, the eerie text appeared during the Covid lockdown period. Lisa said she'd been texting a friend, only for a mysterious "XOXOXO" to appear. However, Lisa thought at the time that her mum didn't sign things this way.

The next day, though, her dad told her that he'd been looking at old letters and had found one from her mum. She'd been 18 at the time, and her dad had been drafted.

Article continues below

"And at the end, half a page, XOXOXOXO all over the page," she added.

News.title: Are you worried about the extreme summer weather? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Are you worried about the extreme summer weather? Take our poll and have your say

With weather forecasters anticipating temperatures to exceed 40C — in what would be the hottest figures ever recorded in the UK - the Mirror readers have expressed concern about climate change

View Image Grass on Wimbledon Common, southwest London, has turned a dry yellow-brown after prolonged heat (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

Temperatures are poised to exceed 40.3C — in what would be the hottest day ever recorded in the UK.

‌



The Mirror readers are divided in their opinion about the rising temperatures, with some arguing more must be done to tackle climate change. However, others are not worried about the extreme summer weather and say they enjoy the opportunities to holiday and have days out in this country.

‌



The current record is 40.3C, which happened during the scorching heatwave of July 2022. Forecasters say it is likely to become warmer than that this summer, following several heatwaves already since May. The East of England the Southeast of England will be the hottest counties during the next scorcher, which experts say will happen at the start of August.

‌



The Met Office’s forecast for the rest of July says conditions are expected to be “warmest in the south”. It adds that temperatures could potentially become “very warm again by the start of August”.

But, what do you make of the extreme weather? Take our poll below, and write a comment at the end of this article, to share your opinion. Share any tips you've found to help cope during the heatwaves.

‌



Met Office names 22 areas facing heavy rain this Sunday as heatwave ends – see full list READ MORE :

But before the return of the sunshine, many regions will experience an unsettled spell. Low pressure will sweep eastwards across the UK during the weekend, and become heaviest across northern England. The Mirror lists the 22 areas expected to see heavy rain on Sunday in this piece.

Note, though, hosepipe bans extended to millions of people could be rolled out even more extensively this summer, the country's drought monitoring group has said, as it warns several parts of the country are on the precipice of water shortages.

Article continues below

The National Drought Group has warned that parts of southern, central and eastern England are close to experiencing the same conditions as more than a dozen other areas across the country.

News.title: Burnham to review early prisoner release scheme after anger over potential freeing of PC Harper's killers
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said he will review an early prisoner release policy, due to come into force this autumn, following anger that two killers of PC Andrew Harper could be freed early.

From September, thousands of offenders in England and Wales will be eligible to be released earlier under the Sentencing Act.

Burnham said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."

He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".

His comments come after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.

PC Harper was killed after he was dragged to his death behind their getaway car. The car's driver, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter but would not be eligible for early release.

The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive governments have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.

Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since 2024.

The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.

Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

Concerning the case of PC Harper, he said: "I feel for the family it's an appalling crime that was committed."

He said the "main perpetrator" of his death would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham also said it was not acceptable to joke about early releases and that it was right Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had apologised for comments he made that were caught on camera.

News.title: Ex-Southern Water boss among four charged over alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests
News.content:
The former chief executive of Southern Water has been charged alongside three others over an alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests to avoid paying financial penalties in the region of Â£45m, it can now be reported.

Matthew Wright is accused of conspiring to defraud the Environment Agency (EA) and water regulator Ofwat between 2012 and 2017 along with Philip Barker, Clive Massey and Mark Gregory, who also worked at the company.

The EA previously asked a judge to issue a summons against Wright and the others charging them with the offence.

Wright's solicitor said his client "denies all wrongdoing and has co-operated fully with the Environment Agency's investigation".

The summons was issued last year but Wright launched a legal challenge which was dismissed by two senior judges on Wednesday.

Wright's lawyers told the High Court in June that the EA did not have the power to issue the summons and it should be thrown out.

But the judges dismissed his claim and ruled restrictions previously preventing reporting of the legal challenge should be lifted.

Separate court listings showed the case against 60-year-old Wright, of Haslemere, Surrey, Barker, 57, of West Chiltington, West Sussex, 64-year-old Massey, of Brandhill, Shropshire, and 63-year-old Gregory, of Southampton, were scheduled to be heard at Medway Magistrates' Court on 14 July.

The four are accused of conspiring between 2012 and 2017 to defraud those conducting the environmental and financial regulation duties of Southern Water, including the EA and Ofwat, by "the implementation of artificial no-flow events at wastewater treatment works".

The court listings show Southern Water has separately been charged with dozens of offences of failing to comply with or contravening an environmental permit condition between 2013 and 2017 at multiple wastewater treatment works.

News.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The ChatGPT-maker said its agent - an AI system which can operate alone after human instruction â was being tested in a controlled environment but, after finding weaknesses, was able to escape the test limits.

They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.

OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was conducting an investigation alongside Hugging Face, whose boss Clement Delangue said in a post on X it was "mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously".

"The investigation is ongoing, and we'll share more learnings from what might be the first incident of its kind," Delangue added.

A government spokesperson said the UK's AI Security Institute was studying the behaviour from the AI system seen in the incident and was continuing to work with OpenAI and other labs to improve safeguards.

They said organisations should step up their cyber-defences by taking steps such as enrolling in the government-backed Cyber Essentials certification scheme.

News.title: Prince George enjoys coastal fun in new video as he becomes a teenager
News.content:
A new video of Prince George has been released by Kensington Palace to mark his 13th birthday.

The video, external, showing a smiling prince waving at the camera in his sunglasses, playing cricket on the beach and climbing rocks, was accompanied by the caption: "Thank you for all the birthday wishes for George today!"

The video was shot in Cornwall at Easter, and follows a new photograph of George which was also published on social media on Wednesday.

George, the elder son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is second in line to the throne.

News.title: Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate
News.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal.

Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-offs in May after admitting they spied on three clubs during the campaign.

An independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time that the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

Since then the club has been the subject of an investigation by the FA, looking into who participated in the spying and assessing the culpability of those who knew it was happening.

The FA said, external Eckert "has been charged with three breaches of FA rule E3.1 in relation to misconduct between December 2025 and May 2026".

Southampton beat Middlesbrough over two legs in the play-off semi-final but, after Saints' expulsion, Boro were reinstated to the final and went on to lose to Hull City.

The English Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the play-offs after they admitted watching training sessions involving Oxford United and Ipswich Town, in addition to filming Middlesbrough before the semi-final.

The EFL can only take action against its member clubs but the FA can punish individuals and hand out bans.

The FA said it is "alleged that the head coach acted in an improper manner and/or brought the game into disrepute by directing and/or authorising the observation of training sessions" of these games.

Eckert has until next Tuesday to respond.

In a statement, Southampton said, external they and Eckert "acknowledge today's charges from the FA relating to a breach of rule E3.1".

The club added: "Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA.

"Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 Championship season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.

"We are unable to comment further while the process remains ongoing, but we will provide an update to supporters as soon as we are in a position to do so."

News.title: Seized maternity notes not given to Lucy Letby defence for trial, BBC learns
News.content:
Maternity notes for the babies Lucy Letby has been convicted of murdering were not made available to her defence ahead of her trial, the BBC has learned.

The neonatal nurse was convicted of murdering and attempting to murder 14 babies at the Countess of Chester Hospital in 2015 and 2016.

File on 4 Investigates has discovered that maternity notes for the babies in the case - which include details of the mother's pregnancy, labour and birth - were seized by Cheshire Police. But they were not reviewed by the prosecution's chief medical expert or disclosed to Letby's defence.

The Crown Prosecution Service said Letby was convicted following two jury trials and that the Court of Appeal dismissed her argument that prosecution evidence was flawed.

Letby, originally of Hereford, is currently serving 15 whole life terms.

Since her trial, and subsequent retrial on one case, there have been concerns raised about some of the evidence presented to the jury.

One concern is that the maternity history of the babies in the case was not adequately considered.

Experts told the BBC that it is critical to fully assess the pregnancy, labour and delivery of a baby when determining why they collapsed and died.

Dr Dewi Evans, the chief medical witness for the prosecution, said the full maternity notes were not relevant to the case.

"I never saw any obstetric notes and I have no idea what happened to them," he said.

"I don't think that maternity care was a particular issue in the Letby case. I think most of the babies I dealt with were born in acceptable condition."

Evans said he did see brief maternity summaries - "usually a couple of paragraphs" - attached to each baby's neonatal notes.

News.title: Nottingham attacks NHS trust faces manslaughter probe
News.content:
The NHS trust that treated Nottingham attacks killer Valdo Calocane is being investigated for corporate manslaughter.

Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020 before he fatally attacked Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates in June 2023, was previously sectioned by Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust.

A statutory public inquiry, which finished hearing evidence in May, was told he had been discharged in 2022 because he failed to turn up for appointments and the team had "lost" him.

The families of Calocane's victims said the NHS trust had "catastrophically failed at every level" and welcomed the investigation.

Northumbria Police confirmed it was carrying out the investigation "on behalf of Nottinghamshire Police".

A spokesperson for the Northumbria force said: "We are in contact with the victims' families and survivors and are committed to supporting them throughout this process.

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment any further."

Nottinghamshire Police has been criticised over its history of interactions with Calocane and its handling of the response and investigation into the attacks.

News.title: The borough where families are slowly disappearing
News.content:
Islington seems, on the surface, a family-friendly area. Parents push buggies through quiet leafy side streets of this popular neighbourhood that is also within easy reach of central London.

But this north London borough has one of the lowest fertility rates in the country and mothers are older on average here than in most other parts of the capital.

Islington is a snapshot of a trend also playing out not only in inner London but also other parts of the world.

The situation has been described by the London Assembly as an "existential challenge" for the city as a whole, so what are the reasons behind this and what can be done about it?

Keen to find out more about family life in Islington, I joined a Zip-Zap baby music class to speak to parents.

Tiphanie Frutuoso and her husband had their first baby this year.

"My husband and I have a one-bedroom flat â a two-bedroom is super expensive.

"Childcare is Â£2,000-Â£3,000 a month."

They are moving back to Luxembourg, partly because childcare is free.

"It's really sad because we love London. We have better job opportunities here," Frutuoso added.

News.title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
News.content:
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.

Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.

Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.

June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: More young women in their 20s are getting type 2 diabetes
News.content:
England is seeing a "worrying increase" in young women in their 20s developing type 2 diabetes, experts at Imperial College London have warned.

The rise has largely occurred since the Covid pandemic and is closely linked to increasing obesity levels, according to an analysis of NHS data from 2011 to 2024, external.

Type 2 diabetes is serious, and can lead to severe complications, such as heart attacks and strokes.

When it develops at a younger age, the disease tends to be more aggressive, raising the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short, according to Diabetes UK.

News.title: Over £100,000 raised for boy, 3, in croc attack
News.content:
More than Â£100,000 has been raised for a three-year-old boy who was attacked in a crocodile enclosure.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

A fundraising page has raised Â£105,000 for the boy and his family after the three-year-old was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital, where he has undergone seven surgeries.

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Military kit still failing women, troops say
News.content:
Women in the armed forces say they are still being issued kit that does not fit properly, five years after a landmark report warned they were at "greater risk of harm" from ill-fitting uniform and equipment.

The 2021 Atherton report said the Ministry of Defence should urgently roll out safer, more appropriate kit for female service personnel by the end of 2022.

Despite improvements, women have been telling the BBC some kit is still poorly fitting, with body armour failing to account for breasts, and shortages of smaller sizes resulting in "competition" among troops.

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) said it ensured everyone had access to the "best equipment they need to protect themselves in combat".

"I never felt that I was neat, tidy, presentable, or in the uniform that I was meant to be in," explains veteran Rhian Brown, who left the service in 2024.

"I never really felt that it protected me or entirely fulfilled the purpose that it was meant to."

News.title: Mid-air 10-person brawl halts easyJet   flight
News.content:
A mid-air brawl involving around 10 passengers forced a Liverpool-bound easyJet plane to fly back to Tenerife, according to air traffic control.

The captain decided to return to the Spanish island about 30 minutes after departure "due to the danger" the fight "posed to the safety of the flight", the air traffic controller said.

Police met flight EZY3352 when it touched down at Tenerife South airport on Tuesday evening, per the crew's request.

The 186-passenger aircraft then continued to Liverpool.

The air traffic controller said in its statement, originally written in Spanish: "Our full support goes out to the crews and passengers who are increasingly having to endure these situations."

EasyJet said the plane "returned to the airport and was met by police due to a group of passengers behaving disruptively.

News.title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
News.content:
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.

The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.

However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."

Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".

But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.

News.title: 'We just need a bed': Baby with 'days to live' can't access lifesaving treatment
News.content:
The parents of a three-month-old boy who they fear has just days to live say they're frustrated at being unable to access lifesaving treatment due to a lack of suitable hospital beds.

Dylan and Catrin Green, from Cardiff, said their "completely healthy baby" Macs started to struggle with his feeding, then caught a cold before later suffering two cardiac arrests.

He has been diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, external - a condition which can lead to heart failure - and now has a "matter of days" on a machine which pumps oxygen into his bloodstream, Dylan said.

He urgently needs a Berlin heart , external- a device used to take over the function of a child's own heart until a donor heart becomes available.

His family said Macs has been stuck at a specialist unit in Bristol for weeks, where his condition has since deteriorated and was now in an induced coma, as the beds he needs were not available.

The two specialist hospitals in the UK where the Berlin heart can be fitted are Great Ormond Street Hospital in London and the Freeman Hospital in Newcastle.

News.title: 'My sister is not just another statistic'  - Jennie's Law is signed
News.content:
Jennifer Poole, a woman murdered by her former partner, will not be "another statistic" her brother has said after a new law in her name was signed off in the Republic of Ireland.

Jason Poole's sister was unaware her partner Gavin Murphy had a history of domestic violence when he murdered her in her Dublin home in 2021.

The Domestic Violence (Judgements) Register Bill 2026, external, known as Jennie's Law, was approved by the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament) and has now been signed off by Irish President Catherine Connolly.

It will result in those convicted of domestic violence against a partner being included on a public register.

World ​Rugby and England and Wales' governing bodies have sought to throw out nearly 380 former rugby union players' lawsuits over neurological injuries, arguing their lawyers repeatedly failed to disclose ⁠key medical evidence.

World Rugby, the Rugby Football Union (RFU) and the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) are facing lawsuits from around 800 ex-amateur and professional players, who say repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows left them with serious neurological conditions.

The claimants' ⁠lawyers allege the governing bodies breached ​their ⁠duty of care by failing to protect them from those risks, but World Rugby argues in its written defence that ⁠it had no such duty and that injuries are an "inherent risk" ​in ⁠rugby.

The case began in 2022 but has been beset by delays over disclosure, as has a parallel action by ex-rugby league players.

World Rugby, the RFU and the ‌WRU have now asked London's High Court ‌to throw out claims brought by former rugby union players because their lawyers have breached court orders requiring them to provide records, including recordings of "neurology interviews" carried out ⁠before lawsuits began.

The Rugby Football League and the British Amateur Rugby League Association are similarly applying for around 130 ex-players' lawsuits to be thrown out.

Neil Block, a lawyer representing the RFU, told the court that "enough is enough".

"These are important documents ... an order was made that we were entitled to have them and we have tried in ‌every way," he said.

Lawyers representing the claimants, however, say they have provided the vast majority of the documents required and that throwing out their claims would be an "extreme response".

"This litigation is of significant public interest ⁠and societal importance for the continuance of contact/collision sports in the UK," their lawyer ‌Susan Rodway said ​in written arguments.

"It would be highly ‌undesirable for a significant number ​of the former players to lose their claims on procedural grounds."

Reuters

News.title: What dating apps are really doing to modern relationships, according to research
News.content:

In recent years, it has become commonplace to see people selecting potential partners with the same gestures (and enthusiasm) they use to scroll through videos on TikTok or browse products in an online store. Swipe right for interest; swipe left to move on. What once involved the drama of meeting someone — glances, hesitation, approaching, rejection, discovery — has been compressed into almost “gamified” interfaces. Dating apps have expanded the possibilities for meeting people, but research in social psychology indicates that more options do not always mean greater satisfaction, more stable relationships, or better outcomes for all users.

Dating apps like Tinder didn’t invent desire or casual sex, social comparison, or the fantasy that there might be someone better just around the corner. Their innovation was to turn all of this into a search engine. But what happens when a human dynamic as old as romantic encounters begins to operate under the rules of a digital platform?

open image in gallery What happens when a human dynamic as old as romantic encounters begins to operate under the rules of a digital platform? ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The “dating market” before the apps

Relationships have always seemed to belong to the murky realm of chance. Two people meet at a party, in a classroom, or in a university hallway. Often through friends who swear that “you two are a perfect match.” But beneath that fog there are identifiable patterns. Finding someone involves searching, comparing, trying, rejection, reputation, and cost. Initial attractiveness itself requires meeting statistically predictable criteria. Love is traditionally celebrated as something that can’t really be rationalized — as fate. But in practice, there’s a structure at work.

Before dating apps, this infrastructure was limited to relatively narrow social circles. People chose from among classmates, neighbors, friends of friends, party acquaintances — people who might reappear in the same social setting after a possible rejection. Scarcity reduced options but increased the significance of each encounter.

Abundance does the opposite: it expands possibilities, but it also trivializes the available options. Faced with the expectation that someone better might be just one swipe away, a relationship no longer competes only with other people nearby but begins to compete with the statistical imagination of all available people.

It’s not just about casual sex

For years, almost everything said about dating apps oscillated between moral lament and technological propaganda. On the one hand, Tinder was seen as an agent of romantic “decadence”. On the other, as an effective liberation for singles trapped in narrow social circles. It remained to be seen what actually changed as this technology began to increasingly mediate interpersonal relationships.

Much of the literature on dating apps suggests that Tinder is a “casual sex app,” but there are important nuances here. In 2017, Belgian researchers developed a questionnaire to measure the main motivations for its use, called the Tinder Motives Scale. The results of the survey, conducted among more than 3,000 young adults in Belgium, identified 13 main reasons for using the platform. These include curiosity, entertainment, validation, ease of communication, and the search for romantic relationships.

In fact, studies show that, in the United States, online dating has become the primary way heterosexual couples meet. This means that the traditional intermediaries in dating — friends, family, work, and school — have been progressively displaced.

At the same time, a longitudinal study of Norwegian students showed that Tinder users were more likely to form romantic relationships over time. In other words, the app may open doors, but part of this “romantic success” may reflect characteristics of the users themselves, and not just this effect.

But it’s also about sex

However, casual sex remains a major motivation for users of dating apps. They tend to report more partners and a higher likelihood of casual encounters and, in some studies, greater exposure to risky sexual behaviors.

Reviews on Tinder and sexual health indicate that sexual motivations, sociosexual, and the search for casual partners appear repeatedly among the predictors of use and sexual outcomes. These results are relatively consistent in Brazil and worldwide.

Generally, studies are unclear as to whether the app leads to promiscuity or whether it is the more sexually liberal users who seek it out more frequently. On this point, it is worth citing a study published in 2026. Instead of simply comparing users and nonusers, the study investigated the initial spread of Tinder on American college campuses.

About the author Felipe Carvalho Novaes is a Professor, PUC-Rio. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

To do so, researchers analyzed an impressive 1.1 million responses from the National College Health Assessment between 2008 and 2019. The results indicated that greater exposure to Tinder increased sexual activity, without producing a corresponding increase in stable relationships or a consistent improvement in the quality of those relationships. In this case, the app appeared to accelerate the pursuit of casual encounters more than it did commitment.

Abundance and inattention

There is also evidence that dating apps reshape the distribution of attention — which could help explain why it’s easier to form casual relationships. Other studies on Tinder have already shown that swiping more does not guarantee more “matches”. Furthermore, women tend to receive more likes than men. And men, in general, need to initiate more conversations.

This pattern helps explain why the abundance promised by dating apps is experienced unequally. The market seems open to everyone, but attention is not distributed democratically. As in other markets expanded by technology, small differences in attractiveness, status, communication skills, or timing can lead to significant inequalities in outcomes.

Impacts on mental health

Mental health is where the story becomes less comfortable for any simple thesis. Some of the literature links the use of dating apps to lower levels of self-esteem, anxiety, depression, loneliness, body dissatisfaction, and psychological distress. However, most of these studies are correlational and cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships.

Recent systematic reviews indicate particularly consistent negative effects on body image and more mixed results for mental health and well-being.

At the same time, the 2026 study cited above found no average decline in mental health among the most exposed students. On some indicators, especially among women, there was even an improvement. This contrast suggests that dating apps may cause harm to certain users and, simultaneously, provide average benefits to others — for example, through validation, romantic attention, or a sense of desirability.

The point, therefore, is not to decide whether Tinder has liberated or corrupted our love lives. What the literature suggests is more interesting: these apps transform dating into a perpetual search market, with endless options, more comparison, more exposure, and more unequal outcomes. It seems that greater supply does not lead to greater satisfaction.

But that doesn’t mean dating apps are the villains in this story. They don’t create our desires for sex, love, status, validation, and novelty. They merely connect these desires to a digital infrastructure designed to scale up and reduce costs. Romance doesn’t disappear. It simply comes to compete with the endless possibilities that lie ahead.

Kenneth Kovar, a resident of New Braunfels, northeast of San Antonio, has been acutely aware of power grid vulnerabilities since Winter Storm Uri in February 2021.

During the multiday freeze that crippled Texas, Kovar, despite not losing main power, found his septic tank inoperable, forcing him to fill toilets with water from his backyard pool.

This experience profoundly influenced his decision last fall to purchase a Ford F-150, hoping to be better prepared for future crises.

"I was interested in trying to find some sort of power backup situation," he explained.

Kovar now utilizes a Ford system that enables drivers of specific F-150 models to directly connect their vehicle to their electric meter, powering parts of their home during outages.

This innovation exemplifies a broader trend among automakers, who are increasingly adapting their electrification technologies for the home energy sector.

This shift is particularly pertinent as grid demand escalates and electric vehicle (EV) sales experience a slowdown.

Car manufacturers are keen to leverage their substantial EV investments to tap into the burgeoning market of vehicle, home, and grid technology, offering solutions for both backup power and enhanced electrical grid resiliency.

open image in gallery Winter storm Uri brought historic cold weather and power outages to Texas ( Getty )

Parth Vaishnav, assistant professor of sustainable systems at the University of Michigan, noted, "They’re trying to look for other businesses that they might sell into."

The Ford system allows drivers of the F-150 PowerBoost hybrid and F-150 Lightning electric pickup trucks to plug a one-foot adapter into a 240-volt onboard outlet.

This adapter, developed with Global Power Products, then connects to a longer cable that attaches to a transfer switch installed directly on the home’s electric meter.

This setup effectively links the vehicle to the home’s breaker box, allowing homeowners to select which devices to power.

Amanda Roraff, Ford’s grid and energy services business acceleration lead, articulated the company’s perspective: "The way we think about it, especially for customers who already have a compatible vehicle is, you already own the power source, it’s in your driveway."

The Lightning can provide power for two to three days, while the PowerBoost Hybrid can last up to five days on a single tank of gas, depending on usage.

Ford touts this solution as a more affordable backup power option, starting around $1,100 for professional installation at the meter, compared to the several thousands required for conventional diesel generators or full-home standby systems.

Currently, this specific setup is available for approximately 200,000 vehicles and is exclusively for outages. Ford also offers a Home Integration System for bidirectional power flow, enabling power transfer between the vehicle and home, and even to the grid.

Beyond Ford, other automakers are also advancing their energy solutions.

Over 630,000 U.S. vehicles reportedly already possess similar functionality, with manufacturers rapidly expanding options toward full vehicle-to-grid support.

South Korean brand Kia, in partnership with EV charging company Wallbox, offers home power backup for eligible vehicles during outages or peak demand, allowing users to reduce utility consumption and even send power back to the grid.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

Tesla’s technology provides similar capabilities, enabling equipped vehicles to connect to homes via additional Tesla hardware.

The Cybertruck offers full vehicle-to-home functionality, while other Tesla models can power specific devices. General Motors is also active in the energy space, with a recent partnership with WeaveGrid allowing owners of certain GM EVs, equipped with the automaker’s home system and proper grid interconnection, to participate in grid reliability programs.

GM’s vehicle-to-home technology can disconnect a home from the grid and supply power from the EV upon detecting an outage. Wade Sheffer, vice president of GM energy, envisions a future where customers have "full control of the energy" through a unified platform.

This burgeoning business is seen as crucial amidst increasing grid demand and a rise in power outages, especially as the EV market faces a slowdown under current U.S. federal policy.

A July Cox Automotive report indicated a 23.8% year-over-year decline in pure EV sales in the U.S. during the first half of 2026, underscoring the potential value of EV and hybrid ownership as a power asset.

However, the technology faces challenges. Industry-wide, these systems require rigorous third-party testing for safety standards, and vehicles and chargers must be programmed for communication.

Utility approval for interconnection can also be a lengthy process, potentially taking years. For consumers, understanding vehicle capabilities and managing the system effectively adds another layer of complexity to home power management.

Despite these hurdles, experts remain optimistic, particularly given strong international interest in EV sales. Scott Samuelsen, engineering professor emeritus at the University of California, Irvine, predicts, "This is going to become very, very popular," highlighting the significant impact of providing home electricity during outages.

Ed Miliband’s appointment as foreign secretary has infuriated Washington, with the White House said to be “deeply concerned” about the pick.

New prime minister Andy Burnham has been warned that Trump “will not forget” Mr Miliband’s years of criticism of him, and that his foreign secretary has “serious diplomatic repair to undertake” in the US.

The pair have clashed for a decade over net zero and Russia, with Mr Miliband once calling Trump a “racist, misogynistic, self-confessed groper” and later accusing him of having “lowered the bar for idiocy”.

Independent readers, though, largely dismissed the row as Trump overreaching.

The dominant view was that it’s not the US president’s place to veto a British cabinet appointment, and that the “special relationship” has too often meant Britain deferring to Washington for nothing in return.

Meanwhile, a smaller number of readers warned that antagonising a sitting US president is reckless when Britain, outside the EU, can’t afford to burn its closest ally.

Here’s what you had to say:

If Trump hates him, he’s the right choice

If Trump hates him, he’s definitely the right choice. Starmer sucking up to Trump, who dumped him anyway, was his undoing. Closer to Canada, good; closer to the EU, even better. Stand up to Trump, and like any bully, he will respect you. We have to work closely with the EU, especially on tech, pharma and defence. Stop looking at the Americans.

punda

Cowards only respond to strength

An excellent choice, Burnham. I could understand Starmer’s desire for diplomacy, but diplomacy doesn’t work with Trump. Cowards only respond to people who stand up to them. Hope this is a confrontational moment.

DHC

For the latest political headlines delivered straight to your inbox, 

Britain must reassert its sovereignty

We in the UK need to learn a lesson from the French and more recently from the Canadians. We do not need to tolerate American interference in our affairs from the American government, American billionaires or anyone else. The French never have and by standing up for themselves they have done far better than we have. Now under Carney the Canadians are doing the same. Those Americans like Trump who think the USA should dominate the world want to convert all their erstwhile friends and allies into effective colonies. We need to work with all the others in this position to clear out all the sources of American influence in our affairs and reassert our sovereignty. In any case Trump has made himself so unpopular in the US itself and all around the world that he will soon be a lame duck president even if he is not already.

Bobcat

The US has no say over our cabinet

What right has Trump and his team got, to determine who is in the Labour Government Cabinet because as far as we know, GB is not another state in the USA under the greasy thumb of his lordship? Get over it, Mr President and focus on your own problems and priorities. Harbouring grudges and bitterness are not attractive attributes for a leader.

WinnieB

A test for Burnham

It will be a test for Burnham not to react to Trump’s tantrum and keep Miliband in post. It’s not the prerogative of the US president to choose the British cabinet.

EEMC2

Imagine the fury if we criticised Trump’s picks

It seems like the US believe they have the right to veto UK government appointments. Can you just imagine the hell and fury from the White House if the British government commented about the Trump administration’s appointments. I realise that we have close ties with the US over many issues but this constant criticism of the UK from the White House is getting ridiculous and needs to be called out.

Fru T-Bunn

None of Trump’s business

I can’t imagine Ed Miliband – or Andy Burnham will be too bothered! It is none of Trump’s business who is appointed. Contrary to Trump’s opinion, he does not have the right to choose ministers in other nations.

Suney

He’s the British foreign secretary, not America’s

As far as I can make out, he is the British foreign secretary and not the US foreign secretary. So the decision isn’t down to Trump. Some people will say we shouldn’t appoint someone Trump doesn’t like, but we’ve seen time after time that Trump is no ally and will turn on anyone, so no way should we pander to his whims.

PaulMG

There’s no such thing as a special relationship

Hated for speaking the truth. It is time the British people wake up, there has never been any special relationship, the special relationship is there only if we bend the knee and do whatever the US government wants. It is a one-sided relationship.

Sunlight

We’ve given Trump too much airtime

Well, we have tried kissing his posterior and that has brought us nothing but grief and loss of respect. Time for our foreign secretary to focus his attention on the rest of the world and Trump is just going to have to think of that what he wishes. We are giving far too much airtime to that country.

SeanF

It’s the climate message that really bothers them

Well, the last thing they want is a net zero enthusiast travelling around the world telling other countries that taking action on climate change might be a good idea. I think that concerns Trump and his cronies far more than anything Miliband may have said in the past.

antmanbee

Don’t attempt to placate Trump

Whatever you do, Ed, don’t attempt to placate Trump. He will see it as another sign of British weakness. And we’ve seen more than enough of that with Starmer.

Cyclone8

Trump doesn’t grasp America’s declining relevance

Nothing to worry about. Trump seems incapable of understanding that turning his back on Europe and Nato also means that as a natural progression, the US will gradually become less and less relevant as time goes by. I understand that the saner US military leaders fully understand this, but as Trump is a very stable genius, he must have a hidden masterplan.

The Dark Side of the Balloon

Remember how they treated Mandelson

Trump’s reaction confirms he’s the right guy. But didn’t they whinge about Mandelson and his comments in exactly the same way, and then love him? But then, Mandelson was Ambassador to the US and hence directly relevant to them, while in the case of Miliband the US is but one of very many countries he will deal with.

ElectiveScot

Miliband’s appointment wasn’t politically astute

Miliband wasn’t a good choice for foreign secretary since a) he has limited experience in foreign policy and b) is not esteemed by Trump. There is much bravado on the thread recommending that Trump is ignored, but that is not politically astute. The UK is outside the EU; realpolitik dictates that it must work with Trump.

Musil

High office demands restraint

Any political person in high office who can’t hold their tongue shouldn’t be in said high office – Lammy, Miliband to name but two. It isn’t about ingratiating yourself and your country but about not using insulting words and terms, about anyone. Agree, disagree with direction, policies but don’t do schoolyard behaviour, you have to be above it, you have to grit your teeth, you don’t even have to be their friend.

leafspot

News.title: Young couple found dead in campervan at cider festival after gas heater leaks
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The deaths of an entrepreneurial husband and wife at a cider festival in the New Forest National Park have been labelled an “absolute tragedy” by a coroner.

Christopher and Kayleigh Coll, who were 45 and 38, respectively, were found dead in their white Nissan van after staying overnight at the New Forest Cider Festival.

They had been working as stall traders at the October 2025 event, selling small trees made of copper wire.

The Colls, who had four children, had succumbed to fatal fumes from a leaky gas heater which should not have been used indoors, area coroner Rosamund Rhodes-Kemp said.

She recorded their cause of death as carbon monoxide poisoning during a hearing at Winchester Coroner’s Court on Wednesday.

She also found that the heater was not screwed in tightly to its gas cylinder.

open image in gallery The heater used by Christopher and Kayleigh Coll ( Solent News )

The Colls, from Blandford Forum, Dorset, were last seen having drinks with Alexander Huxley on 11 October in Burley.

They then went to sleep in their van in the field behind the festival, switching the heater on before bed due to the October chill.

The next morning, Mr Huxley grew worried that the pair had not arrived for the start of the festival, and went to look for them.

When he opened the door to the van, he was “hit with a wall of gas” and heard a “hissing noise”.

He then saw that the couple were dead.

The police said that the windows to the campervan were shut.

The couple had been married around four years. Mr Coll was a business owner and Ms Coll was a trainee accountant.

Ms Coll’s mother, Mara Sivyer, said that they had only used the van “for this one occasion” and it was not designed to be a campervan.

“This was a one off, trying to get their business off the ground and they made a fatal mistake,” she said.

“They slept in it once before but that was summer time so no heating.”

open image in gallery The Colls had been working at the New Forest Cider Festival, pictured, in 2025 ( Andrew Croft/Solent News )

Ms Sivyer described her daughter as an “angel”, adding: “She was the most kindest-hearted person you would ever meet.

“If she thought you needed her last pound, she would give it to you.”

Kelly Simonsohn, Mr Coll's sister, told the inquest: “[Chris] was a good person. He was very loving. He absolutely adored his kids.

“He was very family-centred. He had lots of ideas for the future, a bit like Dell Boy.”

Ms Rhodes-Kemp said that after a toxicology report, it was found the couple had died from carbon monoxide poisoning, but there was no third-party involvement.

“The carbon monoxide would have occurred simply by having it on in an enclosed space.

“On top of that, just to confuse matters further, however it happened, the heater and cylinder have become partially disconnected.

“The heater and gas cylinder connection was not tight. It is a combination of things that have happened.”

The van and the gas heater were taken for testing by the police.

Howard Jonas, an expert gas witness who works for Flogas Britain, said that the cylinder appeared to be in good condition but the heater was not properly attached to the cylinder.

He said that a small knock could cause the heater not to be fitted into the cylinder, but it was unclear how this had happened.

He said that the type of heater being used was a Parabolic heater, which is not designed to be used indoors and must be used in well-ventilated areas.

Mr Jonas said that the heater has no type of sensor to switch itself off.

He said the gas cylinder was “almost empty” and only had 10 per cent of its contents left in it.

Ms Rhodes-Kemp ruled that Mr and Mrs Coll died of carbon monoxide poisoning and gave the conclusion that it was misadventure.

She said that the heater should have a label on it, saying is not suitable for indoor use.

“I will be locating the manufacturers of the heater to see if a warning is on the heater because of the risk of future death,” she said.

“All I can say is I am terribly sorry because it is an absolute tragedy. Two young people to die like this.

"I am sorry for the children and all the friends and family. I really am most desperately sorry.”

Ms Rhodes-Kemp added: “It is just a mistake to close all the windows and turn the heating on. It is an absolute tragedy.

"It was a deliberate act to turn the heater on with a totally unintended consequence.”

News.content:
