Sports.title: Ascot: Jamie Lynch's King George runner guide
Sports.content:
This has all the hallmarks of an epic edition of one of the great races, internationally renowned and internationally reliant this year with the best of France and Japan in round two of their heavyweight clash.

But the race is far more than a rematch, considering there are as many as six other Group 1 winners in the mix, including an all-important Classic-winning three-year-old from Ballydoyle to trigger the generation game. This is what King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes are supposed to look like.

Watch every race from King George Weekend at Ascot live on Sky Sports Racing on Friday 24th and Saturday 25th July.

BAY CITY ROLLER

Trainer: George Scott | Jockey: TBC

"If this, then that." The principle of conditional logic, and the fundamental formula with him: if soft ground, then Bay City Roller. Such a crude conversion does him a disservice, of course, but the fact of the matter is that he goes from Bruce Banner to the Incredible Hulk when he gets the mud.

This is emphasised by his two Group 1 wins under such conditions by seven lengths (in Munich) and 10 lengths, the latter the Coronation Cup in which he marched on mercilessly after Calandagan and co had waved the white flag. His rivals won't be watered down in the King George as they were at Epsom.

CALANDAGAN

Jockey: Mickael Barzalona | Trainer: Francis-Henri Graffard

Racehorses like him don't come along very often. You can see why he's so good, you just see it so rarely, that magical mix of a mile-and-a-half horse who can hit the sexy speeds of a sprinter. He's able to throw in sub 11-second furlongs at will, as well as regularly breaking the 40 mph limit of the middle-distance motorway.

Image: Calandagan (right) won last year's King George

He has never gone faster than he did in the finish of the Grand Prix de Saint Cloud last time, not only a reaction but also a statement with a snarl after what happened to him at Epsom, at the bottom of his list of favourite courses, whereas Ascot would be at the top.

The same can be said for the world's joint-best horse Ombudsman who has been utterly unbeatable at the track…until he met Calandagan. The frequency and fire of his elite-level performances make him a modern great, so much so that he's single-handedly forcing the French to change their rules in order to sprinkle his gold dust at home as well as abroad. But, for now, Ascot is Calandagan's perfect canvas on which to paint his flair-filled works of art.

GOLIATH

Jockey: Christophe Soumillon | Trainer: Francis-Henri Graffard

They call it distance decay, the simple effect that near things are more related and relevant than far things, and, by this stage, Goliath's 2024 King George win qualifies as a far thing, especially as he has never fully reproduced it. His rating in winning that renewal, of 127, was 2lb higher than Calandagan's assessment a year later, and justifiably so given who he beat (Bluestocking) and how he beat her, in a strongly-run race which admittedly hasn't really come his way since.

Image: Goliath won the 2024 King George

However, there has been a spike on the swagger-gram more recently, from the way he won the Grand Prix de Chantilly and the way that he cruised into contention in the Hardwicke, before Soumillon's foot slipped out of his iron. There's a scenario where he shines brightly again.

LAMBOURN

Trainer: Aidan O'Brien | Jockey: TBC

His talent never matched his tagline of dual Derby winner, and this season has furthermore been the firework which fizzles out meekly. His defeat of Bay City Roller at Chester on his comeback was another false positive, as it has all been negative ever since, in the jetwash of Calandagan at Saint-Cloud last time.

MASQUERADE BALL

Trainer: Takahisa Tezuka | Jockey: Christophe Lemaire

Sharing top billing as Japan's best horse of 2025 with living legend Forever Young on the Longines Rankings, robustly rationalised by giving Calandagan all he could handle in the Japan Cup, in a course record, are achievements all the more wondrous when you consider he was only a three-year-old.

He's liable to be more potent and powerful in 2026, and his only race so far did little to dissuade, runner-up in the QEII Cup in Hong Kong to another modern great, Romantic Warrior, when trying to come from last over 1¼m.

He's the best horse that Japan has ever sent to the King George, and if you could ask Calandagan himself who's the toughest opponent he's faced, I reckon he'd say City of Troy first but then Masquerade Ball second, ahead of Ombudsman.

WURTTEMBERG

Trainer: Hiroshi Miyamoto | Jockey: Oisin Murphy

A compatriot of Masquerade Ball but he wouldn't be in the same class nor category. His last three races have come at two miles or above, though it was only the top-tier Croix du Nord who did for him in the Tenno Sho (Spring) in May and that one had beaten the fast-finishing Masquerade Ball in last year's Japanese Derby. A six-year-old, his rating of 116 puts him behind all bar Lambourn and Action.

KALPANA

Jockey: Colin Keane | Trainer: Andrew Balding

She's a millionaire with seven wins on her CV, including back-to-back Fillies & Mares' Stakes on Champions Day, and yet there's still an air of the bridesmaid about her in that she's defined more by her seconds than her firsts.

Image: Kalpana has proven herself to be somewhat of an Ascot specialist in recent times

The key one was in this race last year in which she got Calandagan down to his dregs - the performance of her life - but the Hardwicke last time looked hers for the taking before she bowed to her bête noire Giavellotto. This is a deeper renewal than 2025 but she's got the game to make the podium once again.

MINNIE HAUK

Trainer: Aidan O'Brien | Jockey TBC

Everyone is aware of FOMO, fewer have heard of KIMO, the past tense equivalent, knowing I missed out and the regret or envy therein. It felt like the 2025 Arc was her life's work, amplified by the fact she had a hoof or two on the prize up the straight, and the come down affected her at the Breeders' Cup and maybe ever since. True, she turned the tables on a sub-par Daryz in the Prince of Wales at Royal Ascot but she never laid a glove on Ombudsman, the spark of last summer still missing. The return to 1½m could be the connecting rod to her full force, but by now it's more a possibility than a probability.

ACTION

Trainer: Aidan O'Brien | Jockey TBC

More than a bit-part player in the Derby after his second in the Dante but checked out tamely at Epsom and they leaned into his front-running style all the more in the Irish equivalent. Projects to be pacemaker here, whether it's clarified or not.

BENVENUTO CELLINI

Trainer: Aidan O'Brien | Jockey TBC

If facts hurt your feelings, you need new feelings, not new facts. The same rule applies if facts hurt your argument, but facts don't adequately summarise the snowballing storm that is Benvenuto Cellini, who transmits in feelings not facts and deals in divination not data.

Even with the weight-for-age, a rating of 119 is the equivalent of bringing a knife to the King George gunfight, but the more you rewatch the end of the Irish Derby the more you feel that we could still be just scratching the surface with him, in tandem with the show he put on at Chester.

Since Galileo in 2001, Aidan O'Brien has run only three winners of a Derby in the King George as three-year-olds, but one was Auguste Rodin - with whom Benvenuto Cellini has always had some symmetry, if more in feeling than fact.

JAMIE LYNCH'S VERDICT

A top-tier turnout in prospect, making for one of the races of the season and potentially the decade, but the amazing thing about CALANDAGAN is that there's nothing here to scare him, given the CV he's compiled and the heightened powers he's displayed along the way, all around the world. Armed to the teeth and assured underneath, he's got an answer for whatever or whoever gets in his way.

Sports.title: Kelly promises to let loose in 'spiteful' takedown of Agyarko
Sports.content:
Josh Kelly has promised that his IBF light-middleweight title defence against Caoimhin Agyarko will be "spiteful" ahead of their Saudi Arabia showdown on Saturday.

The fight forms part of the undercard of Anthony Joshua's return to the ring against Kristian Prenga at the Jeddah Superdome.

Sunderland's Kelly won the belt in January against Bakhram Murtazaliev, and told Sky Sports that being champion has given him added belief going into the bout against Agyarko of Belfast.

Image: Josh Kelly celebrates defeating Bakhram Murtazaliev to claim the IBF light-middleweight title

"The thing it has done for me inside is worth its weight in gold," Kelly said of his win over Murtazaliev.

"It's a weird one because, in training and everything, everyone is saying I just look different. These are the closest people to me, watching me go to work every day.

"It's a crazy experience. You don't know what something like this does for you, spiritually, energetically, motivation-wise, everything.

"It's actually taken a lot of expectation off. It's like I can now just let loose, let the reins go and just enjoy everything.

"It's knowing and believing. First, you have to believe, but when you complete the task, you know."

Initially, Agyarko was scheduled to face Brandon Adams in a final eliminator in April, but the American collapsed prior to the weigh-in and was unable to fight.

Rather than the IBF ordering another final eliminator between Agyarko and Murtazaliev, Kelly was given the option of a voluntary first defence, and a deal was struck to face Agyarko.

"We know each other, but he's just another opponent, basically," Kelly said of Agyarko.

"He's just another guy I've got to deal with, a stepping stone in this journey to creating more history. It's not about him, it's about me."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Caoimhin Agyarko says Josh Kelly’s 'mentality and ego' will be his downfall in their IBF super-welterweight clash this Saturday.

Agyarko's last outing was a split-decision victory over Ishmael Davis in December, while Kelly has put eight wins together, including the title victory over Murtazaliev, since his sole career loss to David Avanesyan in 2021.

"There's no complacency," Kelly promised. "No other fight exists except this one.

"I've never overlooked anyone in my career. In fact, I end up overestimating every opponent - I build them up to be the fastest, hardest-hitting guys.

"I'm looking to do bigger and better things in the sport, and this is now a dangerous time to face me because I've got literally nothing to lose.

"I'm just going to go in there and enjoy it, put an absolute spectacle on.

"It's going to be fun. It's going to be spiteful."

Sports.title: Red Bull getting calls from 'good drivers' over future seat - Mekies
Sports.content:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has suggested they are getting calls from "good drivers" about potential future seats at the team but believes they will make the further pace improvements required to ensure Max Verstappen stays.

As Formula 1 prepares for its final race before the summer break in Hungary this weekend, Verstappen's Red Bull future beyond this season remains uncertain.

His contract runs to the end of the 2028 season but contains performance clauses that would allow him to leave at the end of this year. He is thought to have until October to inform the team should he wish to activate a break in the deal.

It emerged last month that the Dutchman's representatives had spoken with McLaren, although the latter's Zak Brown has subsequently made clear that "I've got my two drivers" in Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. Mercedes and Ferrari's drivers are also under contract, seemingly limiting Verstappen's short-term options beyond Red Bull, should he first choose to stay in F1, into 2027.

With it considered normal that Verstappen's representatives would be keeping abreast of potential options for their driver elsewhere, Mekies was asked by Sky Sports F1 at the Belgian Grand Prix whether his team, in turn, had also received enquiries from drivers elsewhere on the grid.

"It's working in both directions," replied Mekies. "It's completely natural and I think that's what you guys were reporting before.

"It's completely natural Max gets called from everyone because he's the best driver in the world and, equally, if you are a top team, you are going to get calls from many of these good drivers around as well. That's natural.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix, Max Verstappen gave blunt responses to questions about his future at Red Bull.

"Is it a distraction for us? Not really. The full focus is to get that car as fast as it can, then you will keep your best driver in the world and we also see there's a massive growth of Isack [Hadjar] alongside Max.

"That for us is the ideal pairing and we try to make sure we can keep that pairing."

Mekies is confident Red Bull will deliver on their ongoing quest to close its remaining gap to the front of the field after steps forward since the start of the season in F1's new era of regulations.

Since a big upgrade of the RB22 three races ago at the Austrian Grand Prix, Verstappen has finished on the podium in two of the last three races, although endured a difficult Silverstone where he spun out late on due to a rear-wing fault.

Isack Hadjar finished sixth from 21st on the grid last weekend in Belgium to extend his run of top-six finishes to six races.

"All we need to do is to continue to progress with the car," said Mekies.

"We started the season a bit more than one second off the pace and I don't think we should be surprised at that.

"I think it's a product of how late the title push was last year - a product of how late the title push was last year, a product of the incredible challenge of the new power unit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After finishing third in Belgium, Max Verstappen has disputed the FIA rating Red Bull's engine as the benchmark in Formula One.

"We started on the back foot but these guys did it again. We were more than a second away and we are now talking about the last two or three tenths for ultimate pace.

"When you are one second away, the drivers are going to be frustrated, Max is going to be frustrated. And we know it's not the position we want to stay.

"To your point, the best way to close the subject is to go and get these last two or three tenths and that's what everyone is focused on."

Red Bull have seen the departure of a number of key figures associated with their past title-winning successes over the last two years, while Verstappen's own race engineer and key ally, Gianpiero Lambiase, is heading to McLaren no later than 2028.

Asked how that sense of 'transition' at the team marries with attempts to keep Verstappen, Mekies said: "It's more simple than what it seems, because ultimately it's only about speed.

"Red Bull and Red Bull Racing only have one objective, it's to win, and it's the same objective that Max has.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

"So, it's not about, how can we prove to him that we can win. We are here to win anyhow.

"It's the same group of people that have done the incredible turnaround last year, that was a few months ago. It's the same group of people that, despite that late push, has managed to absorb nearly one second off our competitors, and they were not waiting for us in these first races.

"Now we are in the hardcore part of it, the last few tenths, the most difficult ones to get, but what we need to do is continue to work as a united group, and that's how we'll produce the best results."

Sports.title: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos in talks to join consortium seeking 30% stake in Liverpool
Sports.content:
The Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has held talks about joining the consortium that is seeking to buy around 30% of Liverpool.

The group led by the former Queens Park Rangers co‑owner Amit ­Bhatia has made a provisional offer of £1.35bn to buy a stake from Fenway Sports Group (FSG), and is talking to other potential investors over supplying funding. Bezos has a personal fortune of around $257bn, according to Forbes, making him the fourth richest person in the world.

The 62-year-old has previously explored bids for the NFL franchises Seattle Seahawks and Washington Commanders without completing a deal, but has never before looked at investing in the Premier League.

Sources with knowledge of the talks have indicated that any deal with Bhatia’s consortium would see Bezos receive equity in Liverpool.

Bezos is executive chairman of Amazon having relinquished day-to-day control when he stepped down as chief executive five years ago. Under his leadership the online retailer has looked to diversify as an entertainment provider in recent years and has bought numerous sports right for its streaming service.

Amazon had live UK rights for 20 Premier League games each season for six years until the end of last year, and broadcasts the Champions League in several European countries, as well as NFL in the United States.

The Bhatia bid for Liverpool is understood to value the club at around £4.5bn, higher than the valuation of Manchester United when Sir Jim Ratcliffe bought 25% of the club two years ago.

While the search for fresh investors is continuing, Bhatia is believed to have secured financial backing from his father-in-law, the Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, whose family wealth is estimated at around £23bn.

Bhatia was a director and co-owner of QPR until yesterday when he transferred his shares to fellow owner Ruben Gnanalingam to pave the way for his consortium’s prospective investment in Liverpool.

An FSG spokesperson has confirmed the talks, saying: “An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club.”

FSG previously sold 3% of the club to the US private equity firm Dynasty Equity in 2023. A spokesperson for Bhatia declined to comment.

Sports.title: World Cup 2026 awards: the Guardian team give their final tournament verdicts
Sports.content:
Match of the tournament

Paraguay 1-1 Germany. There were plenty more games with more goals but none could match the drama of the penalty shootout in this last-32 tie. Germany aren’t supposed to lose in them but they did this time in spectacular fashion. Ed Aarons

Algeria 3-3 Austria was a completely strange fever dream, seeming to exist on a separate plane of reality. I know that sounds grandiose but remember, going into this one the expectation was that it would be a biscotto – a meaningless, pre-arranged kickabout where a draw would see both sides through. For a while in the second half, it looked like that would happen. And finally, in stoppage time, chaos. There were certainly better matches in terms of quality, and maybe a couple that had this beat for drama, but no game was weirder. Alexander Abnos

From the 14 I attended, it has to be Mexico 2-3 England at the awesome Azteca. The buildup seemed to start as soon as the draw was made – fortunately the stars aligned and a grippingly tense game ensued in a venue like no other. It was a high point for England that should cut through despite later disappointments, too. Nick Ames

France 4-6 England was borderline hilarious. Egypt 1-1 Iran in Seattle had plenty of late drama, Iran’s disallowed stoppage-time winner bookended by them twice hitting the woodwork in the final minutes. The draw ultimately proved insufficient for unbeaten Iran, faced with endless hurdles, to progress. Ben Fisher

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The defending champions looked down and out, thinking about their flights home, before a late Lionel Messi-inspired comeback enabled them to claw back a two-goal deficit and win this last-16 match in normal time. Barry Glendenning

The game no one wanted to play. Sid Lowe

Mexico 2-3 England. I have decided that all my answers should relate to things that happened while I was at the tournament and this was one. I mean, I wasn’t there ticking off the “bucket list” of a visit to the Azteca (I think I saw at least half a dozen British hacks claim that), but I did watch it on TV. Besides being like drinking cortisol neat, this was so dramatic, the images so evocative, that even if you are an ardent England fan (as I am) this was pure cinema. Paul MacInnes

View image in fullscreen England’s players sing Wonderwall in front of their fans after their last-16 victory over Mexico. Photograph: José Méndez/EPA

I am biased here in the sense I attended it but Cape Verde 2-2 Uruguay in Miami was superb. Cape Verde’s attitude and discipline were a joy. Such fun to watch. Ewan Murray

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. Incredible drama, despite the questionable behaviour of the referee. Osasu Obayiuwana

Tough to pick from over 100 options, but Mexico 2-3 England with Thomas Tuchel’s men surviving the vaunted Azteca and the best first half Mexico could have mustered narrowly takes this category. Jeff Rueter

Bias says Mexico v England, but Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde was incredible, Sidny Lopes Cabral bending it top right. Max Rushden

For improbable wonder there was Argentina v Cape Verde, for sheer unpredictability there was Mexico v England. Often, though, one is drawn to something more predictable, more familiar: England 1-2 Argentina. Jack Snape

Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde. It’s not a debate. Jacob Steinberg

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The possibility of a shock, a great Messi-inspired turnaround, a couple of great goals, refereeing controversy … what else do you want? Jonathan Wilson

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi (second left) fires a shot past Egypt’s keeper Mostafa Shobeir for Argentina’s equaliser in their 3-2 win. Photograph: Elsa/Getty Images

Player of the tournament

Rodri was the standout player for the best team in a tournament where the big stars came to the party but all ultimately fell short. EA

Kylian Mbappé. Yes, his Golden Boot was padded a bit by that insane third-place game, but the France striker was the best player on what looked to be the best team in the tournament ... at least until that loss to Spain in the semi-final. AA

It’s impossible to look further than Rodri, who looks back to his best and absolutely in his element as the fulcrum of this Spain setup. Otherwise it was good to see a World Cup where the stars largely shone. Jude Bellingham, Erling Haaland, Messi and Mbappé were all one more decisive knockout display away from rising above the rest. NA

Rodri. Michael Olise was majestic, though should have scored a hat-trick against England. Bellingham was equally instrumental for Tuchel’s side – it is crazy to think there were people questioning his inclusion in the squad. BF

Rodri – capitán, líder, leyenda. BG

Lionel Messi. SL

Vozinha. What a man. I think it’s largely because his story is so relatable in these parts – middle-aged man finally receives the plaudits he has always deserved! – but the saves were also top drawer. Add in the pedigree of the teams he either shut out or frustrated, and this was an actual fairytale that didn’t need to be spun by any marketing department. And did you know that he’s 40? PM

Pau Cubarsí. EM

Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper. At 40, and without a club, he was brilliant for the World Cup debutants. OO

While Rodri is an incredibly worthy Golden Ball winner and others made their marks, Erling Haaland leaves this World Cup with the greatest possible souvenirs: a credible if short Golden Boot campaign, a famous first Norwegian foray into the quarter-final stage, and perhaps the biggest boost in star appeal in the lucrative North American market. JR

View image in fullscreen Even the World Cup mascots stand in awe of Erling Haaland. Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Fifa/Getty Images

Hard not to say Rodri although I thought Dani Olmo was great too, and a shout for Pico Lopes. MR

Haaland, Mbappé and Messi have lived up to expectations. But in those moments where a contest teeters – evading pressure with the ball, in transition to defence or staring down a 50-50 – no player has shown his quality more consistently than Rodri. JSn

Rodri. If only England had a player like the Spain captain. JSt

Rodri. As Spain have reverted to a more possession-driven model, their metronome in midfield has been the outstanding figure, setting the tempo and providing control. JW

Goal of the tournament

For sheer drama, it has to be Sidny Lopes Cabral’s brilliant equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina. His reaction was almost as good as the goal itself, clasping his hands to his head before picking out his girlfriend in the crowd to celebrate with. EA

I mean, it’s Sidny Lopes Cabral v Argentina. But I feel that the goal from Uzbekistan’s Eldor Shomurodov against the Democratic Republic of the Congo deserves mention too: an instinctive, oddly satisfying lob from a tight angle. No other goal in the tournament was quite like it. AA

Julián Alvarez had a largely quiet World Cup but his vicious, swerving long-range goal in extra time against Switzerland was a jaw-dropping moment and lit up the cauldron-like stadium in Kansas City. NA

Those seen in the flesh always seem to score more points. A buzz surrounded Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic coming into the tournament and the 18-year-old eliminating a clutch of defenders and blasting in, off balance, from the outside of the box against Qatar only enhanced his reputation. Johan Manzambi’s run and pass in the buildup to Breel Embolo’s opener against Algeria was also a joy. BF

View image in fullscreen Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic is embraced after opening the scoring against Qatar. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

While Morocco’s superior quality would ultimately see them through their group-stage win against Haiti, Wilson Isidor’s breathtaking long-range strike to put the Caribbean nation 2-1 up was as good a goal as any scored in the World Cup. Ever. BG

Sidny Lopes Cabral, of course. SL

I had the privilege of reading the paper by the Seoul Women’s University on the aerodynamic effect known as “drag crisis” which is particularly common when people smack an Adidas Trionda, so as such I thought a lot of the big hits were overrated. I do, however, exempt Sidny Lopes Cabral from that critique. Absolute long-range worldie from the Cape Verde full-back-cum-winger. That it pegged Argentina to parity in extra time of a knockout round only made it more memorable. PM

Harry Kane’s second for England against DRC. EM

Sidny Lopes Cabral of Cape Verde, against Argentina. Magical goal. OO

I will never, in all my years, be able to recreate the sound that left my body as Sidny Lopes Cabral’s audacious effort against Argentina completed its curl between a diving Emi Martínez and his far post. Masterful execution in an unprecedented moment. One of many proud moments for Cape Verde at this tournament. JR

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral unleashes his audacious effort … Photograph: Newscom/Alamy

View image in fullscreen … which flies past Argentina’s keeper Emi Martínez to level the scores in extra time. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

Beyond Sidny Lopes Cabral – the disallowed Uzbekistan one (was it Uzbekistan?) – someone walloped one into the top left-hand corner and it didn’t count. MR

Erling Haaland’s second against Brazil, placed into the bottom-right corner from outside the box to seal the upset, was a microcosm of his effectiveness at the tournament: precise and powerful with a hint of whimsy. JSn

Sidny Lopes Cabral’s equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina was a proper jaw-dropping moment. One of the great World Cup goals. JSt

Wilson Isidor v Morocco. There were more consequential goals, but none struck quite as sweetly or quite as accurately. If Haiti have nothing else, they’ll always have that. JW

Personal highlight

It was a joy to watch Eloy Room’s performance in goal for Curaçao against Ecuador as he broke the World Cup record for the most saves made in a 90-minute match. While Cape Verde’s veteran Vozinha stole most of the headlines for his heroics, the 37-year-old Room clearly enjoyed his moment in the spotlight. “I think I need a statue in Curaçao now,” he joked. EA

Fifa and the stadium authorities typically guard the natural grass pitches heavily, and with good reason. But after the last games in each venue I went to, I loved watching those pitches get taken over by the people whose names you’ll never know but who actually made this tournament run: stadium workers and low-level Fifa staffers, volunteers, security guards, longtime local club representatives and others. Some used the opportunity to have a little kickabout, take selfies, or just run around. An awesome perk for what were almost certainly very hard, stressful jobs over these last several weeks. AA

My first visit to the Azteca was Mexico’s win over Ecuador and I’ve never heard a noise like it. The place really is as magical and monumental as they say. The celebrations afterwards weren’t conducive to a good night’s sleep but were incredible in scale too. Football-wise I’ll also add Messi’s record-breaking goals against Austria in Dallas, which seem an awfully long time ago now but were such a thrill to witness. Those early Argentina games were essentially mass Messi pilgrimages. One more? The view from Monterrey Stadium. Just go, if you can. NA

View image in fullscreen A view of Mexico’s last-32 game against Ecuador from high up inside the Azteca stands. Photograph: Hannah Peters/Fifa/Getty Images

Watching Senegalese journalists pass around a pack of malted milks during their anthem before their collapse against Belgium. And playing eight-a-side with Danny Cipriani, who once spent six weeks training at Tottenham, Harry Kane among his teammates, will stick in the memory. BF

Watching my Irish compatriot Roberto “Pico” Lopes excel while repeatedly putting his body on the line for Cape Verde, his father’s homeland. It would be nice to think Pico’s performances will earn him a life-changing move to a more lucrative league in the twilight of his career but his age could stand against him and he may well be content with being a Shamrock Rovers and Cape Verde legend. BG

Explaining to a mariachi in a gigantic sombrero how it could possibly be that a team in third could get through the group and how it might still be Spain turning up at the Azteca. Alas, it wasn’t. Sharing a birthday with Martin Ainstein and Luis de la Fuente and my family. And watching a motorcade with the Spain bus pass from the sixth-floor window where Lee Harvey Oswald shot JFK was pretty surreal. SL

I loved watching both France eviscerate Sweden and the Instagram reels of Americans acting like they thought the Tartan Army had permanently changed their lives. PM

View image in fullscreen Members of the Tartan Army have a kickabout in a Boston street. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

Players running out to warm-up to the tune of Scotland the Brave, via bagpipes, before the game against Haiti in Foxborough. Scotland’s 28-year World Cup wait was over. The less said about all that happened next, the better. EM

Seeing Vozinha’s mum, against all expectations, travelling from Cape Verde to the World Cup to see her son play. OO

Having covered the nation’s third-to-fifth most popular sport for more than a decade and lived through ICE’s heinous occupation of Minnesota this winter, the sheer scale of interest in soccer was overwhelming and so invigorating – a welcome reprieve in the isolationist second Trump era. Impossible to go through a couple of hours in a World Cup host city without some stranger striking up a conversation about the sport. Long may this remain a part of American society. JR

Shouting Paraguay. Number 10. Cover his mouth. Decision is RED CARD. Jonathan Wilson thinking Robbie Williams was Kevin Pietersen. Mark Langdon’s chow mein bridge. The pancakes at Mile End Deli. Doing a live show in Manhattan and legitimately getting to say “HELLO NEW YORK!” MR

Covering Australia, the tournament petered out from an extraordinary high. Twenty-six minutes into the Socceroos’ opening victory against Turkey, goalscorer Nestory Irankunda revived Tim Cahill’s goal celebration in a ceremonial handover to mark a new generation. JSn

View image in fullscreen Australia’s Nestory Irankunda throws punches while shadowboxing the corner flag, à la Tim Cahill. Photograph: Kaleb Tatum/AP

Being at the Azteca for Mexico 2-3 England. It did not have the most quality but it was hard to beat as an occasion. An epic night at an iconic stadium. A thunderstorm pushing kick-off back, a brilliant display from Bellingham, everyone exhausted when it was over. Things didn’t end well for England but this was easily their greatest away win. JSt

Standing knee-deep in raging floods in Monterrey waiting for a bus having only gone to the stadium to collect a mislaid iPad that I then lost in Houston a week later anyway. That or the weirdly beautiful flyovers outside Dallas. JW

What did you make of the hosts?

The level of interest from the American public surprised me and it was fascinating to meet so many who were interested in what was happening in the tournament. Many people in the US definitely caught World Cup fever. Logistically it was a real test of endurance with so much travelling required between venues and that wasn’t helped by so many being miles from the city centre. And it would have been much better to have played the final in Mexico City or Atlanta’s impressive downtown stadium. EA

I felt unfortunate not to make it to any games in Mexico and only one in Canada. But overall I’m happy that the everyday people who populate the US seemed to show visitors their good side throughout the month. This country has plenty of infrastructure issues I’d like to have seen fixed, but the personal impact is arguably more important, and it seems like the US mostly got that right. AA

If first impressions are everything then I refer you to the often troubling weirdness of the Texas Republican party convention in Houston. But more seriously I was very happy, in the US, to find the hoped-for warmth and openness pretty much everywhere – and in bundles. In their different ways, people really did engage with the World Cup. Less welcome was the US administration’s attempt, duly pandered to by Fifa, to bend the course of the tournament with Folarin Balogun’s reprieve. In Mexico I found a fervent, febrile, fascinating football culture that deserved not to be dwarfed by other co-hosts. NA

Americans love a big-ticket event but it was clear they were hooked by Mauricio Pochettino’s side as they progressed. It was a privilege to witness Canada’s first World Cup game on home soil in Toronto, where there was a match-day buzz and an afterglow despite being held to a draw by Bosnia and Herzegovina. BF

View image in fullscreen Canada fans react to Cyle Larin’s goal during their opening group game against Bosnia and Herzegovina. Photograph: Joosep Martinson/Fifa/Getty Images

While I didn’t meet Donald Trump, the handful of Americans whose acquaintance I did make – hotel staff, a few bartenders and one LA-based reality TV show star – could not have been friendlier. BG

So many people came up to us to say they really hoped we were enjoying this and that we understood that that wasn’t them. We did and they were so nice. SL

I spent two days in Toronto, around Canada Day, and I think they were both welcoming and very keen to hear that they qualified as an actual football nation. People in the US were pleasant, although for travelling fans most experiences will have been complicated by the ubiquitous request for a tip. I did think, though, that sometimes there was an expectation that we should all be delighted to be there. Which we were, but perhaps not for the reasons some wanted. PM

Canada and Mexico? Excellent. US stadiums were first class, as was the extent to which the nation embraced the World Cup. It is just impossible to ignore the stench of the Balogun situation. EM

On an on-field football level? Far from spectacular. The US needs a new player-development architecture to ensure there is a pipeline of high-quality players. They also need a new head coach, with the right vision for the future. Tournament organisation? The fact that Fifa took direct control of it should be a cautionary tale. A local organising committee is always needed. OO

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino speaks to his USA players after their defeat by Belgium which eliminated the co-hosts. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

All three co-hosts fared about as well as I had projected, but each may have exceeded my expectations in terms of how they went about it. Canada were thrilling at times – I covered their 6-0 win over Qatar at BC Place – and had plenty of pluck with Jesse Marsch as their coach-cum-hype man. The USA played some of the prettiest soccer ever seen by a US national team of any gender, and will for ever rue a missed opportunity to do something greater against Belgium. Mexico were one of the biggest bandwagon teams as they barnstormed Group A, then outclassed an Ecuador team on the rise and pushed England to the brink until they ran out of ideas in the final half-hour. Jobs well done across the board. JR

I had six weeks in America. All the Americans were lovely. MR

This tournament put the whirled in the World Cup, its scale ensuring it evaded generalisation. Cities such as Vancouver and Seattle – with downtown stadiums and soccer traditions – were fitting hosts, while metropolises such as Dallas and San Francisco accommodated the month-long novelty without embracing it. JSn

The people in Mexico could not have been more welcoming, even when England beat their side. It was the same in Kansas City, England’s base and where I spent most of my time. On the other hand it would have been better if getting around some US cities was easier. Public transport infrastructure isn’t really a thing in some places. Florida especially. The Boston traffic was ridiculous, too. JSt

A wide range depending on venue but broadly friendly, welcoming and enthusiastic. Would benefit from improved public transport and generally lower volume. Wifi hopeless, coffee weak. JW

Sports.title: Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert charged with misconduct by FA over spygate scandal
Sports.content:
Southampton’s manager, Tonda Eckert, is facing the possibility of a lengthy suspension from all football activity in England, and perhaps beyond, after being charged with three counts of misconduct by the Football Association.

All three relate to the ‘Spygate’ scandal and involve breaching FA rules during covert missions to illicitly observe Championship training sessions involving Middlesbrough, Ipswich and Oxford last season. The 33-year-old has until Tuesday to respond to the charges and may well fear the precedent set by Fifa when it banned Bev Priestman, the English-born former Canada women’s head coach and assistant England women coach, from football worldwide for 12 months. In 2024 Priestman, then in charge of Canada, was found to have authorised a spying mission involving the use of a drone to monitor New Zealand’s training during the Paris Olympics.

Southampton have already been punished for Spygate by the English Football League (EFL) when in May an independent disciplinary commission found them guilty of three counts of football espionage. That ruling stripped Eckert’s team of their right to appear in the playoff off final in addition to ruling that they must start the coming Championship campaign handicapped by a four-point league deduction. The EFL, though, has no power to issue sanctions against individuals in such instances, so the case against Eckert was handed to the FA, who launched a long-running inquiry.

At the start of July the governing body spoke to Eckert, a one-time Germany analyst, at length and now have the power to issue a range of punishments ranging from a warning to a heavy fine to suspension. Yet whereas Priestman’s ban was worldwide, the FA only possess the power to prevent Eckert working in England. The governing body does, however, have the right to ask Fifa to apply any suspension internationally. In 2023 the Italian FA succeeded with such a request when they demanded that the then Newcastle midfeilder, Sandro Tonali’s 10-month suspension for betting irregularities be applied worldwide. In Eckert’s case, an England-only ban would appear almost meaningless were he to be offered a job abroad.

Eckert has already apologised to Southampton fans and admitted he should have known that EFL regulations specifically outlawed spying. A coach who grew up within a European culture that tacitly tolerates observing rivals’ training sessions also spoke of the “bitter irony” that Southampton’s three spying missions had “no impact” on his team’s planning or performances. William Salt, the intern first-team analyst, caught filming Middlesbrough’s training session on a mobile phone before the first leg of a playoff semi final won on aggregate by Southampton before their expulsion, has since been offered a permanent post as an analyst in the club’s academy. Salt has not been the subject of any FA charges.

Southampton’s owner, Dragan Solak has vowed to stand by Eckert and has consistently maintained he will not sack him, but a possible 12 month - or, as some sources are suggesting, six month FA ban – could alter that stance. In a statement issued on Wednesday Southampton said: “Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA. Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League”.

Eckert, who saw Middlesbrough take Southampton’s place in a play off final won by Hull, recently told BBC Radio Solent. “I’ve held my hand up for this judgement on something I have authorised. I am responsible and I apologise for bad judgement.”
