Sports.title: 'I never considered walking away': ANTHONY JOSHUA opens up on his return to boxing in wake of car crash tragedy that killed two of his best friends - and reveals how the power of prayer spurred him on
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua never considered walking away.

Not after the darkest chapter of his life. Not after the unimaginable tragedy that left the boxing world reeling and forced him to confront grief far greater than any defeat inside the ring. And certainly not now, as he prepares to step through the ropes for the first time since the car accident that changed everything.

The crash near Lagos, Nigeria, late last year claimed the lives of Joshua's childhood friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, both 36. The pair had been part of his inner circle for decades, with Ghami serving as his strength coach and Ayodele as his personal trainer.

On Saturday night, Joshua returns to the ring in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, against Kristian Prenga. It is, in many ways, the beginning of a new chapter.

It is his second fight under Oleksandr Usyk's team, but the first after a full training camp together and the first real opportunity to showcase the technical improvements those around him insist have transformed his game. And, perhaps most importantly, it represents the first step towards the blockbuster showdown with Tyson Fury that British boxing has craved for years.

But before any of that, Joshua had to decide whether he even wanted to fight again.

That decision was never really a decision at all.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

He beat Jake Paul in Miami in December, but within days had lost two friends in a car crash

'I never considered walking away, because boxing is my purpose,' Joshua explains ahead of his comeback. 'It's not just about competing. Boxing is therapeutic as well. It gives me purpose.

'As fighters, that's what it gives us. When I'm boxing, I know I'm where I'm supposed to be. It's where I'm most comfortable.

'It gives me direction in life, and that's why I never really thought about walking away. I'm content. This is where I belong.'

Joshua speaks calmly. There is no bravado, no attempt to create headlines. Instead, there is a noticeable sense of perspective from a man who has spent the past year processing an experience no person should ever have to endure.

He is careful when discussing loss, and even more careful not to make himself the focus of it.

'Everyone deals with it differently,' he says. 'For me, I have to put my own emotions to one side because I focus on the parents.

'My emotions can come later, but I look at what the mums and dads are going through because that's what must be hardest.

'I don't make it about me. I make it about them. You have to keep your own emotions under control. That's not how everyone deals with it, but it's the best way for me. I need to be a good soldier. At the end of the day, it's not about me. It's much bigger than me.'

The 36-year-old says he never intended to walk away from boxing because it is his purpose

Daily Mail Sport's Charlotte Daly caught up with Joshua ahead of his return fight

Another source of strength has come from an unlikely place.

Joshua's move to train alongside former undisputed heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk has inevitably led to questions about technical improvements, but the biggest lesson he has taken from the Ukrainian has nothing to do with slipping punches or throwing combinations.

'The importance of prayer,' Joshua says without hesitation while speaking to The Daily Mail in Jeddah. 'Even if you're not deeply religious or don't follow one particular faith, prayer is important. It's something you can take into every training camp.'

Inside Usyk's camp, Joshua insists every aspect of his game has evolved, but one lesson stands above the rest.

'We'd be here all day talking about everything they've added to my game.

'The biggest thing is my relationship with hard work. You can be in one environment and think you're working hard, then you go into another environment and realise what you thought was hard actually isn't hard enough. It isn't good enough.

'So it's really changed my relationship with hard work. I want more from myself. I've put myself in an environment where I know I'll get more out of boxing because I've given more of myself to boxing. These guys push me harder than I was ever pushed before.'

Those working closest to Joshua believe his defence has improved dramatically since arriving in camp. Watching him spar, they see a more patient, more rounded heavyweight than the explosive Olympic champion who first burst onto the scene over a decade ago.

Joshua pictured moments after the tragic crash took place on a major road outside Lagos

Joshua pictured with friends Latif Ayodele (centre) and Sina Ghami who both died in the crash

Saturday offers the first glimpse of whether those improvements translate under the bright lights.

If Joshua comes through against Prenga, attention will inevitably turn to Fury.

The long-awaited Battle of Britain has flirted with becoming reality for years before collapsing at the negotiating table. Now, with both men rebuilding, it feels closer than ever.

Joshua knows Fury will be watching.

Asked what he wants his rival to think after seeing him back in action, Joshua smiles before delivering an answer that perfectly captures the confidence still burning beneath his measured exterior.

'This guy is a f***ing killer. He's a beast. He's strong. He's quick. He's got good footwork. He's got good defence and it's gonna be hard work trying to beat this guy. That's what I'd want him to think.'

Yet for all the excitement surrounding a potential meeting with Fury, Joshua refuses to place it above the moments that have already defined his career.

'It's a huge fight, but it's not for a world title, if I'm being completely honest,' he says.

Sina Ghami had worked with Joshua for years as his S&C coach and sports rehabilitation specialist, while Latif 'Latz' Ayodele became his PT after years of friendship

'It's a great achievement if I beat someone like Tyson Fury, but for me, nothing compares to becoming a world champion.

'You can beat great fighters, but it's different when you're beating them to become a world champion.'

In an era where some of boxing's biggest stars openly question the value of championship belts, Joshua remains unapologetically old school.

He points to changing financial realities, with fighters now earning fortunes outside the traditional title picture, but believes the sport's history still matters.

'There's a lot of talk nowadays about fighters saying belts don't matter anymore,' he says. 'People's attitudes are changing because there are different opportunities now. But personally, the heritage and history of boxing still means everything to me. You can't beat becoming a world champion, in my opinion...

'Unless someone dangles a big enough carrot in front of me... then f*** the belts.'

It draws a laugh, but the message is clear.

For now, Fury can wait. So can championship ambitions.

Joshua's focus is fixed solely on Prenga and proving that, after everything he has been through, he is still exactly where he believes he belongs.

Back in the ring. Back with purpose. And determined that the next chapter of his career is defined not by the tragedy behind him, but by the fights still to come.

Sports.title: Italy set to 'break the bank' for Pep Guardiola as nation's football president confirms talks with legendary former Man City boss
Sports.content:
Italy set to 'break the bank' for Pep Guardiola as nation's football president confirms talks with legendary former Man City boss

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Italy are prepared to go all out to appoint Pep Guardiola as their manager, the country's football federation have confirmed.

Guardiola is currently out of work after leaving Man City at the end of last season following 10 incredible years in England where he won 20 trophies.

Italy, meanwhile, are currently experiencing some of their worst times, with the nation having not qualified for three successive World Cups, while they haven't made it out of the group stages since winning the tournament for a fourth time in 2006.

Previous manager Gennaro Gattuso resigned from the role in April after the Azzurri lost to Bosnia and Herzegovina on penalties in the World Cup play-offs. The head of the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) Gabriele Gravina and Gianluigi Buffon - who was the national team's Delegation Head - also stepped away following that match.

Italy Under 21 boss Silvio Baldini was in temporary charge for the June international break, but with a fresh cycle starting after the World Cup, they are keen to appoint a new boss.

Reports in Italy earlier this week shared news of talks between the FIGC and Guardiola over the role, and Giovanni Malago, who replaced Gravina, outlined their interest in the Spaniard and determination to get a deal done.

Italy are pushing hard to appoint Pep Guardiola as their new national team manager

Italy have failed to qualify for the last three World Cups and currently do not have a manager

'[Financial] exceptions have been made, exceptions that for example may concern the name that is so overbearing in these hours: Pep Guardiola,' Malago told Gazzetta dello Sport.

'Exceptions for obvious reasons that I am not here to explain, but it is not certain that this thing will go through.'

Former Italy boss Roberto Mancini and Azzurri legend Andrea Pirlo are also in the running for the role, although Malago - who said earlier this week that a new coach was 'just a few more days' away - insisted other contenders remain.

'Absolutely not (are Guardiola, Mancini and Pirlo the only contenders),' he added. 'We think about a certain profile and certainly these names fall into that category.'

New Italy technical director Paolo Maldini and his adviser Leonardo, who previously served as PSG's sporting director, met Guardiola in Barcelona last weekend to try and accelerate any potential deal.

The pair are understood to have a superb relationship with the former Man City, Barcelona and Bayern Munich boss, who spent two seasons in Italy during his playing days with Brescia and Roma, and can speak the language.

New Italian Football Federation president Giovanni Malago said '(financial)' exceptions have been made'

Despite the speculation, Guardiola seemed to distance himself from a return to the dugout last Friday when speaking to Fox Sports.

He said: 'From a mental standpoint, I don’t miss anything at all. I started managing at 37 and my entire life has been bound to football.

'Now, I want to try and discover life, to be happy doing other things that have nothing to do with football.'

If Guardiola did end up with the role, he would become just the third foreigner to take charge of Italy.

Hungarian Lajos Czeizler was a member of the technical committee that ran the team in the 1950s, while Helenio Herrera, the legendary Argentine, was joint-manager alongside Italian Ferruccio Valcareggi in the 1960s.

Sports.title: Inside the incredible rise of Madeleine McCann's brother Sean - who 'HATED' swimming: How 'sport-obsessed' mother Kate, 5am wake ups and surviving 'disgusting' training sessions inspired him to Scotland call up
Sports.content:
When Sean McCann stood behind the blocks of the 50m swimming pool at Loughborough University for the very first time, he was an 18-year-old with a dream.

He dreamed of competing for Scotland and Team GB on the senior international stage. And on Saturday, at the age of 21, after years of surviving 'disgusting' training sessions, McCann is on the cusp of realising his life goal.

Almost two decades on from the tragic disappearance of his older sister Madeleine, who was abducted from the family's holiday apartment in Praia da Luz, the Scot will take to the pool to compete in the 400m freestyle heats at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Sean was in the room when Madeleine's abduction unfolded. The 21-year-old, who was two years old at the time of his family's unimaginable tragedy and does not remember the huge global fallout from the case, has received unconditional support from his parents, Gerry and Kate, on his swimming journey.

They have remained a pillar for Sean during his sporting ventures, with Kate having originally introduced him to swimming which he admitted to 'hating at first', with the youngster not wanting to go to lessons.

The couple regularly attend swimming meets to cheer on their son, who has a twin sister named Amelie, and are said to be 'enthusiastic' about distance swimming.

Madeline McCann's younger brother Sean will swim for Scotland at the Commonwealth Games

Sean has had an incredible rise through the swimming ranks with Scotland and Great Britain

One source, who wishes to remain anonymous, expressed to Daily Mail Sport that the parents are 'really, really supportive' and 'are always there turning up', despite the potential they could be put in the spotlight after everything they have been through.

Saturday marks a monumental moment in the young man's career, and takes him one step closer to his ultimate goal of competing at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years' time.

His journey to the Commonwealth Games began at the age of eight, when he finally got over his fear of the pool. McCann joined Charnwood Triathlon Club, with the hope of becoming the next Alistair Brownlee rather than Michael Phelps.

It was there he discovered his talent for swimming. Soon enough, he wanted to train in the pool more and more, so he joined Loughborough Town Swimming Club to quench that desire, before eventually being handpicked to move to City of Leicester.

At youth level, McCann was clearly talented. He came seventh in the 17-year-old age group 400m freestyle at the British Summer Championships in 2022, while he represented Scotland at the Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad and Tobago just a year later.

But it wasn't until he got to the university that has been on his doorstep his whole life that everything changed.

Loughborough University has one of the most prestigious swimming programs not just in the UK but in the world. It has developed stars such as Adam Peaty, who is arguably the greatest swimmer this country has ever seen, Daniel Wiffen, 800m freestyle reigning Olympic champion, and Liam Tancock, former 50m backstroke world record holder. The program has no shortage of heritage.

And McCann took to it like a duck to water. After initially being plopped in the Performance Development squad, McCann sliced a huge chunk off his 400m freestyle time, taking it from 4:01.67 to 3:56.22 in just one year of training at Loughborough.

This seismic improvement saw him promoted to the High Performance squad with Andi Manley, who coaches Wiffen.

Those who have trained with McCann at Loughborough, and elsewhere, made it clear that this remarkable progress is down to his mentality and drive to succeed.

Team Scotland international swimmer, Charlie Hutchison, tells Daily Mail Sport: 'He's a workhorse, just like everybody else in that squad. We do some disgusting training sessions, but he is never one to complain or moan. He just gets on with it.

'This is definitely something he has worked on when he didn't have as many people to race against and then moving to such a competitive group. Just not being demoralised and pushing forward.

'It's great to have him on the team as part of Team Scotland.'

Sean was inspired to start swimming by his mother Kate, although he admits to hating the sport at first

Sean's older sister Madeline went missing in 2007 when Sean was just two years old

Insiders have explained to Daily Mail Sport how McCann used to have to wake up at 5.15am most mornings to make training, with the perceived 'higher' squads swimming at more favourable times.

But McCann was never one to moan during those times, and put in the 'hard yards' to progress into the next squad and make his dreams come true.

Hutchison continues: 'He's on the path to do very well. His rise through the Scottish ranks was on the Scottish junior team. He's gone from strength to strength, dropping almost 12 seconds from when he first joined.'

McCann has now taken his 400m freestyle time down to an impressive 3:50.66, with the seconds just dropping with each passing year. But he is not just a one-trick pony; he has proven to be quite versatile in the art of distance swimming.

The Scot will also be competing in both the 800m and 1500m freestyle at the Commonwealth Games, which is almost like making yourself do a half-marathon, deciding that's not enough, and then doing a marathon straight after.

And if that still wasn't enough, he also has a history with open water racing, the marathon equivalent. This is how Olympian Hector Pardoe, who came sixth in the 10km swimming event at the Paris Olympics, met McCann.

The pair met when McCann was representing the Scotland open water development team at the Mallorca Best Fest event, and Pardoe was asked to drop him a message. They spoke about suit sizes, and the double-Olympian also gave him advice on the physicality of the sport.

In the years since, they became team-mates at Loughborough and even room-mates at the European Open Water Championships in Croatia last year.

Pardoe tells Daily Mail Sport: 'He's a really, really nice guy. He's a very good trainer, trains really hard, is polite, and a good swimmer.

'I've known him for three or four years now; he joined Loughborough in 2023. He's got a lot quicker. I'd previously seen him on the results page at Nationals, as well.

'When I would be chatting to the Director of Aquatics GB Open Water about new swimmers coming through, he would mention a guy called Sean.'

The distance swimmer originally hails from Leicester and qualifies to represent Scotland through his father, Gerry.

Sean will be swimming the 400m, 800m, and 1500m freestyle at the home Games in Glasgow

While McCann is set to complete one dream and don the famous blue hat, which has been worn by many a megastar swimmer before him, for the very first time at a senior level, he is hungry for more.

After this summer has come to an end, McCann has his sights set on representing Great Britain at the next Olympics in LA.

If the Scot wants that dream to become reality, he will have to take off more than five seconds from his current 400m freestyle personal best. The Olympic 'A Entry Standard' qualifying time is 3:45.46, while the 'B Entry Standard', which only grants qualification at your country's governing body's discretion, is 3:47.71.

Nevertheless, with McCann no stranger to shaving huge chunks off his best times, there is genuine belief that he has what it takes to reach the pinnacle of the sport.

'His path to making the Olympics certainly isn't going to be an easy one,' Hutchison adds. 'He is in an event that was strong, went very weak, and now is very strong again. Now he is having to contend with the likes of Jack McMillan, James Guy and Tyler Melbourne-Smith.

'But if he carries on his current trajectory, and he continues in one of the best programs in the world for distance swimming, I have no doubt that he can definitely achieve that.'

McCann will be able to use Saturday's event as a barometer to see how far he is off the very best in Britain. Then it's all steam ahead to LA.

Sports.title: Dark truth of $1.5BILLION 'gas station heroin' secretly rife in sports after cops found it on tragic NBA star, 29, weeks before death
Sports.content:
Dark truth of $1.5BILLION 'gas station heroin' secretly rife in sports after cops found it on tragic NBA star, 29, weeks before death

On April 1, NBA star Brandon Clarke was arrested for overtaking multiple vehicles at more than 100mph in a no-passing zone in eastern Arkansas.

But the officers searching his Corvette had their attention attracted elsewhere. They found a blue duffle bag with multiple small packages containing green powder.

'It's just kratom, it is legal,' Clarke insisted. Kratom is legal in most states but was banned in Arkansas, where he had encountered police.

Six weeks later, Clarke was dead.

'Kratom is an addictive substance. It can, and does, kill,' Dr Josef G Thundiyil, a medical toxicologist and emergency physician with Orlando Health, told the Daily Mail.

Kratom is sold legally in smoke shops, convenience stores and online. Marketed as a natural wellness product, kratom, which has since been dubbed 'gas station heroin,' has grown into an estimated $1.5billion-a-year industry, according to the American Kratom Association.

Memphis Grizzlies star Brandon Clarke died at the age of 29 in May of this year

Police in Arkansas found kratom, otherwise known as 'gas station heroin,' on Clarke during his arrest weeks before his death

In the same botanical family as coffee, kratom is derived from the leaves of a tropical tree native to Southeast Asia and has been used there for centuries. Only recently has it gained in popularity in the US for purported pain relief and stamina benefits.

Sold in brightly-colored cans resembling energy drinks, capsules pass as everyday vitamins or sugar-coated gummies. But experts say looks are deceiving.

'That it's sold very unregulated in tea shops, smoke shops, gives a false reassurance,' Dr Thundiyil explained.

He warned, a 'whole host' of negative and dangerous side effects have been reported amid kratom's boom, including 'severe compulsive addiction.'

'Users describe: I feel it's just as bad as when I was on an opioid, meaning it's very addictive,' he continued. 'And what we have found of the different outcomes, we've seen reported things like seizures and liver failure. But the one that really caught our attention was death.'

A government report showed poison center calls about kratom have skyrocketed. In 2025 alone, they jumped 1,200 percent to 3,400. There were 233 kratom-associated deaths reported between 2015 and 2025, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Many incidents are a consequence of kratom being mixed with alcohol or other drugs.

'[Kratom] has two different ways of working,' Dr Zaid Fadul, a board-certified physician and founder of Bespoke Concierge MD, told Daily Mail. 'At low doses, it can be a stimulant and can cause pain relief.

In the same botanical family as coffee, kratom comes from leaves of a tree native to Asia

Kratom comes in brightly-colored cans resembling energy drinks and capsules look like candy

'Higher doses have different effects. It can be sedating. Any dose for a prolonged period of time, you get chemical dependence, then eventually addiction.'

The risks don't end there. Dehydration is a side effect, triggered by the loss of appetite caused by kratom, Dr Fadul said.

'Two, kratom is going to mask pain,' he added. 'It's not going to treat pain.'

Kratom does not treat injuries. Instead, it lessens pain for athletes to continue training and competing.

'That's when a stress fracture turns into a real fracture,' Dr Fadul said. 'You want recovery for athletes. You don't want pain masking. You want real recovery.'

In an industry where the body is the money-maker, preserving health is key - and kratom puts that in jeopardy.

Given its accessibility and legal status, it is a product athletes may not necessarily have to disclose to teams and risk a trade.

'I get that athletes are hesitant to take opioids, or they want to get off opioids, and so they're looking for alternatives,' Dr Thundiyil said. 'My warning would be kratom is probably not that solution; it's unproven.

Clarke died near Los Angeles, where he had been staying with a friend from college

An investigation into the power forward's death is still ongoing

'The harms are growing. You may be jumping out the pot and into the fire.'

Clarke was discovered with 235 grams of kratom in April.

The Canadian-American star was restricted to two games for the Grizzlies' last season with injury. He missed 73 games, sitting out 26 recovering from surgery on his right knee before another 46 with a right calf strain.

In addition to kratom, Clarke had a THC vape pen and a prescription for a common painkiller used to treat sporting injuries when he was arrested

'That right there is legal pain medicine,' Clarke said in the dashcam video of his arrest. 'That's Toradol.'

Six weeks later, Clarke was found dead on May 12 in the San Fernando Valley. His death is being investigated as a potential overdose after drug paraphernalia was found at the scene.

No official cause has been announced and the inquest is ongoing.

Clarke and a woman attend his sister's 2024 wedding in Mexico City, Mexico

Clarke poses for a picture with his mother, Whitney Triplett, his step father and his half siblings

Clarke is not alone.

UFC veteran Diego Sanchez's former coach Joshua Fabia accused him of being 'strung out' on kratom and other substances in 2021. Fabia claimed the fighter was an 'addict' following their split. Sanchez denied the allegations.

Wrestler Sabu was allegedly given kratom ahead of his final match amid fears he would not show up to the ring, fellow wrestler Joey Janela claimed in a 2025 interview. Janela later claimed that Sabu - whose real name was Terrance Brunk - took kratom 'daily for years' to help him get off other substances.

Sabu died at age 61 in May 2025 three weeks after his final match. GCW, which hosted the bout, denied any involvement in his death.

Meanwhile, the United Football League - the eight-team spring football league - embraced CBD Kratom in 2024 as its official partner, highlighting potential to 'enhance physical performance’ as well as ‘kratom's ability to aid in chronic pain’.

The Missouri Attorney General's Office launched an investigation into CBD Kratom in November for 'deception, fraud, false promises' among other acts. It is one of nearly two dozen kratom companies under investigation by the Missouri AG office. The UFL's partnership ended before the start of this season.

CBD Kratom, meanwhile, said it relished an 'opportunity to demonstrate the strength of our safety standards, compliance practices, and long-standing commitment to consumer education.'

UFC veteran Diego Sanchez (right) denied accusations of being 'strung out' on kratom

Kratom is not considered performance-enhancing by the World Anti-Doping Agency. It was briefly monitored by WADA but removed from the tracking list in 2018.

The United States Anti-Doping Agency, which handles the drug testing for Olympians, explicitly advises against using it over health hazards, but has not banned it.

In Tennessee, where Clarke played for the Grizzlies, kratom was legal when he was arrested. Three months later, Tennessee became the latest state to ban it, with the illegal status enforced from July 1.

Sports.title: Olympics legend Olaf Tufte dies aged 50: Tributes pour in for two-time rowing champion after he was found unconscious on family farm
Sports.content:
Olympics legend Olaf Tufte dies aged 50: Tributes pour in for two-time rowing champion after he was found unconscious on family farm

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Olympic rowing legend Olaf Tufte has died aged 50 after an astonishing career which saw him win two gold medals and compete in seven Summer Games.

He was found unconscious at his family farm and transported to a hospital in Oslo, where he died, according to Norwegian media.

Tufte, who took gold in the single sculls in Athens in 2004 and Beijing in 2008, is survived by his wife and two children.

He also claimed silver in the double sculls at Sydney in 2000 and a bronze in the same event at Rio de Janeiro in 2016.

Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Store said: 'Tufte brought immense joy through sport to us as a nation.

'He was one of Norway’s greatest sporting heroes, a decorated Summer Olympian, one of the finest rowers we have ever had, and a great role model to many.'

Two-time Olympic gold medallist rower Olaf Tufte from Norway has died aged 50

He competed in seven consecutive Olympic Games between 1996 in Atlanta and Tokyo 2021

World Rowing added: 'He closed out his competitive career at the Tokyo Olympics at age 45, rowing in the men’s quadruple sculls alongside teammates young enough to have been born after his own Olympic debut. The veteran mentor, still on the water, still leading by example.

'Alongside his rowing, Tufte ran the family farm, worked as a volunteer firefighter, and built businesses including a concrete company, the clothing brand Tufte Wear and a brewery.'

Tufte's Olympic career spanned from the 1996 Games in Atlanta to the 2021 edition in Tokyo.

But he wasn't done there. After hanging up his sculls, Tufte went into coaching for the 2024 Paralympic Games in Paris and helped Birgit Skarstein to a silver medal.

Beyond the Olympics, he earned six World Championship medals, two of them gold.

Rowing was not just the sport he loved - it was a way of life.

'I know what I do, I know the rowing family, and I managed to do rowing as a lifestyle, not as a moment,' he once told World Rowing.

Tributes have been pouring in for the Norwegian hero.

Tributes have been pouring in for the legendary Norwegian athlete, who also ran a farm

A former rival, Mahe Drysdale, told Dagbladet: 'I was in shock. I simply did not believe it. Olaf was a titan. He seemed invincible. This is a huge shock, both for me personally and for the entire rowing community.

'Olaf was the driving force behind the friendships between us rowers. Only we knew what the others had been through on the road to a championship. We were fierce rivals, but at the same time best friends. It was a way of showing respect and understanding.

'He was a tremendous athlete. But he was even greater as a friend.

'He had a very special ability to make everyone feel important. He brought people together. He was the glue in our environment and the driving force behind the community.

'He never stopped. He simply couldn't sit still. He was active all the time.'

Norwegian rally driver Petter Solberg added: 'Life can sometimes be so unpredictable and unfair. Today, heaven gained a new star – one of its greatest. To most people, Olaf Tufte was a two-time Olympic champion and two-time World Champion in rowing. One of the strongest rowers the world has ever seen, and a legend of Norwegian sports.

'To me, Olaf was also a role model. A friend, a truly great guy, an inspiration and a genuinely wonderful human being. You will remain in my heart forever, Olaf'.

Sports.title: 'It's just so cut-throat, I'm petrified of what's coming next': Man United fans are furious about club's purge of 'ticket touts' - and Sir Jim Ratcliffe's penny-pinching past is to blame
Sports.content:
Go a little deeper into the latest fallout between Manchester United and their fanbase, and it’s about more than just tickets, touts and technology. It has become an issue of trust.

Yes, United’s trust in supporters who say they have been made to feel like ‘suspects’ over the club’s purge on touting that has led to thousands of fans receiving emails over the last week warning that their accounts are being restricted and season tickets put at risk.

But, more significantly, it is once more testing the supporters’ trust in the club and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, whose intentions are under scrutiny again.

‘I feel angry about it – they just want us gone,’ one fan whose account has been affected told the BBC. Another said: ‘I feel like people are punished for their loyalty. They don't want fans, they want customers.’

United have clarified that any season tickets cancelled as part of the crackdown will be resold as season tickets to fans on the waiting list. In other words, this is not an attempt by the club to make money or cut the number of season-ticket holders.

But fans aren’t convinced. They point to supporters being relocated from the South Stand to other parts of Old Trafford to create a VIP area behind the dugouts, or Ratcliffe’s decision to raise ticket prices to £66 and scrap concessions for OAPs and children, as evidence that regular match-going fans are being disregarded by the club.

Manchester United fans (pictured at a protest outside Old Trafford in February 2026) have long had issues with the club's ownership

Many supporters feel disregarded by the club, who raised ticket prices to £66 and scrapped OAP concessions under Sir Jim Ratcliffe

As at other top clubs, there is a concern that tourists and day-trippers who are likely to spend longer in the stadium and more in the megastore will become increasingly valuable

Many are suspicious about what a new stadium will mean for the rank and file, even though in theory the capacity will grow to 100,000.

When plans for Ratcliffe’s grand ‘Wembley of the North’ were unveiled at the headquarters of Foster + Partners in London in March last year, the Manchester United Supporters’ Trust issued a statement challenging the club to make clear how it would impact ‘anxious’ supporters.

‘Will it drive up ticket prices and force out local fans? Will it harm the atmosphere, which is consistently fans’ top priority in the ground?’ MUST asked. ‘Until the questions are answered, our optimism about plans to make Old Trafford the biggest and the best again will be restrained by caution about what the consequences for fans might be.’

As at other top Premier League clubs, there is a concern that tourists and day-trippers who are likely to spend longer in the stadium and more in the megastore will become increasingly valuable in the long-term compared to the traditional fanbase who risk being priced out of the market.

It’s one of the reasons why United’s rather heavy-handed attempt to crack down on touts is being met with such anger and opposition. Fans see it as yet one more measure that makes life harder for them.

‘It’s just so cut-throat, you fear what’s coming next,’ one supporter told Daily Mail Sport. ‘Everything for match-going fans has been negative, there’s nothing positive. No glimmer of hope. Sir Jim Ratcliffe is steering the ship, it’s on him now.

‘I’m petrified of doing what I normally do. What happens before I’m deemed to be a tout too? The club are putting so much time and effort into doing this, there has to be an easier way to target the touts – or is the hope that when people get the emails, they’ve just had enough?’

The first wave of emails went out last week and a second followed on Monday night. It’s understood there might be two more yet. The messages notify season-ticket holders of suspicious activity on their accounts consistent with touts, and request information to satisfy the club there has been no wrongdoing. No sanctions are imposed until fans respond or fail to do so within 14 days.

'There’s nothing positive. No glimmer of hope. Sir Jim Ratcliffe is steering the ship, it’s on him now'

Fans see the crackdown on 'ticket touts' as yet one more measure that makes life harder for them

United have brought in an external agency which uses automated monitoring to flag any potential infringements of the club’s terms and conditions. The club say that the subsequent reviews receive ‘human assessment’, and they understand the concern and distress that anyone receiving the email will have experienced.

United also insist they have a responsibility to remove touts and protect the integrity of their ticketing operation for all supporters. But suspicions remain and frustration grows with a month to go until the new season kicks off.

In the meantime, it’s business as usual at Old Trafford. United launched their new blue away kit on Wednesday, and will wear it in Friday’s second pre-season friendly against Rosenborg in Trondheim.

There were only 20,069 in Helsinki’s 36,000-capacity Olympic Stadium on Saturday for the opening game against Wrexham.

Proof perhaps that Manchester United are no longer the big draw they once were? Who knows. But food for thought as the club once again finds itself at odds with some of its most loyal supporters.

Sports.title: FIFA prosecutor has already punished Argentina for World Cup final antics with instant penalty
Sports.content:
FIFA prosecutor has already punished Argentina for World Cup final antics with instant penalty

Argentina have been at the centre of controversy after their World Cup defeat to Spain on Sunday

View 3 Images Argentina were penalised in December 2022 after some of their celebrations were judged to have overstepped the mark (Image: David Ramos - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Argentina have already faced a hefty fine for their actions after winning the World Cup in 2022. Much talk has centred on what punishment La Albiceleste would face for the wild scenes after this year's final, with FIFA's disciplinary and ethics prosecutor appointed to review events.

‌



Yet the nation has been on the receiving end of a FIFA prosecution once before. Argentina were slammed for the way they celebrated after beating France via spot-kicks in Qatar in December four years ago.

‌



They subsequently faced charges that were related to "offensive behaviour and violations of the principles of fair play" and "misconduct of players and officials"

‌



One instance centred on Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who made an obscene gesture with his Goalkeeper of the Tournament award. He was then filmed in the dressing room mocking France striker Kylian Mbappe.

Argentina were ultimately slapped with an £18,300 fine but no action was taken against any player. The aftermath of Sunday's World Cup final, in which Spain beat Argentina 1-0 at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium, is still unfolding.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Can Argentina Premier League players have visas revoked after World Cup uproar? READ MORE :

Spain star speaks out on Argentina punishment after World Cup final ends in violent brawl READ MORE :

FIFA has initiated an inquiry into possible rule violations, selecting a prosecutor to review the chaotic scenes that followed the conclusion of Sunday's showpiece.

Angry clashes erupted at the final whistle. Argentine midfielder Leandro Paredes seemingly knocked Eric Garcia to the turf and then grabbed the Spanish defender's throat, before shoving Gavi down moments later, an action that initially earned the Argentine a red card.

View 3 Images Emi Martinez celebrating after the 2022 World Cup final (Image: PA)

‌



That sending-off was subsequently erased from FIFA's official logs, however. The governing body later clarified that no formal punishment was issued to the midfielder in the chaotic post-match period.

Additional turmoil occurred when Nahuel Molina seemingly swung at Rodri during the Spanish star's celebrations, while Argentine coach Roberto Ayala supposedly aimed a punch at Dani Olmo before Garcia intervened to separate them.

An official FIFA statement said: “Following a review of the official match reports for the Spain versus Argentina FIFA World Cup final, and in accordance with article 36 of the FIFA disciplinary code (FDC), the FIFA disciplinary committee has tasked a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to look into possible FDC violations related to the post-match events.

‌



“More information will be released by the FIFA disciplinary committee once the prosecutor has finalised their report.”

View 3 Images Argentina players have been slammed for their behaviour after the final whistle (Image: Getty Images)

Last week, FIFA also announced it is evaluating reports from the semi-final tie with England amid uproar over a Falkland Islands display.

‌



Following their 2-1 victory over Thomas Tuchel’s side, the Argentine squad displayed a banner that stated: 'Las Malvinas son Argentinas', which translates to 'The Falklands are Argentine'.

Players who earn their living in the Premier League, such as Tottenham centre-back Cristian Romero, ex-Spurs playmaker Giovani Lo Celso, and Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez, have been criticised for the politically sensitive stunt and could also face personal penalties for holding up the banner.

Sports.title: FIFA bosses to make billions in profit as research shows World Cup 2026 to bring in nearly £4bn
Sports.content:
FIFA bosses to make billions in profit as research shows World Cup 2026 to bring in nearly £4bn

Brand Finance, the world’s leading brand valuation consultancy, found the tournament generated £45bn in "enterprise value". That came from £2bn in sponsorship, yielding a 22-fold return.

Spain celebrate World Cup triumph with open-top bus parade

FIFA is set to make around £3.8bn ($5.2bn) from the World Cup, according to new research.

‌



Analysis by Brand Finance, the world’s leading brand valuation consultancy, found the tournament generated £45bn in "enterprise value". That came from £2bn in sponsorship, yielding a 22-fold return.

‌



Sponsors also added an estimated £5.3bn to their combined brand value during the tournament, the longest in World Cup history held in the US, Mexico and Canada. The research combined Brand Finance's valuation model with sponsorship modelling across 21 official partners. FIFA was the 'ultimate winner' and projected to generate record revenues across the 2023-26 commercial cycle.

‌



View 2 Images England fans at the World Cup semi-final clash against Argentina (Image: World Cup 2026 News Pool (WCNP))

The people of Gaza watch the World Cup final amid the ruins of their homes READ MORE :

The "FIFA World Cup 2026 brand" was valued at £3.8bn, with sponsorship revenue accounting for £1.4bn. That was the single largest contributor to that value. FIFA's commercial success has been underpinned by expansion.

The 2026 tournament featured 48 teams and 104 matches across 16 host cities. Yet demand from sponsors continued to outpace supply.

‌



Richard Haigh, Global Managing Director at Brand Finance, said: "FIFA has built one of the strongest commercial models in sport. It secures sponsorship revenue upfront, regardless of whether an individual sponsor's campaign ultimately succeeds or falls short.

"Sponsors carry the execution risk, but our analysis suggests many are still generating significant value from the tournament. The more interesting question is what happens next.

View 2 Images Captain Harry Kane thanks the England fans at their semi-final defeat to Argentina (Image: World Cup 2026 News Pool (WCNP))

‌



"FIFA continues to expand the World Cup and its sponsorship programme, with discussions around a 64-team tournament already emerging. Historically, bigger events have risked diluting sponsor value. FIFA appears to have achieved the opposite: every expansion strengthened its commercial proposition.

"A t some point, sponsors will inevitably ask where the ceiling is. For now, however, the data suggests FIFA remains uniquely capable of monetising the world's most valuable sporting platform."

England ended their World Cup campaign in style with a thrilling 6-4 victory over France - and a touching display of sportsmanship at the end of the game. Captain Harry Kane and his side were dignified in victory, a total contrast to Argentina's disgraceful behaviour in the semi-final.

Article continues below

France's Kylian Mbappe, 27, scored twice to become the leading World Cup goalscorer in history with 22 goals. England players did not forget the loyal army of fans who had spent a fortune following the team across the United States.

Goalscorer Ezri Konsa, 28, said they reflected on the semi-final defeat, which had been 'painful'. But he added: "We have a special group with special players. We apologise that we could not go that one step further. We hope that we brought some joy back home and to the fans watching here."

Sports.title: Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony set to be 'tear jerker' as Sir Chris Hoy to play key role
Sports.content:
Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony set to be 'tear jerker' as Sir Chris Hoy to play key role

EXCLUSIVE: A dress rehearsal was held in front of 4,000 volunteers, featuring pipers, musicians and sporting stars. "It was amazing," a source said. "But emotional, many were in tears."

Commonwealth Games: England celebrate before 4x400m disqualification

The opening ceremony for tomorrow's Commonwealth Games has been described as a 'tear jerker' that will pull on the heartstrings of athletes and millions of viewers.

‌



For the first time in Games history, it is taking place indoors, and the details are a closely guarded secret. A dress rehearsal was held on Tuesday in front of 4,000 volunteers, featuring pipers, musicians and sporting stars.

‌



"It was amazing," a source told the Mirror. "It was emotional, many said they were in tears."

‌



Sir Chris Hoy, who has spoken of his heartbreaking cancer diagnosis as he seeks to raise awareness, plays a key role. King Charles is expected to tell the audience about the importance of togetherness in his speech to open the Games.

View 3 Images KT Tunstall is one of the headline acts for the opening ceremony of Glasgow 2026 (Image: Glasgow 2026/PA Wire)

Commonwealth Games 2026 athletes start arriving in Glasgow from around the world READ MORE :

KT Tunstall is headlining the show which takes place from 8pm to 10pm at Glasgow’s OVO Hydro. The 14,300-capacity venue more accustomed to hosting the music stars than international sporting events.

‌



Organisers describe the show as “a creative kaleidoscope and Clyde-built journey packed full of music, humour and Scottish surprise”. The King will formally declare the Games open by reading aloud the message he placed inside the King’s Baton at Buckingham Palace on Commonwealth Day, March 10 last year.

View 3 Images Josh Kerr the new one mile World Record holder promises to be one of the stars of the Games

It has spent the past 500 days travelling to all 74 competing nations and territories, each of which decorated its own version, before being reunited on stage during the Parade of Nations at the opening ceremony. Sporting action gets under way before the ceremony itself, with Bowls and Para Bowls holding an extra session between 9.30am and 4.25pm on Thursday at the Scottish Event Campus.

‌



Scottish musicians Callum Beattie, Nina Nesbitt, Nathan Evans, and duo Saint PHNX. and electronic folk duo Valtos will perform during the Parade of Nations, while Brit Award-winning singer Tom Walker was added to the line-up earlier this month. Around 600 volunteer performers are also taking part in the show.

View 3 Images Simple Minds are playing the Games closing ceremony, with tickets still available (Image: Colin Lane/Liverpool Echo)

For the first time since 1954, the BBC will not broadcast the Commonwealth Games. Channel 5 will also show the entire ceremony live from 8pm, both on television and via 5 Streaming.

‌



It will be followed by daily highlights throughout the Games presented by former Olympic sprinter Jeanette Kwakye. The Games run from July 23 to August 2, with around 3,000 athletes from 74 nations and territories competing across 10 sports at multiple venues in Glasgow.

These include the Scottish Event Campus, Scotstoun Stadium, the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome and Arena, and the Tollcross International Swimming Centre. Sir Chris was on crutches last December and "hobbling about" after breaking a leg in a cycling crash which he described as the "worst" of his life.

Six-time Olympic champion Hoy announced in October 2024 that his cancer is terminal. But the 50-year-old has continued to ride his mountain bike thanks to a "stability period" in his treatment. He stressed that he wanted to continue 'living life and enjoying it'. He described it as his worst accident in 43 years on the bike.

Article continues below

Hoy, whose seven Olympic medals include one silver, is Britain's second-most decorated Olympic athlete behind fellow track cyclist Sir Jason Kenny (seven golds). He also claimed 11 World Championship golds and 34 World Cup titles before retiring in 2013.

Simple Minds headline the closing ceremony, and tickets are still available for that event, and some of the Glasgow 2026 events next week. Fans are encouraged not to miss out and get their hands on their tickets today, available at glasgow2026.com/tickets.

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford can play big part in Man Utd's exciting new era - but MUST change
Sports.content:
In his slightly philosophical social media post, Marcus Rashford hit the nail on the head. After spending quality time with his family and friends, Rashford says he will ‘come back a better version' of himself.

And if there is to be a reconciliation with his employers, Rashford needs to be a better version of himself. That means - when he returns to training with Manchester United - being scrupulously professional at all times.

That means matching the work rate of every other player in a reinvigorated United squad. That means selflessness on and off the field.

That also means working assiduously on aspects of his game that still, at the age of 28, need improving. With Michael Carrick having done so well and now in long-term charge, this feels like the start of a new United era.

‌



Bruno Fernandes commits future to Manchester United despite new contract wait READ MORE :

Man Utd release new 2026/27 away kit with striking blue design READ MORE :

And there is no reason why Rashford cannot be a part of it, if he wants to be. New rules agreed between FIFA and FIFPRO, the global players’ union, mean that clubs can no longer have so-called ‘bomb squads’.

If Rashford stays at United - and his contract runs for another two years - he has to be part of the first-team squad. And what Rashford then has to do is prove he is worth his place in the team. Rashford has a lot to prove, as he himself hinted in that social media post.

The cold, hard fact is that Barcelona did not think it was worth paying £26million for his full-time services. The cold, hard fact is that successive England managers have not fully trusted Rashford.

He had a distinctly mixed World Cup - one that was in keeping with his entire England career. Of his 78 caps, 38 have come from the bench.

‌



View 3 Images Marcus Rashford and Michael Carrick have a good relationship (Image: 2020 Soccrates Images B.V.)

Right now, does Rashford get in Carrick’s first-choice starting XI when everyone is fit? You suspect a lot of United supporters would say no.

Is he, for example, a better option than Bryan Mbeumo? Probably not. But he could be - if his focus was complete, if his work rate was stepped up.

Rashford’s numbers in his loan season at Barcelona looked decent enough. In all competitions, 14 goals and 14 assists. But there must have been something that did not fully convince coach Hansi Flick of his worth.

‌



There must have been something that convinced the Barcelona hierarchy they would be better off spending £70million on Anthony Gordon, who also ended the World Cup as Thomas Tuchel’s preferred option. There was also a clause in Rashford’s contract that allowed other clubs - Manchester City and Liverpool excepted - to buy him for £40million, which expired earlier this month.

View 3 Images Thomas Tuchel ended up preferring Anthony Gordon to Marcus Rashford at the World Cup (Image: Eddie Keogh - The FA, The FA via Getty Images)

As expected, no-one triggered that clause. Those scenarios should provoke Rashford into a reaction.

Right now, it is clear the executives at United - headed by director of football Jason Wilcox - would like Rashford’s £325,000-a-week off the books. But they cannot force him out.

‌



And the bottom line is that any interested club will point to the option price Barcelona had and refuse to pay considerably more than that. For want of a better phrase, United could be stuck with Rashford.

But all the interested parties can make that work. Wilcox, Carrick and, most importantly, Rashford himself. If he is true to his promise and comes back from his holiday as a better version of himself, there is no reason he cannot play a key role in United’s new era.

Sports.title: Phil Foden comments on Enzo Maresca speak volumes as he signs new Man City contract
Sports.content:
Phil Foden admits he is relishing working under new Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca - after signing a new and improved deal at the Etihad.

Foden has put his World Cup heartbreak behind by penning a contract that will keep him at the club until 2030. The 26-year-old is one of the most decorated players in the club's history, having won a staggering 20 major trophies.

And he is targeting even more under former first team coach Maresca, who has returned to replace the great Pep Guardiola in the blue half of Manchester.

Foden, who was left out of the England squad for the World Cup, said: "Committing my future to City means everything to me. Playing for this Club is all I've ever wanted to do and it’s always an honour to wear the shirt. It's not lost on me that I’ve been lucky enough to be part of a historic period with so many titles won.

"But we're always looking to the future and trying to win more.

Bruno Fernandes commits future to Manchester United despite new contract wait READ MORE :

Man Utd and Arsenal locked in £40million transfer battle as duo hold talks over deal READ MORE :

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"I can't wait to work with Enzo again. He was brilliant during the Treble season – someone all the players respected and loved working with.

"To have him back here is exciting. Personally, I know I’ve improved so much from working with our coaches and world-class squad and as many of the legends who were here when I first broke through move on, I am excited for the next phase of my career at this great club."

City director of football Hugo Viana added: "Everyone at Manchester City is incredibly proud of Phil.

"He is a unique talent, and his creativity is a joy to watch. But none of what he has achieved would be possible without the focus, dedication and humility to work hard in every moment and absorb all of the knowledge available to him through our coaches and players.

"Given Phil joined City at the age of nine, his continued success is one that is celebrated in every corner of our club.

"At 26, his development is still ongoing, and we look forward to seeing the player Phil can become over the coming years."

Sports.title: Japan's King George star facing the ‘biggest race of his life’ in £2million Ascot showpiece
Sports.content:
Japan's King George star facing the ‘biggest race of his life’ in £2million Ascot showpiece

Masquerade Ball, pipped by defending champion Calandagan in the Japan Cup last year, has come to Britain to take on the world champion racehorse again

View 4 Images Takahisa Tezuka with Masquerade Ball in Newmarket (Image: Megan Rose Photography)

Japan’s King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes star is facing the ‘biggest race of his life’ in Saturday’s £2 million Ascot showpiece.

‌



Masquerade Ball, pipped by last year’s King George winner Calandagan in the Japan Cup, has come to Britain for a rematch with the world champion racehorse.

‌



He is one of two contenders from Japan with the less heralded Wurttemberg, the mount of Oisin Murphy, also taking his chance. The pair arrived in the UK on July 12 after flying from Tokyo to Amsterdam via Anchorage in Alaska before completing the final leg of the journey by road to Newmarket.

‌



Cheltenham Festival veteran Edwardstone retired after finishing career on a high READ MORE :

Grand National-winner’s training partnership to end as ally announces new venture READ MORE :

Masquerade Ball is set to clash again with defending champion Calandagan after only a head separated the duo in the G1 Japan Cup in November. On his only start this year Masquerade Ball finished second to Romantic Warrior in Hong Kong’s G1 FWD QEII Cup in April.

Trainer Takahisa Tezuka said: “I have taken care of Masquerade Ball this year. He has matured and developed a lot from three to four, not just mentally but physically as well. He is a lot bigger and stronger. I was nervous about the journey over, but everything went smoothly. The horse seems very happy, while his training is going better than I expected.

“The King George is one of the biggest races in the UK – it is a dream to bring him here. We have tried to give him the best preparation, so we hope for the best while also enjoying the experience because it is an honour to be involved.

‌



View 4 Images Masquerade Ball and Wurttemberg working upsides (Image: Megan Rose Photography)

“This race is the biggest of Masquerade Ball’s life so far. Calandagan is not the only horse we have to think about, even though there was only a head between us in the Japan Cup, because there are a lot of other strong competitors. We are looking forward to seeing how much our horse has developed since then.”

Masquerade Ball’s jockey Christophe Lemaire said in April that the colt has the potential to be ‘one of the greats’ of Japanese racing.

‌



Tezuka added: “I was very happy with those comments. Christophe has ridden many great horses, including Equinox, so it was an honour to hear that from such a great jockey.

View 4 Images Calandagan: named best racehorse in the world in 2025 (Image: PA)

“The horse’s owner Mr [Teruya] Yoshida loves Ascot Racecourse and, from last year, pushed me to challenge for this race. The King George rather than the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe is our main reason for bringing Masquerade Ball to Europe.

‌



“In Japan, the racecourses are very flat with no undulations, so Ascot will be a very different challenge. The downhill section could be quite difficult, as it is hard to imitate running downhill [in his training], but I am hopeful that he will be able to overcome this.

“I initially thought that a mile and a quarter was Masquerade Ball’s best distance. However, as time has gone on, I think a mile and a half is more appropriate for him.”

View 4 Images Hiroshi Miyamoto with Wurttemberg (Image: Megan Rose Photography)

‌



Wurttemberg arrives on the back of a career-best second in the G1 Tenno Sho (Spring) over two miles at Kyoto.

His trainer Hiroshi Miyamoto said: “The owner gave me the choice of two races, the King George or the Goodwood Cup. I chose the King George because it is a highly prestigious and honourable race. For me, it is the number one race in the UK.

“Wurttemberg has good stamina, having raced up to distances of 3,600 metres, and I think Ascot’s mile and a half with the undulations should be suitable for him.

Article continues below

“Oisin Murphy is the number one jockey here, so we are excited for him to ride the horse. He knows Ascot very well and we will rely on him.”

Sports.title: Southampton boss Tonda Eckert charged by FA over Spygate saga and could face ban
Sports.content:
Southampton boss Tonda Eckert charged by FA over Spygate saga and could face ban

Southampton were booted out of the Championship play-offs after being caught spying on opponents and their head coach Tonda Eckert is still in hot water with the FA

View 2 Images Tonda Eckert has been charged by the FA (Image: Rich Linley - CameraSport via Getty Images)

Tonda Eckert has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association over the 'Spygate' scandal which rocked the Championship play-offs last season.

‌



Southampton were expelled from the play-offs back in May despite beating Middlesbrough over two legs after a staff member was caught spying on an opponents' training sessions.

‌



The Saints were also given a four-point penalty for the 2026-27 campaign, with Middlesbrough being subsequently reinstated for the play-off final, which was won 1-0 by Hull City at Wembley.

‌



Eckert's position was heavily scrutinised following the fallout from the scandal, with an investigation subsequently being launched into the 33-year-old.

It has now been confirmed that Eckert has been charged with three counts of bringing the game into disrepute after spying was authorised against Middlesbrough, Ipswich Town and Oxford United, leaving his future up in the air.

An FA statement confirming the news on Wednesday read: “It’s alleged that the head coach acted in an improper manner and/or brought the game into disrepute by directing and/or authorising the observation of training sessions of Oxford United FC, Ipswich Town FC and Middlesbrough FC ahead of fixtures between these clubs and Southampton FC in December 2025, April 2026 and May 2026 respectively.”

‌



It remains to be seen what punishment Eckert will be handed, with previous reports indicating that the German could be hit with a ban by the FA. They have the power to punish individuals, with the EFL only able to impose sanctions on clubs.

View 2 Images Southampton were booted out of the play-offs despite beating Middlesbrough over two legs (Image: Robin Jones, Getty Images)

Southampton confirmed that they and Eckert acknowledged the charges in a statement of their own, adding: "Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA.

‌



"Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 Championship season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.

"We are unable to comment further while the process remains ongoing, but we will provide an update to supporters as soon as we are in a position to do so."

Bitter rivals Manchester United and Arsenal are locked in a battle to sign Alex Scott.

‌



The England and Bournemouth midfielder is a target of up to eight clubs this summer. Newcastle United, Tottenham and Everton are also keen on Scott.

‌



But United are Arsenal are now in pole position to land Scott in a £40million deal. It's understood Scott's representatives have held talks with both clubs, and that he will make a decision on his future in the next fortnight.

‌



Scott is said to favour a move to the Emirates, but is worried about how much game time he will get for Mikel Arteta's English champions.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
