World.title: Burnham’s Britain: what kind of country has UK’s new prime minister inherited?
World.content:
Burnham’s Britain: what kind of country has UK’s new prime minister inherited?

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 09:26 UTC Full article

UK will have its seventh prime minister in the ten years since it voted to leave EU. It begs the question: what is it about the UK that makes governing it so difficult at this point in time?

By Ben Wellings, Associate Professor in Politics and International Relations, Monash University - When Andy Burnham was handed the keys to 10 Downing Street on Monday, the United Kingdom will have its seventh prime minister in the ten years since it voted to leave the European Union. It begs the question: what is it about the UK that makes governing it so difficult at this point in time?

At the risk of sounding like a broken record, a large part of the answer is Brexit. But Brexit only expressed and exacerbated some of the structural problems the UK still faces today: cynicism, pessimism and political polarization; uncertain relations with the rest of the world; declining living standards for the poorest in society; a sense of social fragmentation; poorly maintained public services… and England knocked out of the World Cup in the semi-finals.

The last point is not trivial, at least in as much as it draws attention to the structure of the UK. The political elephant in the room is England. Specifically, it is the politics of nationhood in England that Burnham needs to address if Labour is to retain office whenever the next election is called.

England needs practical policies to address social and regional inequalities. Importantly, these policies must support a renewed national narrative that explains England’s place in the UK, and the UK’s place in Europe and the world.

Lest this should be seen as a trivial endeavour, it’s worth remembering that Keir Starmer’s lack of a positive narrative meant his political honeymoon with the electorate was very short.

Furthermore, national narratives need to have some grounding in reality. Boris Johnson’s hyperbolic narratives served as an example of how excessive claims – in this case of restored greatness – can erode trust and increase a sense of distance between the audience and the author of such claims.

Establishing a positive national narrative is no easy task. First, it will have to address some inherent contradictions. England is a diverse but singular entity. Through the UK, it has a relationship with the EU built on a newfound – and for many unwanted – sovereignty. It is a nation that values fairness but is increasingly unequal. And that’s before we get to the fact that the contemporary media environment favors, and at times actively supports, a sense of nationhood based on anger and grievance.

Burnham has a partial answer to the English question: the devolution of decision-making powers to local communities. This is a variation on the “take back control” theme – this time from Westminster rather than the EU.

Whereas Starmer was identified as being from southern England (despite being born in Yorkshire) because he supported Arsenal and had “Sir” in front of his name, Burnham wears his northern Englishness on his sleeve. His “Manchesterism” draws on the cooperative traditions of that part of England and inclines him towards greater state intervention in the economy – which will no doubt be resisted in some bastions of London’s financial district, and by tech giants.

So when some people talk about Burnham as the “king of the North”, or when he says he will establish a “Number 10 North” to bring policy focus to places like his Greater Manchester constituency of Makerfield, the “north” we are talking about is not Scotland. It is implicitly the north of England. This is where the next election will be won and lost as Labour confronts the radical right insurgent party Reform UK.

As in Australia with support from One Nation, there is a deep well of pessimism, anger and anxiety that has been exacerbated by the post-pandemic pressure on living costs. In the UK, these pressures compounded existing hardships caused by the imposition of austerity measures and the slow, deflating effects of Brexit on the UK economy.

But this politics of pessimism plays out in the UK’s peculiar structure. It’s worth remembering how unusual the UK is as a nation-state – if indeed we can use that term to describe it. It is comprised of (at least) four different nations. It is not a federation, but an asymmetrically devolved union that retains atypical levels of centralized governmental control.

What used to be an electorate fairly evenly divided between the Conservatives and Labour has now become fragmented between seven different parties across its many devolved jurisdictions with different voting systems. In Scotland and Wales, notionally secessionist parties govern. The government of Northern Ireland is led by a party that claims it wants to reunite Ireland. In England, British nativism is mobilized by the radical and far-right.

It is in this difficult context that Burnham needs to find a narrative for his government that links government policies with “Labour values” and speaks directly to England as a political community. Labour governments tend to be short, but with long-lasting impacts. This suggests a bold policy agenda rather than Starmer-like managerialism. Plans to re-nationalize failing privatized water utilities would be a good place to get some early runs on the board and signal that market-based solutions have their limitations.

As English football fans know, it’s the hope that kills you. Hope among Labour supporters is again high, but it may be the UK’s structural problems run too deep for a change of manager to alter their course. This may make Burnham’s main political task – defeating Reform with its transnational crypto currency financial support – harder.

At least over the summer Burnham and Labour can enjoy the political farce of Nigel Farage scoring an own goal in a self-called by-election in his seaside constituency of Clacton.

Farage resigned as MP for Clacton to defer parliamentary judgement on huge crypto donations from outside the UK. All other parties sensed the trap and declined to field candidates, leaving novelty candidate Count Binface as Farage’s sole challenger. A Binface victory would be a win for the ages.

No one said the English don’t have a sense of humor. (The Conversation)

World.title: PM Burnham first day in office “welcomed” by Russian navy live fire gunnery in the Channel south of Plymouth
World.content:
PM Burnham first day in office “welcomed” by Russian navy live fire gunnery in the Channel south of Plymouth

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 09:15 UTC Full article

Outgunned but unperturbed… HMS Tyne inbound to Devonport on the evening of 20th July after the incident (Photo: Kevin Kelway / Westward Shipping).

In what appears to have been a calculated show of military presence close to the UK, the Russian Navy marked the first full day of Andy Burnham’s premiership by conducting a live-fire gunnery exercise in the English Channel while under close surveillance from the Royal Navy.

The Baltic Fleet frigate RFS Neustrashimy carried out the exercise on Monday 20 July around 40 nautical miles south of Plymouth while being shadowed by HMS Tyne. The drill took place in international waters but within one of the world’s busiest commercial shipping lanes.

The BBC reports the Russian frigate warned OPV HMS Tyne before commencing the firing serial. The exercise reportedly lasted around 30 minutes. An MoD spokesperson confirmed that: “The Royal Navy monitored that exercise throughout, continues to track the vessel’s activity closely, and stands ready to protect UK national security.”

While Russian naval transits through the English Channel are routinely shadowed by RN vessels, live-fire exercises in such close proximity to the UK are rare. Conducting one in the congested waters of the Channel serves as a reminder that Moscow remains willing to use military activity close to NATO territory as a strategic signal, even if fully within the bounds of international law.

There is no official suggestion the exercise was directly linked to the change of government, but the timing is striking. It came as the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, entered Downing Street and Wes Streeting took over as Defense Secretary, inheriting a department facing increasing pressure from an assertive Russia, continued support for Ukraine and growing demands to strengthen the Armed Forces.

According to navyoutlook.com, the 3,500-ton RFS Neustrashimy, commissioned in 1993, is armed with a 100 mm main gun, anti-ship missiles, torpedoes and close-in weapon systems. It is believed she was recently fitted with the PEROED-M counter-drone electronic jamming system. She was observed transiting the Danish Straits on 3rd July after leaving the Baltic Sea on and appears to have assumed Russia’s Channel patrol mission following the departure of the frigate RFS Admiral Grigorovich, which spent around three months operating around the English Channel before returning to Baltiysk in Kaliningrad last week.

A Sky News helicopter filmed RFS Neustrashimy receiving supplies from the PM-82 floating workshop in the North Sea, in international waters off Clacton on 11th July.

RAF Typhoons and a supporting Voyager tanker were observed operating over the Channel in the vicinity of the Russian frigate during the exercise. A French maritime patrol aircraft was also reported to have been monitoring the vessel.

World.title: Chancellor Healey pledges “UK will meet defense commitments to our allies”
World.content:
Chancellor Healey pledges “UK will meet defense commitments to our allies”

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 09:01 UTC Full article

Mr Healey said in his resignation speech that Britain should not let down its Nato allies on defense spending as “our adversaries do not follow timetables set by the Treasury”

Former British Defence Secretary John Healey, who resigned under Sir Keir Starmer in a row over military funding, is now in charge at the Treasury. Prime Minister Andy Burnham appointed him as Chancellor in a surprise move as he named his new top team.

Mr. Healey came out of the starting blocks pledging that the UK “will meet our commitments on defence to our international allies”.

When he resigned as defense secretary last month, Mr Healey hit out at the Treasury for not stumping up the £28 billion military chiefs believed were needed for the defense investment plan (DIP)

At the time, he said he was “certain” that Britain should be spending 3% of GDP on defense by the year 2030, and warned the actual commitment fell far short of this.

Mr Healey wrote in his resignation letter that extra funding in the DIP would only see defense spending rise to 2.68% by the end of the decade, and expressed frustration with Sir Keir Starmer for not setting a clear timetable to reach 3%.

The Nato military alliance has meanwhile tasked all member states with spending 3.5% of GDP on their core defense spending by 2035, in preparation for the growing threat from Russia.

Support from former head of the Army

General Lord Dannatt, who was Chief of the General Staff from 2006 to 2009, said it was a “masterstroke” by Mr Burnham to put Mr Healey in as Chancellor. Speaking to Times Radio, the former head of the Army said there is “no one that knows better than John Healey just what defense needs”.

“It's very much a poacher turned gamekeeper, and physician heal thyself,” he continued.

“If John Healey is going to be true to himself, knowing exactly what the defense budget needs, he's going to have to work very cleverly and very carefully at finding ways of raising more money. ”He is the one behind the desk in Number 11, and has really got to answer his own question.“

Mr Healey said in his resignation speech that Britain should not let down its Nato allies on defence spending as ”our adversaries do not follow timetables set by the Treasury“

The new Chancellor was asked by broadcasters on Monday night if welfare cuts or new taxes could be introduced to meet the 3% of GDP goal by 2030.

He replied: ”Fiscal control is the first duty of any Chancellor. It is mine. And fiscal credibility is the bedrock for economic stability and for national security.

“You heard the Prime Minister this afternoon say, in this more dangerous world, we will meet our commitments on defence to our international allies.”

In one of his first acts as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham announced an £850 million tax cut on energy bills in a bid to tackle the cost of living crisis. This means from October 1 of this year, energy bills will be VAT-free.

According to the government, Forces families will benefit from the saving, which is estimated to amount to £45. (Forces)

World.title: US readies tariffs on some 60 economies over forced labor, with Argentina among them
World.content:
US readies tariffs on some 60 economies over forced labor, with Argentina among them

22nd Wednesday, July 2026 - 07:18 UTC Full article

The proposal, put forward by Greer's office in June following an investigation launched in March, contemplates two tiers

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said his government will announce new tariffs on some 60 economies in the coming days for failing to enforce bans on the import of goods produced with forced labor. “The US has laws to prohibit trading goods with forced labor. Other countries, most of them, don't have a law, and those that do really don't enforce it,” he said on Tuesday in an interview with CNBC.

The levies would be applied under Section 301 of the 1974 trade law and are intended to replace the temporary 10% global tariff that President Donald Trump imposed in February, invoking Section 122, after the Supreme Court struck down his “reciprocal” tariffs on the grounds that he had exceeded his powers. That temporary levy expires on Friday unless Congress extends it, which is not considered likely. Unlike the invalidated route, Section 301 sets no rate caps or expiration dates.

The proposal, put forward by Greer's office in June following an investigation launched in March, contemplates two tiers. A 10% tariff for sixteen economies that have adopted or committed to adopting bans on such imports — among them Canada, the European Union, Mexico, the United Kingdom, Taiwan, Argentina, and El Salvador — and 12.5% for the remaining 44, including Japan, India, South Korea, Singapore, and Vietnam. Together, the targeted economies account for about 99% of US imports. Goods complying with the North American trade agreement would be exempt in the cases of Canada and Mexico.

The measures are not yet in force: the trade office continues to receive public comments following a hearing held on July 7, and Greer did not specify when they would take effect, noting that he must inform Congress and the parties involved. Canada's government has already rejected the initiative, arguing that its legislation against forced labor in supply chains should exempt it from new levies.

The new rates add to other recent trade actions under the same legal instrument. The 25% tariffs on most Brazilian products, announced last week, take effect on Wednesday. On Monday, Trump also signed proclamations to impose additional 50% tariffs in 30 days on a range of Canadian goods, citing trade discrimination against US industries such as automobiles, alcoholic beverages, and dairy. The president had previously threatened tariffs on Canada over the wildfire smoke that affected the US East Coast.

World.title: Baseless conspiracy theories about Argentina's defeat go viral and are debunked
World.content:
Baseless conspiracy theories about Argentina's defeat go viral and are debunked

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:34 UTC Full article

The coach attributed the defeat to the opponent's performance: “We lost because they played better, it's good to acknowledge that.”

In the hours after Argentina's 1-0 defeat to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final, social media filled with posts claiming, without offering evidence, that the result was “fixed.” Fact-checkers and Argentina's own coach, Lionel Scaloni, moved to dismiss those versions.

The narratives, spread on X, TikTok, Facebook, and YouTube, attribute the loss to alleged pressures or hidden interests. Among the most repeated are a supposed FIFA-UEFA deal to crown Spain, an alleged “punishment” over the banner reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” that players displayed after knocking out England, and purported threats to the footballers. None of those claims rested on documents, identifiable testimony, or formal complaints, as verification organizations such as Argentina's Chequeado and Spain's Maldita.es confirmed.

One of the most widely shared items was a video of Lionel Messi's team talk before the match, in which he is heard saying “let's forget everything,” a phrase some users read as a supposed sign of outside pressure. In its full context, the captain was urging his teammates to focus on the game.

Scaloni rejected the speculation when asked by reporters. “I don't look at social media, I don't know anything,” he said, dismissing both an internal squad conflict and a supposed surprise anti-doping test before the match. On the banner, he said FIFA had told them nothing. The coach attributed the defeat to the opponent's performance: “We lost because they played better, it's good to acknowledge that.” The course of the match supported that reading: Argentina did not have a shot on target across the 120 minutes. Spain's ambassador to Argentina, Joaquín María de Arístegui, also rejected the notion of a fix, attributing it to the champions' game plan.

The phenomenon was not new at this World Cup. During the tournament, opposing narratives circulated accusing FIFA of favoring Argentina through refereeing or VAR, which fact-checkers also found baseless. After the final, the story reversed.

Disinformation specialists explain that conspiracy theories tend to grow after emotionally charged events, because they offer simple explanations for complex facts. According to a report by Chequeado, Africa Check, and Full Fact, such narratives attribute events to the secret action of powerful groups and reinforce group identity by avoiding the need to review one's own performance. Major sporting events, which draw millions and stir intense emotions, provide fertile ground for their spread. Fact-checkers recommend being wary of extraordinary explanations without evidence and checking the source of information before sharing it.

World.title: US reacts to Ortega's announcement that Nicaragua will hold no more elections
World.content:
US reacts to Ortega's announcement that Nicaragua will hold no more elections

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:23 UTC Full article

“Daniel Ortega's declaration that under his family's dictatorship Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature,” Rubio said

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Tuesday that his country “will not stand idly by” after Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced that the country will no longer hold elections. In a State Department statement, Rubio called on the international community to “join forces” to respond to what he described as the Nicaraguan government's attacks on the democratic principles of the hemisphere.

Ortega made the announcement on Sunday, during the commemoration of the 47th anniversary of the 1979 Sandinista Revolution, in which he took part in the overthrow of the Anastasio Somoza dictatorship. “There won't be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and power,” he said, in his first public appearance in two months. The 80-year-old president added that he would work with the National Assembly, which he controls, to pass laws barring opposition parties from reaching power through the ballot box. He did not specify how the measure would be formally implemented.

The announcement effectively cancels the elections scheduled for November 2027, after a constitutional reform approved in January 2025 extended the presidential term from five to six years and designated Ortega's wife, Rosario Murillo, as “co-president.” The two exercise control over nearly all branches of the state, including the armed forces, the police, and the judiciary.

“Daniel Ortega's declaration that under his family's dictatorship Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature,” Rubio said in the statement, titled “A Call to Action.” The text added that the Ortega and Murillo government “cannot expect to maintain business as usual with other nations” while undermining the region's democratic foundations. Rubio, who has placed Latin America among his priorities, had already described the Nicaraguan government as a “dictatorship” in June.

The United States, which does not recognize Ortega's presidency, has imposed sanctions and visa restrictions on more than 2,350 Nicaraguan officials and their relatives in recent years. It is unclear whether Rubio's warning will be followed by new pressure measures.

The last election, in 2021, was deemed illegitimate by international observers and by Washington, after Ortega jailed the main opposition candidates; he then claimed about 76% of the vote. Since the 2018 crisis, in which a crackdown on protests left hundreds dead, much of Nicaragua's opposition is in exile or barred from office. In early July, UN experts denounced the mass revocation of lawyers' licenses in the country.

World.title: Conmebol presses FIFA for a 64-team 2030 World Cup and more matches in South America
World.content:
Conmebol presses FIFA for a 64-team 2030 World Cup and more matches in South America

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:08 UTC Full article

The proposal, originally presented by Uruguay's Ignacio Alonso to the FIFA Council in March 2025 and taken up by Domínguez, faces strong opposition

The South American Football Confederation (Conmebol) has stepped up its pressure on FIFA for the 2030 World Cup to be played with 64 teams, which would allow Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay to host more matches than currently planned. A day after the 2026 World Cup final, won by Spain, the body's president, Alejandro Domínguez, treated the format as all but settled in a message on the social network X: “In 2030 the World Cup is coming to Uruguay, Argentina, and Paraguay,” he wrote, proposing to mark the centenary “with a 64-team competition.”

FIFA has not confirmed the expansion. Its president, Gianni Infantino, said the matter “will be examined and discussed in the relevant committees” once the 2026 tournament — the first with 48 teams, up from 32 in previous editions — concludes. A 64-team World Cup would mean 128 matches, double the format in place between 1998 and 2022. The final decision rests with the FIFA Council, made up of representatives of the six confederations.

The proposal, originally presented by Uruguay's Ignacio Alonso to the FIFA Council in March 2025 and taken up by Domínguez, faces strong opposition. The presidents of UEFA, Aleksander Čeferin, of Concacaf, Victor Montagliani, and of the Asian confederation, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, came out against it. Čeferin called it “a bad idea,” and critics warn that a tournament of that size would weaken the quality of play, devalue the qualifiers, and overload the calendar. The 2030 World Cup will already be the most sprawling in history, split among six countries across three continents: the opening matches will be played in South America, marking the centenary of the tournament born in Montevideo in 1930, and the rest in Spain, Portugal, and Morocco.

For South America, the expansion carries a strong sporting incentive: it would guarantee direct qualification for all ten Conmebol nations, including Venezuela, the only one never to have played a World Cup. In Uruguay, the economic dimension is central. According to the weekly Búsqueda, Yamandú Orsi's government told the Uruguayan Football Association that the viability of public investment and possible international financing lines depends on the Centenario Stadium hosting more than one match.

Domínguez has made the demand a fixture of his public appearances. At Conmebol's congress in Quito in April, he placed a captain's armband on Infantino and invoked the centenary to request an exceptional 64-team format, in a staged gesture he closed by announcing South American backing for Infantino's reelection in 2027. The FIFA president, who has promoted larger tournaments during his tenure, initially supported the idea but later declined to comment.

World.title: Falklands Assembly congratulates Burnham and looks to continuity with London
World.content:
Falklands Assembly congratulates Burnham and looks to continuity with London

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 21:01 UTC Full article

The Assembly reaffirmed the principle that, it said, has been and will remain the foundation of its bond with the United Kingdom

The Falklands Legislative Assembly congratulated the United Kingdom's new prime minister, Labour's Andy Burnham, and expressed confidence in the continuity of the relationship between the islands and London, in an official statement issued on Tuesday. The territory's legislative body said it looks forward to working with the new prime minister and his government, and to “continuing the close and productive relationship” between the two sides.

In the text, the Assembly's members also thanked Keir Starmer for his support of the islands during his tenure as prime minister. Starmer left office on Monday, replaced by Burnham after resigning the Labour Party leadership, without a general election.

The Assembly reaffirmed the principle that, it said, has been and will remain the foundation of its bond with the United Kingdom: the democratic wishes of the Falklands people. “We are confident that that principle will continue to guide the new government,” the statement said, also expressing the wish that Burnham have the opportunity to visit the archipelago during his term.

The statement comes at a moment of transition in London. Burnham's new government placed British foreign policy — including the position on the Falklands — in the hands of Chancellor Ed Miliband, appointed foreign secretary. Under the current arrangement, the United Kingdom retains responsibility for the territory's defense and foreign affairs, while the Assembly administers internal matters.

Successive British governments have maintained that the sovereignty of the islands is not open to discussion as long as their inhabitants wish to remain a British overseas territory, a position London reiterates at the United Nations. That principle rests on the 2013 referendum, in which, on a turnout above 90%, 1,513 of 1,517 voters chose to keep the current status.

Argentina, for its part, maintains its sovereignty claim over the archipelago, located about 300 kilometers off its coast, and has on various occasions called for reopening negotiations. President Javier Milei has reiterated that his country will seek to recover the islands through diplomacy.

The Assembly's statement follows a week of tension over the issue, after Argentine players displayed a banner about the Falklands following the World Cup semifinal against England, an episode that prompted a protest from the outgoing British government and FIFA's assessment of possible sanctions. The relationship between the islands and the United Kingdom now awaits the first signals from Burnham's government on South Atlantic policy.

World.title: Archaeologists Exhume Nearly 3,000-Year-Old Remains Near San Salvador
World.content:
Archaeologists exhumed human remains estimated to be nearly 3,000 years old on the outskirts of San Salvador, the Ministry of Culture said in a statement. The remains form part of a pre-Hispanic burial discovered at the Pasaje 4 archaeological site in Antiguo Cuscatlán, a district in the metropolitan area of San Salvador (municipality of La Libertad Este). Officials estimate the remains date to around 850 B.C.

The burial also contained a small Usulután-style ceramic vessel shaped like a sea turtle. Excavators additionally uncovered two ancient cassava (yuca) cultivation furrows preserved beneath layers of volcanic ash from eruptions in different periods — one associated with the Plan de la Laguna eruption around 850 B.C. and another linked to the Ilopango Caldera eruption between approximately 431 and 539 A.D.

The human remains were found face down (in a prone position, oriented about 17 degrees east of north). They will undergo radiocarbon testing to confirm their exact age. DNA analysis will also be conducted to help determine the individual’s sex and other biological details. Archaeologist Carlos Flores Manzano, a doctoral candidate at Yale University who directed the excavation under the supervision of the National Directorate of Cultural Heritage, noted that the burial appears to have been prepared before the volcanic event rather than resulting from it.

According to the official report, the area may hold a similar number of remains to those found at Structure E3-7 at the Chalchuapa archaeological site in western El Salvador. There, salvage excavations in 1977–1978 recovered the remains of 33 individuals, widely interpreted as evidence of human sacrifice and among the earliest such documented cases in the Mesoamerican region.

That assemblage included 26 complete skeletons, four partial skeletons, and three isolated skulls. Many were found face down; some showed signs that hands or feet had been bound or were absent, along with evidence of mutilation and decapitation. The individuals whose sex could be determined were adult males, and researchers have suggested they may have been war captives.

The Antiguo Cuscatlán finds build on earlier archaeological work in the same zone, including a 1987 rescue excavation by Paul Amaroli and Gregorio Bello-Suazo. Further laboratory analysis of the newly recovered remains and associated materials is expected to refine the dating and provide additional insight into pre-Hispanic occupation and agricultural practices in the region prior to major volcanic events.

World.title: Costa Rica Faces a Proposed 12.5 Percent US Tariff
World.content:
Costa Rica is among 60 economies that the United States has targeted for new tariffs tied to a federal investigation into forced labor in global supply chains, and formal announcements could come within days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer signaled on Tuesday that the measures are nearing completion.

Greer described the pending action during a televised interview, casting it as a response to trading partners that, in Washington’s assessment, have failed to keep goods produced with forced labor out of their own markets and, by extension, out of the United States.

The proposal sorts the 60 economies into two tariff tiers. The Office of the US Trade Representative determined that the large majority had neither established nor effectively enforced a legal prohibition on importing forced-labor goods, and it proposed a 12.5 percent rate for that group, which includes Costa Rica. A smaller set of economies that maintain at least a partial ban but that Washington considers to enforce it inadequately, among them Canada, Ecuador, the European Union, Indonesia, Mexico, and Pakistan, would instead face a 10 percent rate.

For Costa Rican exporters, the more consequential detail is what the new tariff would replace. Costa Rican goods currently enter the United States under a temporary 10 percent duty the Trump administration imposed in February, after the US Supreme Court struck down an earlier round of tariffs the administration had sought to justify under a separate legal authority.

That temporary duty is scheduled to lapse on July 24. The Costa Rican Ministry of Foreign Trade, known as Comex, has stated that the proposed 12.5 percent rate would substitute for the expiring 10 percent rather than stack on top of it, although earlier US filings were read by some analysts as implying a combined burden nearer 22.5 percent, a discrepancy that remains unresolved pending the final notice.

The stakes are considerable given how much Costa Rica sells northward. The United States is our single largest trading partner, absorbing roughly 47 percent of all national goods exports in 2025, a total Comex has valued at about $10.8 billion.

The investigation has advanced rapidly. USTR opened the proceedings on March 12 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the same statute Washington has invoked to answer what it regards as unfair trade practices in other disputes. The process included consultations with the governments involved, public hearings in Washington in late April, and a comment period that drew hundreds of written submissions before USTR published its findings in early June.

Costa Rica has already lodged its objection. On July 6, the final day of the public comment period, Comex Minister Indiana Trejos submitted the country’s formal defense, asking Washington to exclude Costa Rican products and to preserve the zero-tariff access negotiated under CAFTA-DR, the free trade agreement linking the United States, Central America, and the Dominican Republic.

Trejos argued that the investigation had produced no evidence that Costa Rican exports are made with forced labor, and she framed the country’s manufacturers as reinforcing rather than displacing US production through integrated regional supply chains. The submission was prepared in coordination with business chambers, industry associations, and individual companies, which had pressed the government to mount a joint public and private response and to build a technical case for exemptions.

Costa Rica is not the only economy in the region caught up in the review. Several other Latin American countries appear on the list, including its Central American neighbors Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, alongside larger economies such as Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, Chile, and Mexico. Costa Rica’s exposure comes despite a relatively favorable standing on international measures of the problem, where it ranks among the lowest-risk economies in Latin America.

The forced-labor tariffs are also arriving amid a broader run of US trade actions against individual countries. Brazil was hit last Thursday with a 25 percent tariff on a range of products, and Washington has signaled further country-specific measures in recent days. With the July 24 expiry of the current duty now approaching and formal announcements expected imminently, the window for Costa Rican exporters and trade officials to press their case is narrowing.

World.title: US Issues Chikungunya Alert for Costa Rica Travelers
World.content:
If you are heading to Guanacaste this month, pack insect repellent and treat mosquito bites as a real risk rather than a minor annoyance. The U.S. Embassy in San José has told American travelers to take active precautions against chikungunya after health officials confirmed the mosquito-borne virus is now spreading within the local mosquito population along part of the province’s coast.

The warning, issued on July 13, centers on Playa Langosta and the wider Santa Cruz area — the same beach community near Tamarindo where Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health declared an outbreak on July 1. Of 45 suspected cases investigated at that point, four were laboratory-confirmed and 17 were classified as probable, and those infected included both Costa Ricans and foreign visitors.

What has changed since then is the scale. The Health Ministry’s most recent count puts the national total at 21 chikungunya cases for 2026, up from the 16 reported when the embassy first published its alert. Cases have also been recorded beyond the Guanacaste coast, including in parts of the Central Valley — a shift that widens the map of where an infected mosquito could bite you.

The phrase health officials keep using is “local transmission,” and it is worth understanding what it means for your trip. It signals that the virus is now circulating among mosquitoes living in the area, not simply arriving in the bloodstream of travelers who caught it elsewhere. In practical terms, that raises the odds of being bitten by an infected mosquito while you are on the ground, which is exactly why the embassy stopped short of a routine reminder and issued a formal health alert.

Chikungunya spreads through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the same insect behind dengue and Zika. Symptoms usually appear four to eight days after a bite and hit fast: a sudden high fever above 39°C (102°F), severe joint pain and swelling, headache, nausea, and a general wiped-out feeling. Most people recover within one to two weeks, but the joint pain can linger for weeks or months, and it is more than enough to confine you to your hotel room for the rest of a vacation. There is no vaccine in routine use for travelers, so avoiding bites is your only real defense.

That defense is straightforward. Use an EPA-registered repellent containing DEET, picaridin, or IR3535, and if you are also wearing sunscreen, put the sunscreen on first and the repellent second. Cover up with long sleeves and pants where the heat allows, and spend downtime in air-conditioned or properly screened rooms. Around your rental or hotel, tip out anything holding standing water — buckets, plant saucers, uncovered containers — because Aedes mosquitoes breed in surprisingly small amounts of still water close to where people sleep. If you develop symptoms during your trip or in the days after you fly home, see a doctor and mention that you were in Guanacaste.

The U.S. warning followed a matching move from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which updated its Costa Rica travel notice to Level 2, “Practice Enhanced Precautions,” on July 16. The CDC advises pregnant travelers to avoid the affected area entirely, noting that newborns infected with chikungunya face a risk of severe illness.

Costa Rican authorities say containment work is ongoing. In the Playa Langosta area alone, crews have fumigated roughly 5,000 homes with specialized equipment and carried out targeted interventions at 638 properties, including inspections and the removal of mosquito breeding sites.

The Ministry of Health has urged residents and visitors across Guanacaste and neighboring communities to reinforce the same precautions the embassy is now echoing to Americans. None of this makes Guanacaste off-limits — the coast remains one of the country’s busiest tourist regions — but it does mean a bottle of repellent belongs in your beach bag this season.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Wins First UTS Tournament in South America
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima claimed the title at the Ultimate Tennis Showdown’s first tournament in South America, defeating 17-year-old Brazilian Guto Miguel in a tightly contested final at Rio de Janeiro’s Maracanãzinho arena. The American completed a remarkable turnaround by beating Miguel 3-0 on Saturday, July 18, with quarter scores of 15-14, 17-14 and 15-13. Although the score appeared one-sided under the UTS system, all three quarters were decided by three points or fewer.

Nakashima earned $368,800 for winning UTS Rio, which was also his first appearance in the alternative tennis competition. “It was a great couple of days here,” Nakashima said after the final. “I really enjoyed my first experience here in Brazil and first UTS experience.” His path to the championship was far from straightforward. Nakashima opened the tournament with a 3-1 victory over top seed Francisco Cerúndolo before losing 3-2 to Miguel in Sudden Death during the round-robin stage.

The loss left Nakashima relying on quarter and point differentials to reach the semifinals as the fourth qualifier. Once there, he produced one of his best performances of the tournament, recovering from the loss of the opening quarter to defeat Nick Kyrgios 3-1. Nakashima won the final three quarters against Kyrgios by scores of 20-10, 17-12 and 20-10, ending the Australian’s bid for his first UTS title.

Miguel provided the tournament’s biggest surprise. The Brazilian teenager defeated Kyrgios, Nakashima and Cerúndolo during his run to the final, winning all three matches in Sudden Death. Miguel entered the event as a late replacement for Ugo Humbert but quickly became one of the central figures of the three-day competition.

He began by stunning Kyrgios 3-2, winning the first two quarters before surviving the Australian’s comeback. Miguel then defeated Nakashima by the same score and overcame Cerúndolo 3-2 in the semifinals after losing the opening quarter 23-11. Miguel had already enjoyed a breakthrough season after becoming the first Brazilian-born player to win the boys’ singles title at Roland Garros.

His victories over three established professionals in Rio offered another indication of his potential, even though Nakashima’s consistency proved too much in the final. Brazilian fans had initially expected João Fonseca to lead the home challenge. Fonseca defeated Tallon Griekspoor 3-1 in his UTS debut but was eliminated after Kyrgios swept him 3-0 in only 37 minutes.

Fonseca, Kyrgios and several other players finished the round-robin stage with one victory, leaving quarter and point differentials to determine the four semifinalists. Fonseca later defeated Corentin Moutet 3-1 in a classification match to finish sixth. Cerúndolo also recovered from an opening defeat, beating Cameron Norrie 3-0 to qualify for the semifinals. The Argentine eventually finished third after his Sudden Death loss to Miguel.

UTS Rio was held from July 16 through July 18 on an indoor hard court at the 11,000-seat Maracanãzinho. It marked the tour’s first appearance in South America and the second event of its 2026 season after an April tournament in Nîmes, France. The distinction is important: UTS had already staged an event in Latin America when Guadalajara, Mexico, hosted a tournament in 2025. Rio was the competition’s first stop on the South American continent.

Created by coach Patrick Mouratoglou, UTS replaces traditional games and sets with eight-minute quarters. The first player to win three quarters takes the match, while a 2-2 tie leads to Sudden Death, where a player must win two consecutive points. Players receive only one serve, fans may make noise during points and each competitor can use a bonus card that makes the next point worth three.

Rio also introduced a single eight-player round-robin table, with each player facing two opponents before the top four advanced to the semifinals. The event ultimately produced two significant results for UTS: a debut title for Nakashima and a breakthrough week for one of Brazil’s most promising teenagers.

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Says She Faces Nine Threats, One Involving a Sniper
World.content:
President Laura Fernández said yesterday that she has received information about roughly nine alleged plans to attack her, including one she described as involving a sniper, and that the reports have been passed to prosecutors for investigation. She made the statements at a press conference following a meeting of the National Security Council at Casa Presidencial, adding that she had not spoken about the matter publicly before because she considered the information sensitive and confidential.

According to Fernández, the roughly nine threats are directed at her physical safety and, in some cases, extend to members of her cabinet and her family. She said the intelligence behind them came for the most part from police and prison sources, and that the files had already been referred to the Ministerio Público, our prosecutorial authority. She said she intends to request a written account of how far those investigations have advanced. No supporting evidence for any of the alleged plots has been made public, and none of the claims has been independently confirmed.

Fernández presented the disclosures as part of a wider push on security policy, and she used the same appearance to criticize the leadership of the Judicial Branch, whose senior figures did not attend the council meeting. She described their absence as a “tantrum” and a slight against Costa Ricans, said she could formally denounce them, and indicated she wants the council to convene at least once every two months. She said the meeting had also covered the progress of security legislation and the effectiveness of the courts.

The president spoke without offering documentation, names, or details that would allow the alleged plots to be assessed by anyone outside the government. She said the protocols governing her own protection and that of her ministers were already known, and that the aim now was to confirm what prosecutors had done with the cases already referred to them.

The claims arrive against a backdrop of earlier, similarly unproven security scares surrounding the presidency. Fernández took office in May, succeeding her political mentor, Rodrigo Chaves, whose government announced in January that it had uncovered an alleged plot against the then-president; authorities never produced concrete evidence in that instance.

In June, Fernández was evacuated during an explosion while touring an area of illegal mining in the country’s interior, and in the days before that the government said it had received information about an alleged plan said to be taking shape inside a prison. As with those episodes, the accounts released yestarday rest at this stage on the government’s own characterization rather than on any publicly verifiable proof.

For now, the matter sits with the Ministerio Público, and any determination about whether the reported threats amount to credible plots will depend on the outcome of that review. Fernández, for her part, signaled that she does not intend to alter her public schedule, saying she would continue in the role regardless of who might wish her harm.

World.title: Belize City Council celebrates 2 years of eBuses!
World.content:
Belize City Council celebrates 2 years of eBuses!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize City Council is celebrating the second anniversary of its eRide Project, which introduced electric buses to Belize City.

The Belize City Council says that more than 370,000 rides were completed over the past two years.

“The eRide Project represents a major step forward in the Council’s efforts to provide sustainable, people-centred transportation and build a cleaner, more climate-resilient Belize City.

Your Belize City Council remains committed to modern solutions that improve mobility, protect our environment and serve our people,” the council said.

World.title: Belmopan City Council, CET and partners host motorcycle repair training in Belmopan
World.content:
Belmopan City Council, CET and partners host motorcycle repair training in Belmopan

By Zoila Palma: The Belmopan City Council hosted a completion ceremony for participants who completed the Motorcycle Repair Training Program.

The program was implemented by the Belmopan City Council in collaboration with the Government of Venezuela and Cayo Centre for Employment Training.

“Your enthusiasm, dedication, and commitment to learning have made this journey a success. We wish you all the best as you put your new skills into practice and embrace new opportunities as we continue to Move Belmopan Forward,” the Belmopan City Council expressed.

World.title: International News: Panama, China renew Maritime shipping agreement
World.content:
International News: Panama, China renew Maritime shipping agreement

By Zoila Palma: Panama and China have reached an agreement to renew a maritime shipping treaty that provides preferential treatment for Panamanian-flagged vessels operating in Chinese ports.

The agreement follows concerns raised by Panama over increased inspections and tighter controls on its ships in China, AFP reports.

The Panamanian Foreign Ministry said Monday that, following negotiations in Beijing last week, the two countries had “reached a consensus” and would move forward with procedures to renew the agreement, which is set to expire later this year. The pact provides preferential tariffs and streamlined bureaucratic procedures for Panamanian vessels.

Local media reports indicated that nearly 500 Panamanian-flagged vessels were detained for inspections in China in 2026.

Acting Foreign Minister Carlos Hoyos said Monday that the number of inspections has since returned to “historical levels,” following discussions between the two governments.

Tensions increased after a Panamanian court cancelled the concession held by Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison, to operate two ports at the Panama Canal.

World.title: International News: Hegseth estimates U.S. war with Iran has cost $37.5 billion
World.content:
International News: Hegseth estimates U.S. war with Iran has cost $37.5 billion

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has estimated that the war with Iran has cost the United States $37.5 billion so far, as Republicans prepare a $95 billion funding package to support the military and other priorities of the Trump administration.

Hegseth made the disclosure Tuesday during a heated Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, where protesters repeatedly interrupted his opening remarks, American Press reports.

The hearing came days after the Pentagon announced that three additional U.S. service members had died in the conflict, bringing the American death toll to 17, while more than 100 others have been injured since early July.

Hegseth described the proposed funding as an “urgent, necessary” injection of money, warning that the military could face critical shortfalls without it.

Democrats, however, sharply criticized the administration’s handling of the conflict.

The funding request comes amid growing public concern over the conflict, rising gas prices linked to disruptions in oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and concerns over U.S. munitions supplies.

World.title: Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance
World.content:
Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Hattieville construction worker has been fined more than six times the value of a sledgehammer he admitted stealing from a man who hired him for a day’s work after he would not give him an advance in payment.

Forty-two-year-old Felix Larance Petillo appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday and was charged with stealing a red Truper-brand sledgehammer, valued at $50, from a construction worker who had hired him.

Petillo initially pleaded not guilty and was offered bail of $1,000. However, while waiting to secure bail, he returned to court and changed his plea to guilty.

Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison fined him $300, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay or serve two weeks in prison.

According to the allegations, the construction worker hired Petillo on July 19 to assist with removing cement material from a demolished house on Locario Street in Hattieville.

Later that evening, Petillo reportedly asked for an advance payment for work scheduled for the following day. When the construction worker refused, Petillo allegedly threatened to take some of his tools.

The following morning, the construction worker discovered that his sledgehammer was missing and reported the matter to police.

Police later detained Petillo, who reportedly admitted placing the tool inside a mechanic’s vehicle. The mechanic subsequently handed the sledgehammer over to police and was not charged.

World.title: Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen
World.content:
Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Belize City that left a 67-year-old businessman injured on Tuesday morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. at Handy Money Loans on Handyside Street.

Police said the suspect entered the establishment under the pretense of pawning a cellphone before producing a firearm and demanding money.

The robber reportedly fled with approximately $80 in cash after firing a single shot at the businessman, Miguel Angel Guerra.

Guerra was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving medical treatment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-year-old taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has received disclosure in the murder case stemming from the September 2025 shooting death of Gaston Barrow at Old Belize.

Vaccaro, a resident of Cumberbatch Street, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday.

He was provided with 154 pages of disclosure, five compact discs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s evidence. The matter was adjourned until September 7, 2026, when a preliminary inquiry is scheduled to begin.

Vaccaro was first arraigned for Barrow’s murder on October 6, 2025, and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Police said Barrow and another man, Hank Carr, were shot at the Old Belize compound on the night of September 28, 2025. Barrow was pronounced dead on arrival at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while Carr was treated and later released.

Investigators allege Carr was driving a vehicle with Barrow in the front passenger seat when a gunman near a taxi opened fire. The shooter reportedly entered the taxi and escaped towards the nearby police checkpoint.

Police later reviewed surveillance footage from the area, which reportedly led to Vaccaro’s detention and subsequent charge.
