World.title: Germany's growing interest in Africa: A win for both sides?
World.content:
Germany is deepening its footprint across Africa, as Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul embarks on his third trip to the continent in 2026. His top-level talks will focus on security, skills development and investment.

Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is currently visiting Nigeria as part of a multi-country trip across Africa, with a preceding major stopover in Mauritania, and an upcoming call on South Africa.

The trip follows up on prior journeys by Germany's top diplomat to Africa, with Wadephul having visited Ethiopia and Kenya in January, and Morocco in April.

Wadephul says these repeated travels to the continent are a strategic necessity for Europe as part of Berlin's expanding engagement with Africa.

"This is my third trip to Africa now. Why? Africa is a continent of both destiny and opportunity for Europe," he told reporters, highlighting the continent's economic potential while also emphasizing its persistent security challenges.

In Nouakchott, Wadephul met with Mauritanian President Mohamed Ghazouani alongside several other German diplomats Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Mauritania: Security, migration and counterterrorism

As the first destination on the current tour, Wadephul's stop in Mauritania focused on various interlinked issues such as security cooperation, migration management and regional stability.

Geopolitical analyst Fidel Amakye Owusu believes that "Germany will go to Mauritania because of migration," highlighting the growing use of Atlantic migration routes by people desperate to reach Europe.

In fact, the foreign minister's visit came just days after the UN refugee agency reported at least 144 deaths along this route near the Mauritanian coast.

Wadephul's trip to the country, however, also focused on opportunities for deeper security cooperation with Mauritania; his delegation visited the Mourchidates, an all-female Islamic spiritual guide group trained and deployed by the state to counter extremism.

DW's Silja Fröhlich, who accompanied Wadephul on the trip, noted that the foreign minister's interaction with the Mourchidates women was one of the main highlights: "In Mauritania, he was visibly moved by women working with the UN to prevent extremism and violence — women who, despite living in a deeply patriarchal society and often carrying personal ties to the very conflict they are confronting, are determined to protect their communities," she explained.

Support for such a grassroots initiative is also a reflection of Germany's intent on bolstering community‑based approaches to preventing radicalization.

Germany hopes to intensify its involvement — and investments — in Nigeria Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Nigeria: Economic partnership and youth‑driven innovation

The second leg of the trip took Wadephul to Nigeria, where he met with various entrepreneurs, creatives, influencers, filmmakers and students.

"We are looking for new global partners. This is the very reason that I am here: that we are looking to Africa and to the countries in Africa. I view Nigeria as some kind of a powerhouse, a striving nation, growing faster and faster and with a lot of creative ideas," the foreign minister commented, describing Nigeria as an African powerhouse, particularly in the creative industries.

Vocational education, skills development and collaboration in science, technology and innovation were highlighted as key areas for future cooperation, with discussions also centering on expanding economic and commercial partnerships and attracting greater German investment into priority sectors.

Nigeria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Ministry in a statement said that the country "looks forward to productive engagements that will further consolidate the existing friendship, and open new avenues for collaboration in support of inclusive economic growth, regional stability and shared prosperity."

Local content creator Shalom Onyuinye said that Wadephul's recognition of Nigeria's growing cultural momentum around the world marks a significant shift in the global perception of Africa's most populous country.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul wants to support and boost Nigeria's creative enterprises Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

South Africa: Germany's closest economic partner in Africa

Wadephul's trip across the continent is due to will conclude in South Africa — Germany's most significant economic partner in Africa; more than 600 German companies operate there.

German direct investment in South Africa reached €7.99 billion ($9.1 billion) in 2023, with South African investment in Germany totaling €2.6 billion, according to Germany's Federal Foreign Office.

Analyst Owusu thinks that South Africa's advanced and diverse economy as well as its role as Africa's chief manufacturing hub make the country attractive to foreign investors; he also noted that German investment could generate substantial benefits in the long run — for both sides.

However, against the backdrop of recent xenophobic attacks across the country, the foreign minister is also expected to double-down on shared democratic values between the two nations.

Furthermore, this upcoming leg of the trip is expected to focus on industrial cooperation, energy transition partnerships and strengthening ties with South Africa's business and political leadership.

Germany's FM stresses Europe's 'need' for skilled workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's growing interest in Africa

Wadephul's visit to Africa also builds on a partnership established last year, when Germany and the African Union (AU) launched their first‑ever strategic dialogue on foreign and security policy at the AU headquarters in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

This new framework aims to deepen cooperation on global security crises and multilateral engagement, for which Germany pledged funds exceeding €100 million in total.

"Especially at a time of major global geopolitical upheaval, reliable cooperation with our African partners is essential," Wadephul remarked at the launch of the initiative.

The foreign minister stressed at the time that Europe and Africa were "closely interconnected politically, economically, and in terms of security, and face many of the same challenges," stressing that "a strong Africa is in Germany's interest."

Silja Fröhlich contributed to this article

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: Female coaches want more representation in African football
World.content:
Female head coaches will be a rare sight at the Women’s African Cup of Nations. However, there are some promising signs.

When it kicks off in Morocco on July 26, the Women's African Cup of Nations (WAFCON) promises to provide great goals, games and memories as 16 teams compete for the continental title. While the focus will be on the stars on the pitch, there may also be some attention on the fact that very few of the head coaches are female.

Cameroon's appointment of Valentine Nguel just weeks before the tournament, brought the number of WAFCON nations with female coaches to four – along with Zambia, Kenya, and South Africa. Still, the vast majority are men. Other teams have appointed female assistants in order to comply with a rule passed by FIFA earlier this year, which requires women's teams to have at least one female coach on the bench.

Africa may be moving slowly in the right direction with two head coaches of 12 at the 2025 WAFCON (16.7%) to four of 16 (25%) in 2026, but there is still a long way to go.

Desiree Ellis has been named Africa's women's coach of the year four times. Image: Nour Aknajja/Sports Inc/empics/picture alliance

South Africa leads the way. Desiree Ellis is one of the world's most successful female coaches and led South Africa to the 2022 title. The four-time African Women's coach of the year would like more countries to follow the example set by hers.

Helping female coaches

"Our federation took a stand long ago that all female teams will be coached by females," Ellis told DW.

"That needs to happen and federations need to be brave and appoint female coaches. They need to not just appoint them but give them support, otherwise they are not going to succeed."

South Africa is one of 14 members of the Council of Southern Africa Football Associations (COSAFA). Even before the FIFA regulation announced in March, this regional organization already had a rule in place making it mandatory for women to form part of the coaching teams.

"This is to force federations to provide more opportunities for female coaches, and we can see that in South Africa, it's yielded good dividends," Ellis said.

Jackline Juma says female coaches in Africa are not given the same support as their male counterparts get Image: Talanta FC

Jackline Juma is head coach of Kenya's U-20 women's team and would like to see something similar set up all over the continent.

"We don't have many female coaches in charge of African female teams… It's because they still don't trust women, don't give them chances, the support is not as much as for male coaches," Juma told DW.

She believes that such attitudes mean help is needed.

"At least, get restrictions when it comes to club licensing so that for female football teams, priority should be given to female coaches as head coaches so this would give us a good number of female coaches rising up."

Juma suggests that the first assistant coach should also be female with men allowed to fill out the coaching staff after that.

Setting pathways

More jobs coupled with role models like Ellis can inspire a new generation of female coaches and Vicky Huyton, who founded the Female Coaching Network in 2014, told DW that while just 20% of female national teams have female coaches, they account for 90% of major championships.

Inspiring young girls is, however, just the beginning of what can be a long and difficult journey to the upper reaches of the sport. While there are some countries that have made strides, some federations still have much to do in this field to enable coaches to reach their full potential.

"I am contacted quite often by amazing female coaches in Africa –various countries, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria." Huyton told DW.

"Often they say 'I have a passion, I have a want but I have nowhere to go.'"

Huyton would like to see a clear pathway in place for all young coaches.

"They don't know how to take that route and that's not necessarily the coach's fault, that's the federation or governing body who aren't reaching out to these women and saying 'if you want to be national team coach, this is what you have to do.' I honestly think that in some sports even the governing bodies don't know how to get them there."

Huyton admits that all around the world there is a long way still to go but that there is a fundamental lesson that Africa can learn from Europe.

"From a level-one grassroots coach volunteering once a week, what does that pathway look like to go all the way to a national team coach?" she asked.

"It's really important to understand what the journey looks like. People think that women don't want to coach…it isn't true."

Sarina Wiegman has coached both the Netherlands and England to Women's Euros titles Image: Priscila Bütler/SPP/IMAGO

Reasons for optimism

The lack of representation at the top level is not confined to Africa. Men are a common sight on the benches of women's games all over the world, including Europe. At the Women's Euro 2025, just seven of the 16 teams had female coaches, an increase from past tournaments but still fewer than half.

England's national team may be European champions and led by a woman, but female coaches are still a minority in the country's Women's Super League, regarded by most as the strongest domestic competition in the world.

In Africa, progress is being made and while it is slower than many would like in terms of women rising to senior positions, there are reasons to be optimistic, according to Ellis.

"Now, you have Lamia [Boumehdi] who has just won CAF (Confederation of African Football) coach of the year, being appointed as U20 coach of Morocco," Ellis said.

"You have Adelaide [Koudougnon] qualifying Ivory Coast for the first time to the U17 tournament, you have Carol [Kanyemba] of Zambia going to back-to-back World Cups with the U17s, you have Mildred [Cheche] going to the U17 World Cup with Kenya. There are a lot of future coaches coming up."

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Iran war: Trump threatens bridges over Hormuz Strait attacks
World.content:
Skip next section Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Signs of ships avoiding second choke point off Yemen after Houthi warnings: tracker data

Houthi supporters rallied in Sanaa in support of the announcement of a maritime blockade earlier this week [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Houthi threats to ships headed to or from Saudi Arabia's western shoreline could further impact commercial shipping, data trackers are warning.

The Houthis, who have de facto control over much of Yemen, have declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia and told ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Red Sea on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. It provides access to western Saudi coastal cities like Jeddah and Yanbu.

Data provider Kpler said shipping in both waterways was "under pressure," saying traffic in both straits had fallen sharply.

Ship broker Clarksons issued a similar warning, saying four vessels had registered new courses on Wednesday, avoiding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and heading north through the Suez Canal towards the Mediterranean instead.

"The threat of Houthi hostile actions against Saudi Arabia ... has begun to have an overall effect on tanker activity," Clarksons wrote. "There are reports of several tankers, having ​loaded in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu port in the Red Sea, that have shifted course towards the Suez Canal rather than sail south towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while ​others are holding their positions waiting for further instruction."

For ships headed to places like India, Pakistan, Indonesia or Australia, doing this would add well over 10,000 nautical miles (more than 20,000 kilometers) and weeks at sea to the typical travel distance.

"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday warned that the actions "threaten regional security, undermine freedom of navigation, challenge the rules-based maritime order and jeopardize uninterrupted flow of global commerce."

The Reuters news agency cited an advisory from the European Union's Aspides naval mission in the Red Sea as saying that ships with links to Israel, the United ​States or Saudi Arabia ‌were at a higher risk of being attacked by the Houthis and were advised to avoid voyages through the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until the threat level decreases.

World.title: What's holding up the Gaza stabilization mission?
World.content:
A multinational stabilization mission is supposed to ensure the reconstruction of Gaza. Without political consensus among Israel, Hamas and the Arab states, its implementation remains uncertain.

Morocco recently signed an agreement to participate ​in the International Stabilization Force (ISF) in Gaza.

This agreement "reflects the shared determination to contribute, through concrete ​humanitarian and security actions, to the ​establishment of a climate of peace and security in the region," Morocco's state news agency MAP reported in July. According to the report, Morocco's contribution includes military personnel, police and gendarmerie forces and a field hospital.

Morocco is the first Arab country to join the planned international security mission for the Gaza Strip. Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Albania are also part of the force, while Jordan and Egypt have agreed to supporting roles only.

However, it remains to be seen whether the ISF can ever be deployed on the scale originally envisioned by its initiators.

The force, which is linked to the "Board of Peace" established by US President Donald Trump, is intended to do far more than simply secure humanitarian aid: It's seen as the security cornerstone of the planned post-war order for Gaza.

No traditional UN peacekeeping mission

The International Stabilization Force is tasked with securing the reconstruction process, protecting humanitarian aid deliveries, and training new Palestinian security forces. In the long term, it is intended to support a political transition.

However, in contrast to traditional United Nations peacekeeping missions, it will be organized outside the usual UN command structures even though the UN authorized the force. This structural difference makes the ISF one of the most ambitious — and one of the most challenging — international projects for the Gaza Strip.

"The involvement of international actors requires at least a minimum level of political stability," Gil Murciano , executive director of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, told DW. The real problem, he said, is not the mission itself, but the lack of a political framework in which it needs to operate.

Marcus Schneider, head of Germany's political Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Regional Project for Peace and Security in the Middle East in Beirut, is also skeptical about the mission's prospects for success.

"Israel wants to secure military freedom of action, while potential troop-contributing countries are primarily interested in a traditional peacekeeping mission," he told DW, adding that "these differing expectations pretty much rule each other out."

This view is echoed by the International Peace Institute (IPI). According to a recent analysis , a stable, legitimate Palestinian administration is needed first; otherwise, the ISF risks becoming yet another international transitional project.

As long as reconstruction is tied to a political framework, the population of Gaza remains in limbo Image: Dawoud Abu Alkas/REUTERS

Israel, Hamas, and the Arab states still differ on Gaza's future

In particular, Israel, Hamas, and the Arab states have differing views on what role the ISF should play. From Israel's perspective, security is the top priority.

"The Israeli government has made its position very clear: as long as Hamas does not agree to disarm, the reconstruction of Gaza should not begin," Murciano said. This ties reconstruction to a political condition that has not yet been agreed upon.

In Schneider's assessment, the actors involved are pursuing different political goals. While Israel wants to preserve its military freedom of action, many potential troop-contributing countries expect a clearly defined mandate with manageable risks. However, these expectations are currently difficult to reconcile.

The stance of Hamas — which is designated as a terrorist organization by the US and the EU, among others — further complicates the planning. Although the organization has signaled a willingness to withdraw from the civilian administration of Gaza, it has so far refused to fully disarm.

From Israel's perspective, this means that a key prerequisite for the mission's deployment remains unmet; at the same time, many international actors argue that reconstruction and political stabilization should not wait until all security issues have been resolved.

Is the Board of Peace Trump's private UN? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The role of the Arab states in Gaza

Arab states play a key role in Gaza's future as they are considered the most important financial backers for reconstruction. They could also lend the mission the necessary regional legitimacy. However, many governments want to avoid sending troops and billions in aid to Gaza without a solid political roadmap.

Morocco's commitment is seen as an important signal, even though it does not change the fact that other major regional powers have so far remained cautious.

The Washington-based think tank Arab Center Washington DC highlights this dilemma. While many Arab states are, in principle, willing to support the reconstruction of Gaza, participation in an international stabilization mission would be possible for them only within the framework of a credible political process, a report stated.

Gaza's reconstruction as a prerequisite for security

The real challenge lies in solving this stalemate, predicts Murciano. "Reconstruction itself is an essential component of security," he said. Anyone who separates the two processes risks further entrenching the political stalemate, he added.

Whether the ISF will ever be able to assume its intended role remains uncertain. While planning is well advanced, the mission still lacks the political conditions needed for deployment.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Congo: Ebola deaths increase to 1,000
World.content:
Authorities in Congo have said the latest outbreak of the Ebola virus has killed 999 people since mid-May. That fatality rate is far higher than in previous outbreaks. No vaccines or treatments exist for the new strain.

The World Health Organization (WHO) on Wednesday published an overview of new data documenting the rapid spread of the current Ebola outbreak in Congo.

Democratic Republic of Congo Ministry of Health data documenting cases traced between May 15 and July 19 shows that 2,473 people in Congo and neighboring Uganda have been infected by the latest Bundibugyo strain of the virus, with 999 documented deaths.

The spread — the fastest ever recorded for Ebola — has continued unabated as no vaccines or treatments exist for this new strain of the virus.

Until now, the deadliest outbreak — which raged from 2013 to 2016 and infected 28,000 people, 11,000 of whom died — took some eight months to reach the grim 1,000 death mark.

Ebola spreading faster than officials can track

Health officials in Congo say some 80% of new cases have emerged through unknown transmission chains, suggesting it is spreading far faster than authorities can track.

In DRC, fighting Ebola means fighting misinformation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Overall, 82% of contacts linked to confirmed cases are being traced by authorities. This is well below the 90%-95% rate WHO officials say is needed to contain the virus.

The highly contagious Ebola virus is spread via bodily fluids, such as blood, semen and vomit, and is often fatal.

To date, infections in the central African nation of 116 million have been recorded in five of Congo's 26 provinces. The epicenter of the current outbreak lies in Ituri province, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.

Healthcare workers forced to flee

The severity of the situation is being compounded by attacks on health workers as well as the generally poor working conditions that these individuals face.

Many healthcare workers have been forced to flee affected areas in fear for their own safety, and others say they have not been paid in months.

Speaking in Ghana on Tuesday, Director-General of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya told attendees at the Africa Health Summit that international efforts to stop the spread of the virus must be intensified.

"If we don't stop this outbreak, it could become one of the worst ebola outbreaks the world has ever documented," Kaseya said.

World.title: Can India become the next semiconductor hub after Taiwan?
World.content:
India is investing billions to build a domestic semiconductor industry as major industrial powers seek to diversify supply chains beyond Taiwan.

More than 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are made in Taiwan, an island at the center of ongoing rivalry between the US and China.

Any disruption to Taiwan's chip industry would likely send shockwaves through the global economy, with modern semiconductors used to make everything from smartphones and electric vehicles (EVs) to aircraft and military systems.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, chip shortages forced automakers to halt production — exposing how dependent the world had become on a handful of manufacturers in East Asia.

The result has been a global race to build more resilient semiconductor supply chains. The US, Japan, South Korea and also the EU have all launched multi-billion-dollar programs to attract chipmakers.

India is now mounting its biggest push yet to become part of that network and enter the global arena as the next electronics powerhouse.

India's chipmaking ambitions

Last week, the Indian government approved a $13.2 billion (€11.4 billion) semiconductor program labeled Semicon 2.0. The project builds on the $9 billion India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) launched in 2021 and aims to develop the entire chip ecosystem — from chip design and fabrication to advanced packaging, specialty materials, equipment manufacturing and workforce training.

US giant Micron Technology has established a semiconductor assembly and test facility in India Image: Jonathan Raa/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Thousands of engineers working for companies such as Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and Texas Instruments already design some of the world's most sophisticated chips from research centers in the Indian cities of Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Noida.

But analysts warn India has been lagging behind in large-scale manufacturing. In the semiconductor industry, this is the area that brings both economic value and strategic importance.

"India already has the expertise to design sophisticated semiconductor chips," said V Kamakoti, director of the Indian Institute of Technology in the city of Madras.

"Indian engineers working for both domestic companies and multinational firms have successfully designed and delivered complex chips," Kamakoti told DW. "The bigger challenge is manufacturing them."

So far, India's progress has been concentrated in chip packaging and testing rather than manufacturing the chips themselves.

Kamakoti said the next step is building a domestic fabrication ecosystem that can turn those design strengths into large-scale production.

Taiwan's AI surge fuels global power, amid growing risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hopes of a $100 billion market by 2030

Micron Technology, a US memory chip maker, Kaynes Semicon and CG Semi, two Indian semiconductor assembly and packaging companies, have begun commercial production under the first phase of India's semiconductor program.

Indian Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw says the next phase is intended to move more of the semiconductor value chain into India.

"Convincing global companies is no longer that difficult," said ISM chief executive Amitesh Kumar Sinha, pointing to the 12 approved fabrication and packaging projects, three of which are already in commercial production.

The government wants to build a domestic semiconductor market worth between $100 billion and $110 billion by 2030 and meet up to three-quarters of India's electronics demand through locally designed and manufactured chips.

A costly industrial leap

Becoming a major chip manufacturer, however, is one of the toughest industrial challenges any country could take on.

A leading-edge fabrication plant can cost more than $20 billion, requires uninterrupted electricity, vast quantities of ultra-pure water and an extensive network of suppliers producing specialized chemicals, silicon wafers and precision equipment.

Chip market contest: Who will win the race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kamakoti argues that India should first prove it can manufacture mature 28-nanometer (28 nm) chips reliably at scale before attempting the most advanced 3 nm processors used in high-end smartphones and AI systems.

"28 nm [chips] will meet the majority of India's needs. Once that succeeds, we can gradually move to more advanced technologies," he said.

Riding the AI boom

India's ambitions are being helped by forces beyond its control.

In a time of geopolitical tensions and the rapid growth of AI, companies are rethinking their supply chains and demand for semiconductors is expected to rise sharply over the coming decade.

Sambit Sahu, a semiconductor industry veteran with more than three decades of experience at Qualcomm and Intel, says India must build capabilities across the semiconductor value chain from chip design and intellectual property to fabrication and manufacturing.

"The rapid growth of artificial intelligence will drive demand for semiconductors for years to come, creating a window of opportunity for India," Sahu told DW.

"Building a semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem will be expensive and technically challenging, but with sustained investment and supportive policies, India could emerge as an important manufacturing hub over the next decade."

High-tech boom and expensive housing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, not everyone is convinced India can narrow the manufacturing gap quickly.

A senior semiconductor industry executive, who preferred to stay anonymous, says India is likely to remain stronger in chip design than fabrication for the foreseeable future.

"India has built world-class capabilities in chip design, but manufacturing is a different challenge," he said. "The biggest opportunities in the near term are in packaging, testing and mature-node manufacturing."

Semicon 2.0 marks India's most ambitious attempt yet to enter the semiconductor race.

Whether it succeeds will depend less on the billions India has pledged and more on its ability to turn those commitments into factories, skilled workers and a competitive manufacturing ecosystem.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: France: Minister quits over pesticide bill — but is staying
World.content:
Environment Minister Monique Barbut submitted her resignation in protest over the reintroduction of pesticides that scientists say harm human health as well as bees. But President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept it.

French Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut announced Wednesday that she would "submit her resignation today" to President Emmanuel Macron in protest to the reintroduction of harmful pesticides.

However, Macron did not accept her resignation, and Barbut will stay in her post due to the "urgency to address the consequences of climate change," her team said in comments carried by the AFP news agency.

Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon later said that Barbut will stay in office.

What Barbut said about her resignation

In a post on LinkedIn, Barbut wrote that "contrary to the commitments that had been made to me, the government prevented any debate on the removal of this measure," adding that there had been "one environmental setback too many," since was appointed last October.

"Politics is not my world, and if this is what politics is about, it definitely never will be," said the former head of WWF France and the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD).

What is in France's pesticide bill?

Barbut's statement comes just after lawmakers appoved a bill that will allow the pesticides acetamiprid and flupyradifurone to come back into use. They have been banned in France since 2018 and 2019, respectively.

Scientists say that the chemicals are dangerous to human health and are harmful to the bee populations that make agriculture possible in the first place.

Proponents of the bill argued that France's beet, apple, and hazlenut farmers need the pesticides to compete against their EU counterparts.

The substances are not banned in the EU but some member states limit their use.

07/22/2026 July 22, 2026 Germany, France move forward on nuclear production deal with Russia

A German regulator has cleared the way for a Germany-based subsidiary of a French nuclear fuel company to do joint work with Russia's state-owned Rosatom.

Despite banning nuclear power plants in 2011, Germany is still home to facilities producing nuclear fuel rods, which use fission — different from the fusion process used in traditional nuclear power stations.

The decision underscores how nuclear energy has largely remained exempt from the EU's sanctions against Russia following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Germany's Environment Ministry expressed regret at giving the go-ahead, indicating that it did not have much choice as the venture does not fall under any ban.

The EU has so far been unable to come to an agreement as to how to extend sanctions to include Russia's nuclear sector.

World.title: El PP se pliega a Vox y Les Corts Valencianes aprueban los primeros presupuestos en España que incluyen la “prioridad nacional”
World.content:
Las cuentas de la Generalitat, presidida por Juanfran Pérez Llorca, salen adelante con los votos de los populares y de la formación de extrema derecha

Vox llevaba meses advirtiendo al PP de que, si no se incluía expresamente su “prioridad nacional” en los Presupuestos de la Generalitat Valenciana para 2026, no los apoyaría. Este miércoles, la formación de extrema derecha ha impuesto su exigencia y el pleno de Les Corts ha aprobado las cuentas de 33.305 millones de euros del Consell, presidido por Juanfran Pérez Llorca, que incluyen la polémica expresión en varias partidas relativas a ayudas sociales y de acceso a la vivienda.

Son los primeros presupuestos con rango de ley de una autonomía en España en los que se ha dado entrada al concepto que popularizó en los ochenta el dirigente francés de extrema derecha Jean-Marie Le Pen. Hasta ahora, la prioridad nacional solo se contemplaba en los acuerdos de gobierno alcanzados este año entre el PP y Vox en Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León, y Andalucía.

Los votos del PP (40) y de Vox (13) se han impuesto a los del PSPV-PSOE (31) y Compromís (15) y han superado la mayoría absoluta al sumar 53 por 41 de la oposición.

Un exultante José María Llanos, portavoz de Vox, ha afirmado desde la tribuna: “Prioridad nacional por ley. Los primeros presupuestos donde se incluye el concepto. Y ha llegado para quedarse, más pronto que tarde llegará a la normativa nacional”. Luego, ha hilvanado un discurso muy crítico con la inmigración y ha sostenido que se establecerán puntos de empadronamiento como “primera barrera” para que “el dinero de los valencianos vaya antes que a nadie a los valencianos”.

La bancada del PP, tras la votación de este miércoles. Mònica Torres

Tras el pleno, Pérez Llorca ha asegurado que el PP “no se pliega ante nadie” y lo que busca es “diálogo y consenso”. Ha insistido en que el PP pone “el énfasis en el arraigo” de la prioridad nacional de Vox. “Aquí se han hecho afirmaciones que son completamente falsas. Este presupuesto no distingue entre color de piel, entre inmigrantes y personas nacidas aquí. Jamás lo toleraría. Aquí se ha puesto en valor darle esa prioridad a aquellas personas que llevan más tiempo censadas en un municipio, y es algo que hacen también los alcaldes socialistas en todos sus municipio”.

Su portavoz, Fernando Pastor, ha defendido la estabilidad política de la Comunidad Valenciana frente “al caos, al lío y al desmadre que hay en Madrid”, en referencia al Gobierno del socialista Pedro Sánchez que cuenta con presupuestos prorrogados.

En los pasillos en Les Corts, la líder del PSPV-PSOE y ministra de Ciencia y Universidades, Diana Morant, ha acusado a Pérez Llorca de haber “convertido el apartheid en ley”, ha reiterado que el Gobierno estudiará la aplicación de la “prioridad nacional para recurrir la ley ante el Tribunal Constitucional (TC) si efectivamente se produce discriminación” y e “impacto social” en el acceso a la vivienda y las ayudas sociales.

El portavoz socialista, José Muñoz, durante su intervención. Mònica Torres

El portavoz socialista, José Muñoz, ha subrayado que la prioridad nacional va dirigida en realidad contra los pobres, porque el PP y Vox padecen “aporofobia”. Y ha señalado al consejero de Hacienda, José Antonio Rovira, de dedicarle una peineta, un gesto obsceno de desaprobación, tras la votación. “He tenido un pronto, uan reacción refleja, porque los socialistas nos acusan de convivencia con Vox, cuando el PSOE gobierna con apoyo de Bildu, de los etarras”, ha señalado el consejero a este periódico.

Desde Compromís, el diputado Carles Esteve ha ironizado con las “caras” de los diputados del PP tras la votación, incidiedo en que Pérez Llorca se haya levantado de su asiento para “darle las gracias” al portavoz de Vox. “Estáis hipotecando el futuro de los valencianos”, ha reprochado a los populares.

El Consell, presidido por el PP, con el apoyo parlamentario de Vox, aprueba sus terceras cuentas, las primeras con Pérez Llorca como president, que accedió al cargo en diciembre del pasado año, tras la dimisión de Carlos Mazón. El expresidente y diputado autonómico ha llegado al hemiciclo poco antes de la votación.

La prioridad en el texto de la ley

La prioridad nacional se refleja en varias partidas, ya aprobadas por el PP y Vox en comisión, de la siguiente manera: “Desarrollar medidas que faciliten el acceso de jóvenes a una vivienda en zonas rurales despobladas, colaborando en las actuaciones de dinamización del entorno rural, incorporando el principio de prioridad nacional, adecuado a la legalidad vigente, que procure la asignación prioritaria de los recursos públicos a quienes mantienen un arraigo real, duradero y verificable en la Comunidad Valenciana, con el objetivo de asegurar la relación efectiva y afectiva del solicitante a la región”.

“Este principio supondrá: Exigencia de arraigo real y prolongado, basado en empadronamiento histórico en la Comunitat Valenciana y España. Refuerzo de los criterios de vinculación económica, social, familiar, laboral y formativa como elementos que evidencian la relación efectiva y afectiva del solicitante con el territorio. A tal efecto, se valorará, al menos, con sujeción a la legalidad, la trayectoria de cotización y actividad laboral, la existencia de familiares de primer grado que residen en la Comunitat Valenciana, así como cualquier otro criterio que acredite vinculación real y duradera de los solicitantes con la región”.

El mismo texto se repite en otra partida para “facilitar el acceso a una vivienda pública en régimen de propiedad o alquiler de la Generalitat Valenciana” o para acceder a la renta valenciana de inclusión. En todas ellas se contempla la incorporación del “principio de prioridad nacional”, con la inmediata acotación: “adecuado a la legalidad vigente”.

El 31 de julio se votará en Les Corts la llamada ley de acompañamiento, que tiene un mayor peso político en la aplicación del principio de prioridad nacional en las distintas líneas de actuación del Consell.

Valencia marca el camino de los pactos entre PP y Vox al convertirse en la primera comunidad autónoma en incorporar la “prioridad nacional” a sus presupuestos, aunque otras, que aún negocian los suyos, podrían seguir sus pasos. La vicepresidenta tercera y consejera de Economía y Hacienda de la Junta de Andalucía, Carolina España, ha eludido confirmar si los próximos presupuestos autonómicos lo incluirán.

La también portavoz del Ejecutivo regional ha optado por repetir el mismo argumentario que incide en actuar dentro del marco de la ley del que lleva tirando el presidente Juan Manuel Moreno cada vez que ha sido preguntado en las últimas semanas por el encaje de esa premisa xenófoba de Vox, incluida en el pacto de gobierno de coalición entre el PP y los ultras. “Haremos un presupuesto y gobernaremos para todos los andaluces y para que Andalucía siga avanzando, siempre dentro de lo que marque la ley, la Constitución y el Estatuto de Autonomía”, ha dicho España. Ya en 2024, con mayoría absoluta, el Gobierno de Moreno recortó la ley de Igualdad andaluza para suprimir la obligación de que la Cámara de Cuentas incorporara un informe sobre la fiscalización del cumplimiento de la perspectiva de género en los presupuestos andaluces. Informa Eva Saiz.

World.title: El terremoto más allá de La Guaira: los pueblos costeros venezolanos se aferran al mar
World.content:
Poblaciones como Chichiriviche de la Costa, Puerto Cruz y Cepe están casi aislados desde el sismo del 24 de junio

Es mediodía en la costa venezolana, pero la brisa asemeja el atardecer. Las olas se cruzan a destiempo, haciendo que todo en la lancha se silencie y se sienta, cuando menos, como una montaña rusa. “Hay que sentir el mar para poder atravesarlo”, dice Will desde el motor ahogado de su peñero. La lancha ha servido para transportar donaciones a pueblos como Puerto Cruz, Puerto Maya y Cepe, a dos horas en lancha de La Guaira, la ciudad costera más afectada por los terremotos del 24 de junio. Los sismos dejaron a estas poblaciones costeras parcialmente incomunicadas de Catia del Mar, su principal fuente de provisiones.

Brisón es un término que se escucha en el litoral central venezolano para describir esa brisa extraña —no muy fuerte, no muy fría, pero poco frecuente— que empezó ese día, justo a las seis de la tarde, en plena fiesta de San Juan, cuando se abrió la tierra. Desde entonces, el mar tiene un comportamiento distinto y sus habitantes no quieren bañarse en la playa. Le tienen más respeto al agua que a la tierra firme. Ese día, durante el sismo, el mar se recogió varios metros, dejando en la arena a las lanchas que suelen anclarse en el agua, a metros de la orilla. “Me da miedo que mi hijo, el menor, se bañe y que se lo lleve el mar si se vuelve a recoger, porque eso fue muy fuerte”, dice Brígida en Puerto Maya, con lágrimas en los ojos.

Apenas los terremotos terminaron, se activó una alerta de tsunami en Venezuela que obligó a cada habitante a abandonar el mar. Durante días, los vecinos de los pueblos de la costa se reunieron para dormir en las plazas o en sus emblemáticos patios de secado del cacao. “No sabemos qué significa esto. Solo sabemos que nosotros no habíamos vivido algo así y que nuestros ancestros jamás lo vieron”, dice Enrique Liendo desde su hamaca en Cepe, a la orilla de la playa.

Enrique Liendo descansa en una hamaca junto a la playa en Cepe, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO

Dieciocho días después, hubo una réplica con epicentro en el mar, que volvió a despertar la preocupación de todo el litoral. “El mar está como el mar de diciembre, que hay que tenerle respeto”, dice Laurimar Salazar desde su silla de ruedas en Puerto Cruz, dirigiendo la reparación de su restaurant Mamita, que se desplomó en los terremotos. “Aquí todo el que viene yo lo atiendo, así tenga que ir a Caracas a comprar mercancía de ahora en adelante”, suspira.

En Chichiriviche de la Costa, Puerto Cruz, Puerto Maya y Cepe no hubo pérdidas humanas y el daño de las casas no es comparable a la destrucción generalizada de La Guaira. Pero no tienen cómo abastecer sus negocios y despensas, pues su principal proveedor era Catia La Mar y ahora tienen que ir hacia otros pueblos alejados por tierra o, los más privilegiados, hacer mercado en otras ciudades. “El primer día, si recibíamos un kilito de arroz, era súper bien recibido, pero el otro día tuve que ir a Carayaca a hacer mercado y eso queda a una hora en carretera desde aquí”, dice Rosa María Liendo en Chichiriviche de la Costa.

—¿Cómo están las cosas por aquí?

—Tranquilas.

Marbelis Meléndez estaba bajo la sombra de un árbol, en la orilla de la playa de Puerto Maya, cuando llegó una lancha con dos personas que no eran del pueblo. “Vengan a ver cómo quedó mi casa, necesitamos ayuda”, dijo, sin saber quiénes eran. “Aquí no ha venido nadie, no sabemos qué podemos hacer para que nos den los saquitos de cemento que necesitamos para volver a construir nuestra pieza”. Junto con su prima Brígida, emprendió un camino desde la playa, atravesando dos ríos a pie y subiendo una colina, para mostrar al menos cuatro casas caídas y otras seis con sus paredes rotas por los terremotos.

La mayoría de las casas que se cayeron medían un poco más del tamaño de una cama matrimonial y estaban hechas artesanalmente de bloques con cemento a medio terminar y ajustadas a veces con cartones, a veces con bahareque, siempre sin friso. “Esta es mi piecita. Esa pared me cayó encima y tuve que sacar a mi mamá viva de los escombros”, dice Brígida, refiriéndose a la señora Marcimina, quien desde ese día se ha dedicado a recoger bloque por bloque para llevarlo desde su pieza al desagüe, tapando la única salida de agua que tienen en la zona.

Vista aérea de viviendas afectadas en Puerto Maya. MAXWELL BRICENO Marbelis Meléndez en Puerto Maya. MAXWELL BRICENO La vivienda de Marbelis Melendez presenta daños estructurales tras el terremoto del pasado 24 de junio. MAXWELL BRICENO Marcimina Meléndez observa los escombros de una pared de su vivienda que colapsó sobre ella, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO Karina Blanco posa frente a su vivienda, que colapsó por completo durante el terremoto, en Puerto Cruz. MAXWELL BRICENO Vecinos preparan cemento para reconstruir un local comercial afectado por el terremoto, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO Viviendas y comercios afectados por el terremoto del pasado 24 de junio, en Puerto Maya. MAXWELL BRICENO

“¿Y ahora qué hago? ¿Para dónde agarro si la tierra se está abriendo?”, pensaba Karina Blanco mientras veía cómo su casa se derrumbaba. Desde que llegó con su mamá hace 21 años desde la Colonia Tovar hasta Puerto Maya, su casa siempre ha estado en amenaza de caerse por estar junto a la quebrada: “La primera vez que creció el río me tumbó una pieza. Cada vez que me decían que crecía el río, yo agarraba mis cosas y las subía para allá. Sé que en La Guaira fue más fuerte que aquí, pero la verdad es que uno necesita, y si me dieran una casa en otro lado, yo la aceptaría”, dice preocupada.

En uno de los negocios frente a la cancha de bolas criollas funciona una antena de Starlink que mitiga la falta de telefonía en el lugar. Hace unos meses que se cayó la antena de la única operadora que prestaba servicio en el pueblo (que es del Estado) y, desde entonces, todos dejaron de tener señal. Cuando se va la luz, no hay ni wifi ni antena. Y esto sucede más de cinco horas al día, por un racionamiento eléctrico no oficial y rotativo, que arropa a muchos de los pueblos fuera de Caracas desde hace años, pero que ahora se prolonga, después del terremoto.

Las lanchas, que son el gran medio de comunicación entre los pueblos de la costa, tienen limitado el abastecimiento de combustible. Deben navegar más de una hora hasta el Puerto de La Zorra para recargar. Por estos días, suelen juntar los bidones del pueblo en una sola lancha, para llenar todos los que puedan y compartirlos. Con la poca gasolina que les llega salen a pescar y llevan insumos a otros pueblos.

Wiliams Alvarez entrega cajas con ayuda humanitaria para su distribución entre las comunidades afectadas por el terremoto. MAXWELL BRICENO Pescadores salen a una jornada de pesca en Cepe, el incremento del oleaje dificulta la pesca y el acceso maritimo a los pueblos costeros. MAXWELL BRICENO Vista aérea de Puerto Maya, en La Guaira, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO Residentes esperan el abastecimiento de combustible en Puerto Maya, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO Vigilia en memoria de las víctimas del terremoto del pasado 24 de junio, en Chichiriviche de la Costa, La Guaira, el 14 de julio. MAXWELL BRICENO Un pescador transporta un pescado tras una jornada de pesca, principal actividad económica de la comunidad. MAXWELL BRICENO Un habitante de Puerto Maya transporta bidones vacíos de gasolina para las lanchas pesqueras, principal medio de transporte y sustento para las faenas de pesca. MAXWELL BRICENO

La pesca también sufre, porque el terremoto cambió el lecho marino. En Trinidad, la isla contigua al oriente de Venezuela, el suelo se levantó seis metros después de los sismos; la NASA también confirmó que los terremotos provocaron un desplazamiento de la superficie terrestre de hasta 60 centímetros, que alteró drásticamente la geografía local; y, en Chichiriviche de la Costa, los pescadores han visto cómo donde antes había arena ahora hay rocas, y donde existía una profundidad de 10 metros, hoy hay más. “Después del temblor sí estábamos sacando muchos peces, pero llevamos como dos días que no se encuentra nada por ahí”, explica Enrique Liendo.

Los locales confían en que el turismo va a llegar. “Creemos que ahora va a empezar a venir más gente para este lado porque La Guaira se quedó sin playa”, dice Will desde su lancha. Mientras tanto, seis turistas de Barquisimeto llegaron a Choroní, y de ahí a Cepe, como los primeros aventureros. “Teníamos un viaje programado y como vimos que aquí todo estaba bien, nos vinimos”. Esa es la razón por la que La Morocha abre todos los días, con la esperanza de que alguien llegue; Richard prepara la guarapa de parchita en el congelador y Micaela De Fisher, la maestra jubilada del pueblo, abre su posada también a diario. Saben que hay que seguir.

World.title: Ivory and a rhino skull among 5,800 items handed to RVO
World.content:
Some 5,800 prohibited objects including elephant ivory have been anonymously handed in to the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) over the past year, a more than fivefold increase on the previous year.

“Never before has so much been handed in,” says The Hague-based RVO, including “moving boxes with a thousand [pieces of] ivory jewellery, a rhino skull with a gunshot wound, crocodile leather bags, musical instruments and an elephant’s leg.”

The objects also included taxidermy animals such as a long-eared owl, peregrine falcon and turtles. Pictures on broadcaster NOS show ivory binoculars and crocodile leather bags.

The sale and trade of elephant ivory are strictly regulated under European CITES laws (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), with permits required for the possession and trade of protected plants or animals.

Most of the items, which can be handed in at a drop-off bin in The Hague or even by post, are destroyed to prevent them from (re)entering the illegal trade. The RVO says it uses a small number of the items for research and education.

World.title: Thuisbezorgd hides costs and fakes discounts: consumer group
World.content:
The food delivery platform Thuisbezorgd.nl hides compulsory charges and advertises fake discounts, the Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said on Tuesday, calling on the company to stop and to compensate affected customers.

Mandatory costs should be clearly shown before a customer starts ordering, the association said, but Thuisbezorgd’s app and website do not reveal compulsory “service” charges – for items such as bags, plastic packaging and sauce – until part-way through or at the end of an order, adding an average of €2 to €4 to the bill.

The association also said the company broke rules on special offers. Under Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) rules, a struck-through sale price must be the lowest the seller charged in the previous 30 days. In one case, the association found Indian snacks that had previously cost €3.75 being offered “on sale” from €7.50 to €6.

“We have been in talks with Thuisbezorgd since March, but the platform is still confronting customers with hidden costs and fake discounts,” said Consumentenbond director Sandra Molenaar, noting the company has more than six million users in the Netherlands.

Because the practice has probably been going on for years, the association estimates the hidden costs run into the hundreds of millions of euros in total. A Thuisbezorgd spokesperson said the company did not recognise the association’s accusations.

The Consumentenbond said it had also found hidden costs at Uber Eats, which made changes in June, though no fake discounts. The findings are part of a wider campaign against hidden charges and misleading offers that also named Bol and Amazon last week.

The association can press companies to change but cannot impose penalties; that is a matter for the ACM, which has fined firms including Leen Bakker, G-Star and Jysk in the past.

Three men have been arrested over the theft of a shipment of smartphones with an estimated street value of around €5 million from the Schiphol area, the Royal Military Police (Koninklijke Marechaussee) have said.

The suspects are two 24-year-old men from Amsterdam and a 39-year-old from Zoetermeer.

The shipment went missing on June 18, prompting an investigation, led by the Noord-Holland public prosecution department, into an organised crime group.

One of the suspects works for a transport company at Schiphol and is thought to have passed confidential information to the group, the military police said. Further arrests have not been ruled out.

World.title: Two trams collide on Rotterdam’s Erasmus Bridge, 15 injured
World.content:
Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when two trams collided on the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam on Wednesday morning, the regional safety board has said. One of the trams was derailed by the impact.

The crash happened at around 11.10am, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Footage shows one tram coming to a halt as it drove onto the bridge from the direction of the city centre, before a second tram approached from behind and ran into it, apparently without braking.

The seriously injured person was trapped and had to be freed before being taken to hospital. The safety board initially reported 18 injured and two seriously hurt, but later revised the figures.

Transport company RET said it could not yet say what caused the rear-end collision, adding that it was shocked by the footage and that its thoughts were with the victims and passengers. Two cars were also damaged, the fire service said.

The power to the overhead lines was switched off and the bridge closed to traffic, halting tram services on lines 3 and 5.

World.title: Man jailed for 15 months over threats to Groningen butchers
World.content:
A Groningen court has sentenced a 23-year-old man to 15 months in prison for sending death threats to butchers in the province and neighbouring Drenthe.

Prosecutors requested a four-year sentence, saying he had a terrorist motive. But the court ruled there was insufficient evidence for such a charge, saying instead he acted out of radical environmental and animal-rights beliefs.

Because four months of his sentence are suspended, the man, known as Bas V., will be released immediately, having already served his time in pre-trial detention. He is bound by a three-year probationary period.

The crime

Last September, Bas V. sent threatening emails to 12 butcher shops demanding they close. “You get one warning, nothing more. If the shop isn’t closed tomorrow, I will come with a machete and stab everyone to death,” read the email.

The court stated: “The texts on his phone say something about his mindset, but not that he wanted to disrupt society with them.”

Bas V., who admitted to sending the emails, was arrested after seven of the butchers filed a complaint. Police found a machete in his home and notes on his phone saying he also needed a pistol with a silencer to “kill people responsible for the humiliation of animals,” according to broadcaster NOS.

The national broadcaster also says that Bas V. was found by experts to have a gaming addiction, a cannabis addiction, ADHD and autism, and will be placed in a protected living facility to receive treatment.

World.title: House prices rising fastest in Groningen, slowest in Amsterdam
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

House prices are climbing fastest in Groningen and slowest in the Randstad, figures from the national statistics office CBS and the Land Registry showed on Tuesday.

Homes in Groningen province cost 7.9% more in the second quarter than a year earlier – the biggest rise in the country – while in Noord-Holland prices went up just 2.4%.

House prices rose 4.2% nationwide, the tenth quarter running that they have climbed, though more slowly than the 5.2% jump in the first three months of the year. After Groningen, the steepest rises were in Drenthe, Gelderland and Friesland, all above 5%.

Of the four biggest cities, The Hague rose most, at 4.5%, while Amsterdam barely moved, up 0.8%. Fewer homes sold than a year earlier in both Amsterdam and Rotterdam.

Nearly 59,000 homes changed hands across the country, 2.7% more than the same quarter last year.

As the conflict between the US and Iran escalates, the foreign affairs ministry has tightened its advice for people wanting to travel to the region.

With Iran targeting US allies in the Middle East in response to American attacks, the Dutch government has advised against travelling to Qatar, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates – which includes the popular holiday destination of Dubai – unless absolutely necessary.

That falls under the ministry’s orange travel advisory, which discourages all travel unless there’s an emergency, such as the death of a family member.

The travel advice for Bahrain has moved up to red, meaning the ministry says the Dutch embassy cannot offer help. “Whatever your situation is, don’t travel there,” the ministry said. “It’s too dangerous.”

The US, UK, Canada and Australia have also updated their travel alerts for Gulf countries in recent days.

Check the ministry’s website for the latest travel advisories.

World.title: Explosive attacks fall as task force targets young offenders
World.content:
Attacks using explosives fell by more than 17% in the first half of this year, the first substantial drop since the wave of explosions peaked in 2024, according to the government’s Offensive against Explosions (OTE) working group.

The number of explosions or attempted explosions decreased from 705 during the first half of 2025 to 581 during the same time, putting the OTE on track to achieve a 10% decrease this year.

But explosions remain a serious safety threat – and it’s mostly young people who use them to commit crimes. Almost half of all arrested suspects were minors, reports NU.nl, with fewer than one in six suspects older than 30. A large proportion of offenders are under the age of 25.

“Every attack is one too many,” said Carola Schouten, mayor of Rotterdam and chairwoman of the OTE. “But it is good to see that the number of attacks is starting to decrease nationwide… This requires continued attention and joint commitment on all fronts.”

Young offenders

Specifically, the task force is focusing on reducing the number of young offenders, finding and prosecuting those who hire them and their intermediaries and limiting the availability of explosives – in this case mostly powerful, illegally trafficked fireworks, often procured from neighbouring countries like Germany or ordered online.

“This is done, among other things, by disrupting the production, transport, storage and trade in such explosives,” said the OTE, which is also setting up a joint Europol task force with Germany and Sweden, and lobbying with France and Sweden for tighter EU rules on powerful fireworks.

But given the young age of offenders, prevention is the name of the game. The OTE has begun a pilot focusing on conflict mediation among young people, while parents, caregivers and those who work with them are being given support to make “young people more resilient to (online) temptations to crime”.

Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK.
