Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. World.title: President vetoes legal rights for same-sex couples in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to sign an agreement granting them certain rights. The proposed law would have marked the first time that Poland had recognised same-sex relationships in domestic law. However, Nawrocki argued that such a move would threaten the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. The measures in question were approved by both houses of parliament in May and June with the support of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The proposed law would have allowed couples, both same-sex and opposite-sex, to enter into a new type of contract, signed before a notary and then submitted to the registry office. It would have granted them some of the rights available to married couples, including joint property and tax settlement, access to their partner’s medical information, exemption from inheritance and gift taxes, and the right to decide about their partner’s burial if they died. However, the two main opposition parties – the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) – voted against the legislation, and Nawrocki himself also made clear that he intended to veto it. The government’s majority in parliament has approved a bill that would grant same-sex partners some of the rights available to married couples. However, President Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has made clear he will veto the law https://t.co/hx8viUN6QH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 29, 2026 On Friday morning, the president confirmed he would not be signing into law the two bills passed by parliament that would have introduced the new system. He said that the measures would effectively “introduce civil partnerships through the back door”, and that such partnerships are “intended to replace or substitute the institution of marriage”. “As the guardian of the constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the special status of marriage defined in article 18 of the constitution as a union between a woman and a man, placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” he added. Nawrocki also argued that the proposed measures were contrary to the principles of social justice because they would have granted such couples some of the privileges of marriage but without all of the same obligations. He also noted that the proposed new type of contract could be terminated far more easily than a marriage. “Marriage, which best secures family stability, cannot become one of many equally valid options offered by the state administration,” declared the president. “The family is a community fundamental to the survival of the nation.” However, Nawrocki added that, as he has previously said, he remains open to legislation that would grant loved ones rights relating to healthcare and various administrative issues. But only if it “does not create an alternative to marriage” or “introduce ideological changes to family law”. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision was condemned by Tusk, who called it “an expression of contempt toward people and their right to happiness and a normal life”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, accused the president of “turning his back on the two million Poles living today in informal relationships”. However, she pledged that “the veto will not halt social change”. If such change “cannot go through the door, then [it will go] through the window”. Kotula noted that Poland has already begun legally recognising same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union member states, after being ordered to do so by the European Court of Justice. While “not all benefits are yet available” to such couples, “this is something that I intend to deliver”, she added. Prezydenckie weto to wyraz pogardy wobec ludzi i ich prawa do szczęścia i normalnego życia. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 However, the government’s ability and willingness to take such action, even when it cannot be vetoed by Nawrocki, is hampered by internal disagreements over the issue within Tusk’s coalition. The Left (Lewica), from which Kotula hails, and Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party are generally in favour of strengthening LGBT+ rights. But they have met with resistance from more conservative elements in the coalition, in particular the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). The measures vetoed today by Nawrocki were already a compromise within the government: earlier plans to introduce same-sex civil partnerships were watered down to instead simply allow same-sex couples to sign a contract granting them certain rights. However, opinion polls show that the Polish public itself is in mostly in favour of recognising same-sex relationships. State research agency CBOS last year found its highest-ever level of support for the introduction of civil partnerships, with 62% of Poles in favour. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships. World.title: Charles Bridge Undergoes Careful Cleaning as Restorers Protect Historic Stonework
World.content:
The Prague Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) has started regular maintenance work on Charles Bridge, with restorers and specialists currently removing algae, moss and unwanted vegetation.

The work is aimed at protecting the bridge’s sandstone elements from long-term damage caused by moisture and biological growth.

According to TSK, the maintenance will continue over the coming weeks and will not affect pedestrian access or tourism on one of Prague’s most visited landmarks.

Specialists are carrying out the work using climbing equipment and a support boat, allowing them to reach areas that are difficult to access from the bridge itself. The method enables detailed cleaning while avoiding any need to close the bridge to visitors.

Experts say removing vegetation is an essential part of preserving Charles Bridge. Plants and microorganisms growing on the stone surface can retain moisture, which gradually weakens the masonry and accelerates natural deterioration.

Restorers use traditional cleaning techniques

The maintenance is being carried out manually using traditional restoration methods. Workers remove algae and other growth with controlled water pressure, silicone brushes and specialised tools.

After cleaning the stone surfaces, restorers inspect and repair the joints between individual blocks. Damaged sections are cleaned to a depth of around two to three centimetres before being refilled with traditional lime mortar designed to match historical construction techniques.

Charles Bridge is among the most valuable architectural landmarks in the Czech Republic. Construction began on July 9, 1357, under the reign of Emperor Charles IV, after the previous Judith Bridge was destroyed by floods.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum. It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Brasil Fest Returns to Brno With Performances and Public Parade
World.content:
You don’t need a plane ticket to experience the rhythms of Brazil—just a train to Brno.

Brno will once again become a hub of Brazilian culture as the city welcomes the return of Brasil Fest Brno, the largest event of its kind in Central Europe.

The three-day festival kicks off on Thursday, with a full schedule of concerts, dance performances, and street parades bringing a tropical flair to Brno’s historic center.

On Saturday, the festival’s main parade will move through the city center, joined by hundreds of dancers and musicians from across Europe and Latin America.

The route starts at Moravské náměstí and ends at Zelný trh. This year, for the first time, the parade will include a five-meter puppet of the Brno dragon, decorated in the Brazilian national colors.

The festival’s programme will open on Thursday, July 30, with a special concert by Hamilton de Holanda Trio at Špilberk Castle’s Summer Cinema.

The Brazilian mandolinist, winner of the 2025 Latin Grammy Award for Best Jazz Album, is one of the leading figures of contemporary Brazilian music.

On Friday, the festival will move to the city centre with free performances at Moravské náměstí and náměstí Svobody. Visitors can look forward to the Ritmo Factory Big Show, an energetic performance combining Brazilian-inspired percussion, dance and capoeira, followed by a concert from Mirla Riomar, a singer from Salvador da Bahia known for blending Afro-Brazilian traditions with a modern sound.

The main highlight of Brasil Fest Brno will arrive on Saturday, August 1, with the traditional carnival parade through the streets of Brno. Hundreds of dancers, drummers, capoeira performers and other artists will fill the route from Moravské náměstí to náměstí Svobody and Zelný trh, creating a colourful spectacle inspired by Brazil’s famous carnival celebrations.

A warm-up programme will begin earlier in the afternoon, followed by the parade at 16:00.

The evening programme at náměstí Svobody will continue with a Brazilian dance show featuring multiple dance groups, followed by performances from artists including Ely Janoville 4tet and Brazilian singer-songwriter MADDU, whose music reflects her northeastern Brazilian roots and combines poetic songwriting with a powerful stage presence.

The festival will conclude on Sunday, August 2, with a Family Day at Lužánky Park, offering workshops, games and creative activities for children. Young visitors will be able to make carnival masks, enjoy face painting, try dancing and join a special children’s carnival parade through the park.

World.title: Experience Czech History: Ride a 19th-Century Steam Train!
World.content:
Looking to swap your car for something more adventurous?

Take a step back in time aboard the narrow-gauge railway that winds through the Osoblaha region in the Bruntál district, near the Czech-Polish border.

This charming line, originally opened in 1898, still runs today, offering passengers a scenic ride through rolling countryside, forests, and quaint villages.

The railway stretches just over 20 kilometers, connecting Třemešná ve Slezsku to Osoblaha, and is the only narrow-gauge track of its kind in Czechia still in regular seasonal use.

From May to November, visitors can hop aboard historic steam or motor locomotives. With windows down and the rhythm of the train echoing across the fields, it’s a peaceful way to experience this remote corner of the Moravian-Silesian Region.

Find more info here

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kolej na Brochowie (@kolejnabrochowieofficial) History

The railway was built with a narrow 760 mm gauge, and its construction began in the spring of 1898. The first official train ran later that same year, on December 14. After World War I, it became part of the newly formed Czechoslovak State Railways (ČSD). During World War II, in 1938, the line was seized by the German Reich Railways, which introduced eight-wheel carriages and specially designed trailers for standard-gauge wagons. Despite heavy damage to the region during the liberation battles of 1945, the track itself remarkably survived. However, the condition of the trains was poor, and restoring operations required significant effort. By the mid-1980s, the railway underwent extensive renovations, bringing both the track and rolling stock up to modern safety standards. Today, it’s a beloved heritage line, not just for tourists, but for railway enthusiasts from across Europe.

World.title: Prague Airport Unions Declare Strike Readiness Over New CEO Appointment
World.content:
Five trade unions at Václav Havel Prague Airport and ČSA Handling have announced strike readiness over the appointment of Radomír Lašák as the new head of Letiště Praha.

The unions’ announcement does not currently affect airport operations. Prague Airport confirmed that all flights are operating normally and passengers should not expect disruptions, delays, or cancellations.

The labour groups oppose Lašák’s appointment, pointing to his previous role in the management of Czech Airlines before the carrier entered bankruptcy proceedings. They have also raised concerns about the transparency of the selection process for the airport’s top executive position.

Trade union representatives are seeking more information about possible future changes to the airport’s management structure, financial strategy, and personnel policy. They argue that employees have not received sufficient guarantees about the company’s future direction.

Additional concerns emerged after Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the government was considering a possible stock market listing of part of Prague Airport’s shares. Unions fear that such a move could bring changes to the airport’s operations and affect job security.

Finance Minister Alena Šillerová rejected the concerns, saying there was no reason for employees to worry. According to her, Lašák was selected as the strongest candidate through an open recruitment process, and the government is not planning mass layoffs or major organisational changes.

Šillerová is scheduled to meet with trade union representatives on Tuesday to discuss their concerns directly.

The announced strike readiness remains in effect from July 21 until it is officially withdrawn. If Lašák’s appointment receives final approval from the government’s personnel committee, he will replace Jiří Pos, whose term as head of Prague Airport ends at the end of August.

World.title: Prague Petřín Cable Car Ticket Price to Rise to 100 CZK After Reopening
World.content:
Passengers using the iconic Petřín Cable Car will pay more when the service resumes in September.

The city council has approved a new fare of 100 CZK for a single ride, up from the previous 60 CZK.

The increase comes after a two-year shutdown during which the historic line underwent major reconstruction. The cable car has been out of operation since September 2024, with new vehicles built in Switzerland now undergoing final testing before returning to service.

The first passengers are expected to board the renewed cable car in September, but the experience will come at a higher cost.

Passengers who purchase tickets electronically will pay a discounted fare of 90 CZK.

Children under 15 and seniors over 65 will continue to travel free of charge. The ride will also remain included in Prague’s 24-hour and 72-hour public transport tickets, as well as long-term travel passes.

The Petřín Cable Car, one of Prague’s most popular attractions, connects the Újezd area with Petřín Hill and provides access to one of the city’s most visited viewpoints. The service has been closed while the track, technology and vehicles were being upgraded.

The newly manufactured cars feature a modern design and are currently completing mandatory operational tests before the official reopening.

World.title: Five Legendary Ballets in One Night at Prague’s Hybernia Theatre
World.content:
Prague’s Hybernia Theatre is hosting a series of special evenings dedicated to classical ballet, bringing together some of the most celebrated scenes from the world’s best-known productions.

The upcoming Classic Ballet Gala will take place on July 22, 25 and 29.

More info about the program here.

The performance will feature students and graduates of the conservatory, presenting excerpts from legendary ballets including Don Quixote, Swan Lake, The Nutcracker, Sleeping Beauty and Le Corsaire.

Rather than focusing on a single full-length production, the gala will offer audiences the opportunity to experience highlights from several major works in one evening.

The young dancers will perform in specially prepared costumes and under the guidance of experienced teachers, including former soloists of the National Theatre Ballet. The artistic concept and dramaturgy of the evening are overseen by Pamela Morávková and Jiří Horák.

The programme will combine the dramatic energy of Don Quixote, the romantic atmosphere of Swan Lake, the fantasy world of The Nutcracker, the fairy-tale elegance of Sleeping Beauty, and the adventure of Le Corsaire.

Founded in 1945, the Prague Dance Conservatory is the oldest and largest institution of its kind in the Czech Republic. Over eight decades, the school has educated generations of dancers, choreographers, ballet masters and teachers who have performed on stages in the Czech Republic and abroad.

Its students regularly take part in international competitions and represent Czech dance at festivals and cultural events around the world.

World.title: Look Up! JAS 39 Gripen Jets to Fly Over Prague on Wednesday
World.content:
Prague residents will have the chance to see JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets flying above the city on Wednesday, July 22.

The aircraft will take part in a ceremonial event at the National Memorial on Vítkov.

The flyover is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. and will be carried out as a training flight connected with the ceremony.

According to information from Prague 4 City Hall, the jets will approach the capital from the east, flying over areas including Běchovice, Dolní Počernice and Žižkov.

The aircraft will then turn south over Prague Castle before continuing their return route through Podolí, Nusle and Hostivař. After completing the flight over the city, the jets will head back to their base in Pardubice.

The route means residents in several parts of Prague may be able to see the aircraft, depending on weather conditions and visibility.

Military aircraft flights over the capital are relatively rare but not unusual. In March 2024, crowds gathered in central Prague to watch a large military flyover marking the 25th anniversary of the Czech Republic joining NATO.

That event included five fighter jets and an Airbus aircraft, which flew over landmarks including Charles Bridge. The fighter jets later returned to their bases, while the Airbus landed at Prague’s Václav Havel Airport.

The Czech Air Force regularly uses ceremonial flights to mark important national events and military anniversaries, while also serving as training exercises for pilots.

World.title: Mayor: Budapest’s busiest M3 metro to be extended after EU funding secured!
World.content:
Budapest’s busiest metro line is set to be extended after the Hungarian government confirmed funding for the long-awaited northern expansion of the M3 metro.

The announcement was made on Wednesday by Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy during the presentation of the government’s new Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan. The project will be financed through European Union funds.

The extension will take the M3 metro line beyond its current northern terminus at Újpest-központ to Rákospalota-Újpest railway station, creating a new interchange with suburban rail services.

Mayor welcomes ‘historic day’

Reacting to the announcement on Facebook, Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony described the decision as a “historic day” for public transport in Hungary. He said the capital had long argued that no seven-year EU budget cycle should pass without a major metro investment in Budapest.

Karácsony also criticised the previous Orbán government, saying its policies had cost the country valuable time and funding, but added that the new government had managed to “save what can still be saved” by securing EU financing for transport projects.

Plans already prepared for further extension

According to the mayor, detailed plans have already been completed for extending the M3 metro line all the way to Káposztásmegyer, one of Budapest’s largest residential districts. However, he said that, given current financial and time constraints, only the first phase as far as Rákospalota-Újpest can be delivered for now.

Karácsony nevertheless described the project as a major step forward because it can be coordinated with planned suburban railway developments, improving connections for both Budapest residents and commuters travelling into the capital from surrounding towns.

Part of wider rail modernisation programme

The metro extension forms part of the government’s newly announced 10-year railway investment programme, worth approximately HUF 3,550 billion (EUR 9.7 billion). Read more about it here!

Alongside the M3 metro line extension, the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan includes new InterCity trains, a replacement fleet for Budapest’s HÉV suburban railway, station modernisation projects, preparations for an airport rail link and upgrades to major railway corridors across Hungary.

The government says the programme is intended to modernise Hungary’s rail network and strengthen cooperation between national and Budapest transport developments.

World.title: Orbán declares “We’re fine” as Fidesz launches ‘resistance’ campaign against Hungary’s new government
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán insisted that “we’re fine” as Fidesz sought to regroup after its heavy election defeat, unveiling a new strategy that frames the party as the leader of a nationwide “resistance” against what it calls Hungary’s new “authoritarian” political system.

Speaking outside Fidesz headquarters alongside the party’s newly elected parliamentary group leader János Bóka, Orbán accused the new government of dismantling the rule of law through constitutional amendments and pledged that Fidesz would fight back using “every peaceful means” available.

Fidesz forced outside after server seizure

The press conference was held outside the party’s headquarters after prosecutors reportedly seized Fidesz’s servers as part of the ongoing investigation into the National Cultural Fund (NKA) case. Orbán claimed the seizure left the party without internet access and unable to operate its internal systems.

“We did not expect to be holding this press conference under these circumstances,” he said.

He described the investigation as politically motivated, arguing that authorities had effectively paralysed the party by confiscating its communications infrastructure and membership database.

Orbán: Hungary is no longer a democracy

The former prime minister said Hungary had entered a fundamentally new political era following the latest constitutional amendment, comparing the situation to the final years of Hungary’s communist Kádár era. According to Orbán, the amendment unlawfully restricted who can stand in parliamentary elections, depriving voters of their democratic choice.

He also argued that the removal of former President Tamás Sulyok marked the collapse of constitutional checks and balances. Orbán claimed the current political system is “illegitimate” and declared that Sulyok was “the last legitimate President of the Republic”, quotes 24.hu. He added that Fidesz would not recognise public office holders appointed under the new constitutional framework.

Fidesz launches “resistance” campaign

Orbán said the party’s newly adopted “Declaration of Resistance” commits Fidesz to restoring Hungary’s democratic rule of law. While he declined to explain exactly how the party intends to organise its campaign, saying he would reveal more details during his upcoming speech at Tusványos, he stressed that all action would remain peaceful.

According to Orbán, Fidesz will continue participating in parliamentary work rather than boycotting the legislature. He also said the party does not intend to dictate the pace of opposition activity, describing Fidesz instead as a “service centre” supporting all Hungarians who oppose what he called political authoritarianism.

“We’re fine”

One of the most striking moments came when Orbán was asked whether Fidesz had been weakened following last week’s political setbacks and poor polling. His response quickly became the headline of the press conference.

“We did not support the creation of this system. We’re fine.”

Orbán argued that the real question is how long former Tisza Party voters will tolerate what he described as an increasingly authoritarian government. He predicted that resistance would gradually become a broad national movement rather than one based on party politics or ideology.

Stay up-to-date: Fidesz’s parliamentary group elected new leader after previous one stepping down

Szijjártó’s new job praised

Orbán also defended former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó, who recently left Parliament to take up a senior position at Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD. He said he had fully supported Szijjártó’s decision.

“A very important role still awaits him in Hungarian public life. That won’t be tomorrow, but the day after tomorrow. It is also important that he is working in a place that holds enormous value and opportunities for Hungary.”

Bóka added that outstanding personnel issues within the parliamentary group would be settled before Parliament’s autumn session begins.

More on Orbán and Fidesz: Former prime minister says from now on, their mission is “to restore the democratic rule of law”

Private US trip

Responding to questions about his recent visit to the United States during the FIFA World Cup, Orbán insisted he had travelled privately and paid for the trip himself. He confirmed that he had held unofficial, non-public meetings while in the US but declined to reveal any details.

Joking about the cost of attending the tournament, Orbán remarked that he was glad the World Cup only takes place every four years because he could not afford it annually.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary’s Public Prosecutor resigns
World.content:
Hungary’s Public Prosecutor, Gábor Bálint Nagy, submitted his resignation on Wednesday, according to a statement published on the Prosecutor General’s Office website.

‘The prosecution service must not become a political tool’

In a statement also sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), Nagy said safeguarding the independence and authority of the justice system, including the prosecution service, is one of the cornerstones of a democratic institutional framework.

He stressed that the prosecution service “must not become an instrument in the struggles of political actors” and should not serve as an arena for day-to-day political interests or power battles.

“To make this unequivocally clear, today I submitted my resignation through the acting President of the Republic in a declaration addressed to the Deputy Speaker exercising the powers of the Speaker of the National Assembly, initiating the termination of my mandate with effect from 25 August 2026,” Nagy said.

His resignation is set to take effect on 25 August 2026, subject to the relevant constitutional procedures.

PM Magyar reacts

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar reacted on Facebook:

“The Public Prosecutor has just resigned. With this, the country has rid itself of another Orbán puppet who was obstructing the democratic transition. Gentlemen, who will be next?”

World.title: Four Hungarian paramedics beat intoxicated patient unconscious three times
World.content:
Four paramedics in southern Hungary have been charged with repeatedly assaulting an intoxicated patient inside a hospital detoxification unit, allegedly beating him until he lost consciousness three times.

According to the Baranya County Prosecutor’s Office, the incident took place in November 2025 at the Emergency Clinic of the University of Pécs Clinical Centre. Prosecutors have requested suspended prison sentences and a ban preventing all four defendants from working in healthcare, the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) reported.

Patient allegedly assaulted after trying to leave detox unit

According to the indictment, the man had been taken to the emergency department after suffering a head injury in the street. Because he was intoxicated, he was placed in a detoxification room.

Prosecutors say the patient did not want to remain there. He reportedly shouted and repeatedly punched the door while attempting to leave.

The indictment alleges that the four healthcare workers, who were employed as paramedics and registered nurses, entered the room on several occasions and assaulted the man, sometimes together and sometimes individually.

Allegations include punches, kicks and spitting

According to prosecutors, the patient was punched and slapped in the head and face, kicked in the head and legs, had his coat pulled over his head, and was spat on by one of the defendants.

The prosecution alleges that the assaults caused the man to lose consciousness on three separate occasions.

The charges relate to repeated assault committed in a group by persons performing a public duty, along with other offences.

Trial to determine criminal responsibility

The case will now be heard by the Pécs District Court, where the defendants will have the opportunity to respond to the allegations.

The prosecutor’s office is seeking suspended custodial sentences rather than immediate imprisonment, while also requesting that the four defendants be prohibited from practising healthcare professions if convicted.

The charges have been filed, but no verdict has yet been reached.

World.title: Hungary unveils EUR 10 billion railway modernisation: New trains, airport rail link and faster journeys promised!
World.content:
The Hungarian government has unveiled what it describes as one of the largest railway development programmes in the country’s history, committing around HUF 3,550 billion (EUR 9.8 billion) to modernising the national rail network by 2035.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy presented the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station in Budapest on Wednesday.

According to the government, the programme is intended to reverse decades of underinvestment, improve reliability, modernise rolling stock and make rail a more competitive alternative to driving.

Dávid Vitézy and Péter Magyar at the press briefing. Photo: MTI

Railway seen as a national strategic priority

Speaking at the launch, Magyar said railway development was not simply a transport policy but a matter of national strategy, affecting economic competitiveness, regional development, labour mobility and Hungary’s international connections.

He argued that rail investment should become a long-term national project extending beyond individual government terms, noting that many European countries are increasingly prioritising rail transport because of its environmental and economic benefits.

The prime minister also criticised the previous government’s approach, saying Hungary must catch up after years of neglect.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy and Prime Minister Péter Magyar. Photo: Facebook/Vitézy Dávid

Six priorities for Hungary’s rail network

The Baross Gábor plan is built around six main objectives:

faster, more reliable rail links to every county seat;

preserving and modernising regional railway lines;

expanding suburban rail services around Budapest and major provincial cities;

strengthening cooperation with Budapest on transport projects;

increasing rail freight capacity to reduce road traffic; and

improving international rail connections.

Among the longer-term ambitions are preparations for a rail link to Budapest Airport, further studies into high-speed rail, and closer cooperation with neighbouring countries, including the proposed Visegrád high-speed railway network.

New InterCity trains, HÉV fleet and station upgrades

One of the centrepieces of the programme is the renewal of Hungary’s ageing rolling stock.

The government plans to purchase at least 35 new InterCity trainsets and 42 new HÉV suburban railway trains, while preparations will begin immediately for the comprehensive renovation of Hungary’s ten busiest railway stations.

The programme also aims to eliminate many permanent speed restrictions, expand rail capacity, improve digital passenger services and better integrate train and bus timetables.

According to official figures presented at the event:

the average age of Hungary’s railway vehicles is 43 years;

almost half of all railway seats lack air conditioning;

around 40% of the rail network is subject to speed restrictions; and

approximately one-quarter of the Hungarian State Railway’s (MÁV) rolling stock is currently out of service.

The government’s target is to significantly reduce the average age of trains, improve reliability and eventually achieve an average station-to-station speed of at least 100 km/h on main railway lines.

Projects already taking shape

While the government presented the plan as a new long-term strategy, many of the proposed projects have previously been discussed by Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy.

Expected developments include:

new tram-train routes around Miskolc and Debrecen;

modernisation of the Budapest–Szeged, Budapest–Miskolc and Budapest–Lajosmizse railway lines;

upgrading the Szabadbattyán–Lepsény section towards Lake Balaton;

improvements to the Budapest–Vienna corridor;

further planning for the proposed Warsaw–Prague–Bratislava–Budapest high-speed railway; and

replacement of ageing HÉV trains serving Szentendre, Ráckeve and Csepel.

Several previously suspended railway projects around Budapest are also expected to resume under the programme.

Funding from EU sources and international financing

According to Vitézy, the programme’s HUF 3,550 billion budget would come from several sources. The current funding plan includes:

HUF 1,100 billion from EU Cohesion Funds;

from EU Cohesion Funds; HUF 700 billion from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF);

from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF); HUF 400 billion in loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB);

in loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB); HUF 400 billion through concession-based investments; and

through concession-based investments; and HUF 950 billion earmarked for projects in the EU’s 2028–2034 funding cycle.

The government says the programme aims not simply to deliver individual infrastructure projects, but to create a faster, more reliable and passenger-focused railway system capable of competing with road transport by 2035.

World.title: Video: PM Magyar spat on at Budapest railway station before major rail announcement
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar was spat on by a man at Budapest’s Nyugati railway station on Wednesday morning, shortly before unveiling the government’s new railway development strategy alongside Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy.

The incident, which was captured on video, occurred as the two politicians were at Nyugati railway station ahead of a press conference presenting the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

Man confronts prime minister

According to footage published by Hungarian media, a man approached Magyar and Vitézy at Nyugati station.

The man reportedly shouted: “How could you? You dared to come here?!” When he received no response, he spat at the prime minister from behind.

Magyar reacted calmly, wishing the man “good health” before commenting:

“This is what remains of the faces of Fidesz.”

He then added that perhaps this was why former Transport Minister János Lázár had not travelled by train.

Political tensions still high

It is not the first time a politician from the governing Tisza Party has reported being spat on in public. In November 2025, MP Kriszta Bódis said she had been spat on in the street.

Commenting on this new incident on Wednesday, Bódis wrote that those serving in public life must sometimes endure unfair treatment, adding that she believed years of political hate campaigns had contributed to such behaviour and expressing hope that public discourse would improve.

World.title: ‘They knelt on my head’: New witness testimonies reveal alleged abuse in Hungary’s ‘gold convoy’ scandal
World.content:
Newly obtained witness testimonies have shed light on one of the biggest political and diplomatic scandals of the final weeks of Viktor Orbán’s government, with Ukrainian cash couriers alleging they were subjected to physical abuse and unlawful detention after a dramatic counter-terrorism raid in Hungary in what has since been called the “gold convoy” scandal.

The testimonies, published by Hungarian investigative outlet 444.hu, were given by the seven Ukrainian couriers between 27 May and 10 July via video link as part of an investigation into suspected unlawful detention. The witnesses describe what they say happened after Hungary’s Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) stopped their convoy carrying more than HUF 27 billion (EUR 74 million) worth of gold and foreign currency on 5 March.

The allegations are the couriers’ account of events and have not been proven in court. However, 444 reports that the testimonies are largely consistent with one another and do not contradict internal documents or previous witness statements from Hungarian authorities that have emerged during the investigation.

‘Someone knelt on my head’

According to the testimonies, the convoy had collected the shipment from a Raiffeisen Bank branch in Vienna before obtaining the necessary customs documentation at Vienna Airport. After crossing into Hungary, police reportedly inspected the documents at the Austrian-Hungarian border and allowed the vehicles to continue.

The situation changed after the convoy passed Budapest. Witnesses say police directed the vehicles into a MOL petrol station near Vecsés, where heavily armed TEK officers surrounded them. The couriers allege they were forced onto the ground, handcuffed, blindfolded with masks placed over their eyes, searched, and separated.

One courier recalled:

“When they removed my bulletproof vest, they stepped on my head. Then someone crouched beside me and knelt on my head.”

According to the testimonies, officers repeatedly demanded to know where weapons were hidden, despite no firearms reportedly being found during the operation.

The confiscated assets. Photo: MTI/Magyarország Kormánya

Convoy leader alleges beating while in custody

The most serious allegations concern convoy leader Hennadiy Ivanovych Kuznetsov, a retired Ukrainian intelligence officer.

He told investigators that he was questioned extensively about his previous military and intelligence service before his health deteriorated while in custody. Kuznetsov claimed that instead of receiving his medication, several officers forcibly attempted to move him into a wheelchair.

He alleged that during the incident he was repeatedly struck in the face and kicked in an injured leg.

“I screamed incoherently,” he reportedly told investigators, adding that he could not identify those involved because several officers wore masks.

Kuznetsov also claimed he was injected with an unknown substance before later being taken to hospital. According to previous testimony from former TEK director János Hajdu, the convoy leader was treated at two Budapest hospitals while remaining in TEK custody.

Viktor Orbán and János Hajdu. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Other witnesses report hearing screams

Several other couriers said they heard shouting during the interrogations. One witness said that while being questioned, he heard “terrible screaming” coming from another room that lasted for about a minute and sounded as though someone was in severe pain.

According to earlier evidence cited by 444, a senior official at Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) was also informed by colleagues that shouting could be heard during the questioning, although the official said they did not know what had caused it.

Background: Hungary’s ‘gold convoy’ affair

The case became one of the most controversial episodes before Hungary’s April general election.

The convoy was transporting cash and gold belonging to Ukraine’s state-owned Oschadbank from Austria to Ukraine. Lawyers representing both the Ukrainian bank and Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank have consistently maintained that the shipment was fully documented and legally transported with the required permits.

Despite this, the previous Orbán government suggested the shipment could be linked to money laundering and, without presenting public evidence, hinted at possible connections to financing the opposition Tisza Party.

Subsequent investigations took a different turn. The confiscated assets have since been returned to the Ukrainian bank, while Hungarian prosecutors are reportedly preparing to close the money laundering investigation against the couriers due to a lack of evidence of any crime.

Meanwhile, the investigation into the conduct of Hungarian authorities has continued.

On 29 June, former TEK director János Hajdu was formally named as a suspect on suspicion of unlawful detention involving the mistreatment of detainees.

Earlier reporting by Hungarian media also suggested that prosecutors have examined the role of several former senior officials involved in authorising the operation, while previous reports claimed the raid itself had been ordered at the highest political level.

World.title: Hungary submits landmark bill to open Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
The Hungarian government has submitted a new bill to Parliament that would pave the way for the most comprehensive disclosure yet of Communist-era state security files, fulfilling what it describes as a promise left unfulfilled since the country’s democratic transition more than three decades ago.

According to the government’s statement, the legislation was finalised after a public consultation and seeks to replace previous piecemeal measures with an entirely new legal framework governing the disclosure of documents created by the Communist dictatorship’s secret services.

Government aims for greater transparency with opening Communist-era files

The cabinet argues that previous governments have repeatedly attempted to uncover the activities of the Communist-era state security apparatus since the regime change, but none of those initiatives proved either comprehensive or successful.

It said the continued secrecy surrounding the identities and activities of informants who monitored innocent citizens has undermined public trust in state institutions and politicians. The government maintains that confronting the country’s past and ensuring the transparency of public institutions are essential pillars of a democratic state governed by the rule of law.

According to the proposal, the legislation is intended to restore public confidence, provide moral redress for victims of the Communist regime and deepen historical understanding by making agent files available to the public as extensively as possible.

Historical archives to make records widely accessible

A key element of the bill is the expanded role of the Historical Archives of the State Security Services. The institution would be tasked with making previously classified documents available in the simplest and broadest possible way.

To facilitate public access, the government plans to launch a dedicated online platform where documents can be searched and viewed digitally.

Parliament has already approved preparatory measures for the disclosure process through earlier legislation. The newly submitted bill is designed to regulate the entire process from publication to data protection.

Disclosure to happen in several stages

The government also outlined a timetable for releasing the records. The first documents expected to become publicly available will be the so-called “six cards” (hatos kartonok) and the notorious magnetic tape archives, shortly before the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.

The six cards contain information relating to the recruitment of informants into the Communist-era surveillance network. Meanwhile, the magnetic tapes are digital copies created in January 1990 containing several state security databases:

the G database, covering operational records;

the H database, containing the network register of informants; and

the K database, the Central Counterintelligence Registry.

According to the government, these databases were copied onto magnetic tapes without systematic organisation at the time.

Throughout the remainder of the year, authorities plan to gradually publish the surviving B dossiers, which include recruitment files, evaluations of recruited individuals, the identities of people connected to the network and records indicating from whom informants gathered intelligence.

Privacy safeguards remain part of the process

Before any material is published, officials will review the documents to determine whether disclosure would infringe the fundamental rights, privacy or human dignity of individuals mentioned in the files. Particularly sensitive personal information—including details concerning an individual’s health, pathological addictions or sexual orientation—will only be made accessible under strict legal conditions.

The government says the legislation seeks to strike a balance between the public interest in understanding the past, academic freedom, individuals’ rights to informational self-determination and the protection of national security interests that remain relevant today.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar’s first major misstep? What the presidential nomination really revealed

A promise dating back to the democratic transition

The government says the legislation represents a significant step towards historical accountability and will help both researchers and the wider public better understand Hungary’s Communist past.

By opening the archives, the cabinet argues it is delivering on a commitment first made during the democratic transition more than 30 years ago, while creating a legal framework intended to reconcile transparency with privacy protections and national security considerations.

World.title: Survey: Doctors enjoy highest degree of trust in Romania, but half of respondents question vaccines
World.content:
Around 54% of Romanians have a lot or very much trust in doctors. At the same time, half of Romanians disagree or are hesitant when it comes to the safety of vaccines, according to a new Poll/Int Romania Barometer conducted by the Political Rating Agency (ARP)

According to the survey, 72.1% of Romanians believe that Romania is heading in the wrong direction, while only 16.9% believe that the country is moving in a good direction. Another 11% did not express an opinion.

Compared with April, the public perception has changed very little, indicating that dissatisfaction with the country's direction remains at a high level. The authors of the report emphasized that the lack of trust is not limited to the political class, but affects several areas of society, as cited by Digi24.

Asked who they trust the most, Romanians first indicated doctors. More than half of respondents (54.1%) say they have a lot or very much trust in this professional category.

Teachers rank second, with 48.9%. Far behind are private companies (27.5%), banks (27.4%), town halls (27.3%) and foreign investors (24.9%). The press is trusted by only 16.2% of respondents, while influencers and social media content creators rank last, with only 7.7%.

The report also showed important differences between population groups. For example, young people have less trust in the press and more trust in influencers, while people over the age of 60 show the opposite tendency. In addition, people aged between 40 and 60 have a lower level of trust in doctors and teachers compared with other age groups.

The barometer showed that only 56.7% of respondents believed that vaccines are generally safe. The rest either disagreed or hesitated to provide a clear answer, which, according to the authors, indicates a significant erosion of trust in vaccination.

Regarding children's immunization, the level of support is higher. Almost two-thirds of respondents (64.9%) believe that it is important for children to receive vaccines recommended by doctors. Even so, more than one-third of survey participants do not express firm agreement with this statement. Trust in vaccines was lower in rural areas, among people with lower levels of education, and among AUR voters or undecided voters.

The survey also revealed a high level of distrust regarding the quality of products sold in Romania. Around 52.8% of respondents said that international products sold in Romanian stores are of lower quality than those sold in Western countries.

Only 20.3% believed they are at the same level, and 6.5% said that products in Romania are actually of better quality than those in Western countries.

According to the report's conclusions, the population's level of trust is closely linked to electoral preferences.

The survey was conducted between June 30 and July 3, 2026, on a representative sample of 1,774 adults, through telephone and online interviews. The maximum margin of error is ±2.8%.

World.title: Nearly half of Romanians would accept authoritarian regime that ensured order, stability
World.content:
Around 46.3% of Romanians would accept an authoritarian regime if it provided more order and stability, according to the latest INSCOP survey.

On the other hand, 47.2% of survey participants believe that democracy is preferable, even if it sometimes involves more conflicts and political debates. The rest chose not to answer.

Those who declared that they prefered democracy in a significantly higher proportion than the average were Liberal (PNL) and USR voters, men, young people under 30, people with higher education, and residents of large urban areas.

AUR voters, people aged between 45 and 59, those with primary education, and rural residents prefered a less democratic regime because it provides more order and stability, in a higher proportion than the rest of the population.

Split down party lines, 59% of AUR voters said they would prefer a less democratic regime. Around 45% of Social Democrat (PSD) voters said the same, and so did 27% of PNL voters and 14% of USR voters.

There is, however, a pro-democracy majority. Roughly 60.6% of respondents said that it is more important for power to be democratically controlled, even if decisions are made more slowly. At the opposite end, 29.5% believe that it is more important for decisions to be made quickly, even if power is controlled democratically to a lesser extent. The share of non-responses is 9.8%.

Those who stated that it is more important for power to be democratically controlled, in a higher proportion than the average, were PNL and USR voters, people aged between 45 and 59, those with higher education, residents of Bucharest and large urban areas.

Those who believe that it is more important for decisions to be made quickly, in a significantly higher proportion than the rest of the population, were AUR voters, people aged between 30 and 44, those with primary education, and rural residents.

“The majority continues to support democratic control of power even at the cost of a slower decision-making process, which shows that democratic principles still maintain an important basis of legitimacy. The tension between these two attitudes reflects the existence of a vulnerable democratic culture, in which a significant part of society is willing to relativize democratic norms when it perceives that they no longer provide order, efficiency and stability,” said Remus Ștefureac, director of INSCOP Research.

The Informat.ro – INSCOP Research BAROMETER is a monthly opinion poll conducted by INSCOP Research at the request of the Informat.ro news platform, in partnership with the Strategic Thinking Group think tank. Data were collected using the CATI method (telephone interviews), with a simple random sample size of 1,100 people, representative of significant socio-demographic categories (gender, age, occupation) for Romania's non-institutionalized population, aged 18 and over. The maximum accepted margin of error of the data is ±2.95%.

World.title: Romanian prime minister Ilie Bolojan congratulates new Moldovan PM Vasile Tofan
World.content:
Romania’s acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan sent congratulations to Vasile Tofan, who was confirmed as the Republic of Moldova’s new prime minister on Tuesday, July 21.

"I assure him of the full support and cooperation of the government of Romania. It is important that we continue to move forward with the projects on our bilateral agenda, from transportation and energy interconnection projects to those in the fields of culture and education," acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan wrote on X.

He also praised "Chișinău's progress in the EU accession process: As I have said on other occasions, Romania remains its most active and dedicated supporter."

Vasile Tofan’s cabinet was approved by the Moldovan Parliament on July 21, receiving the votes of the 53 deputies of the governing PAS party out of 101.

Asked where he would like to make his first foreign trip during an interview, Vasile Tofan indicated Romania, mentioning the strategic partnership linking the two countries. "We have not yet agreed on the first visit. I believe we have a strategic partnership with Romania. I would like it to be Romania," replied the new prime minister.

"Now I understand that the political situation in Romania is a little more complicated than ours, but if you ask me where I would like to go on my first visit, I would like to go to Romania," Vasile Tofan added during the program "În PROfunzime" on ProTV Chișinău, in reference to Romania’s ongoing political crisis.

He also said that a second important destination would be Brussels. As PM-designate, Tofan said he would accelerate Moldova’s accession to the EU.

In the same interview, Tofan said he has two citizenships, "like all well-intentioned Moldovans" (with dual citizenship), those of the Republic of Moldova and Romania. He added that around a third of all Moldovans are in the same situation.

Tofan, 44, studied at Erasmus University Rotterdam and Harvard Business School, and speaks fluent English, French, Dutch, Ukrainian, and Russian.

He worked as an investor through Horizon Capital, a fund with approximately USD 1.6 billion in assets under management, focused on Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova. He led investments in the companies Purcari, Glass Container Company, and Maib. He was a member of the boards of directors of AmCham Moldova, Startup Moldova, and Media Alternativa (TV8/1TV).

Earlier this month, the previous Moldovan PM, Alexandru Munteanu, announced his resignation amid an investigation by Ziarul de Gardă into the state-owned enterprise MoldATSA, the body charged with air traffic safety in the Republic of Moldova.

World.title: Romania’s weather agency issues red alert for Tulcea county amid widespread storm warnings
World.content:
The National Meteorological Administration (ANM) issued a red weather warning for Tulcea county as heavy rain, strong winds, and severe thunderstorms are expected to affect parts of Romania through Thursday morning, July 23. Yellow and orange alerts have also been issued for several other regions, with forecasters warning of torrential rain, hail, and damaging wind gusts.

The red alert for Tulcea is in effect from 6:00 p.m. on Wednesday until 6:00 a.m. on Thursday. Forecasters expect exceptionally severe weather, including torrential rainfall, frequent lightning, wind gusts exceeding 80-90 km/h, and storms. Rainfall totals are forecast to reach 90-110 liters per square meter, with isolated areas receiving more than 120 l/sqm.

An orange warning covering the same period has been issued for Galați, Brăila, and Constanța counties, as well as the eastern parts of Ialomița and Călărași counties. These areas are expected to experience heavy downpours, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h, with rainfall amounts of 30-50 l/sqm and isolated totals of up to 90 l/sqm.

A yellow alert is in place overnight for eastern Muntenia, southwestern Moldova, and parts of the Eastern Carpathians, where thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, and wind gusts of 50-70 km/h are forecast.

Earlier on Wednesday, ANM issued yellow and orange warnings for large parts of the country, including Oltenia, Muntenia, Dobrogea, southern Moldova, southern Transylvania, and mountain areas, as storms moved eastward during the day.

After the red warning expires, Tulcea county will remain under an orange alert from 6:00 a.m. until noon on Thursday, with additional heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h expected.

ANM said it will update its forecasts depending on the evolution and intensity of the weather system.

World.title: Four Romanian female tennis players included in 2026 US Open main draw
World.content:
Four Romanian players have been accepted directly into the women's singles main draw of the 2026 US Open, according to the entry lists published on Wednesday, July 22, by the United States Tennis Association (USTA).

Sorana Cîrstea, ranked 17th in the WTA rankings, is the highest-ranked Romanian representative on the US Open entry list. She is followed by Jaqueline Cristian (WTA No. 41), Elena-Gabriela Ruse (WTA No. 73), and Irina-Camelia Begu, who will compete using a protected ranking, reserved for players who have been absent from the tour for an extended period due to injuries, according to Mediafax.

The 2026 US Open will take place from August 23 to September 13, with the main draw singles matches beginning on August 30.

The entry lists were compiled based on the ATP and WTA rankings of July 20. The last woman accepted directly into the main draw is Anastasia Zakharova, ranked world No. 102, while in the men's draw the last direct entrant is Filip Misolic, who entered using a protected ranking.

In the women's competition, world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka will attempt to win her third consecutive US Open title. Other leading favorites include Elena Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, and Iga Swiatek.

In the men's competition, world No. 1 Jannik Sinner will attempt to reclaim the trophy he lost last year to Carlos Alcaraz. The former recently defeated Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final to win his fifth Grand Slam title. Alcaraz, who missed the last two major tournaments due to a wrist injury, is on the entry list and hopes to return to the tour during the North American hard-court season.

The US Open initial field includes 17 former Grand Slam singles champions (11 women, six men), including 10 former US Open champions.

Among the countries represented at the US Grand Slam, the United States has the largest delegation, with 28 players accepted directly into the main draws, 14 women and 14 men.

The 128 places in each main draw will be completed by players receiving wild cards from the organizers and by athletes who qualify through the preliminary tournaments scheduled during the week preceding the start of the main draws.
