World.title: Air traffic at Bucharest airports reaches record 8.45 mln in first half of 2026
World.content:
Bucharest’s two airports, the Henri Coandă International Airport and the Băneasa "Aurel Vlaicu" International Airport, welcomed 8.45 million passengers in the first half of 2026, according to the National Company Bucharest Airports.

Traffic data for the first six months of this year indicate a significant 5.08% growth from the same period in 2025.

Air traffic growth was also reflected in the number of aircraft movements. During the first half of the year, 68,367 landings and take-offs were recorded, 3.37% more than in the January–June 2025 period.

"The results we have achieved are the effects of the new management strategy, focused on attracting new airlines, expanding the number of routes operated from Bucharest, increasing operating frequencies on existing routes, and, last but not least, optimizing the quality and safety of airport infrastructure," said Bogdan Mîndrescu, General Director of the National Company Bucharest Airports, cited by Economedia.

Henri Coandă Airport exceeded the threshold of 7.7 million passengers, but the absolute record belongs to Băneasa Airport, which reached 745,674 passengers in the first half of the year, 50,956 more than the total number of passengers recorded at this airport throughout the entire year of 2025.

"The National Company Bucharest Airports recorded solid and sustainable growth, with the priority of CNAB's management being to ensure optimal conditions for this development, with major concern for maintaining the strictest standards of safety and security for passengers and air operations at the Capital's airports," Bogdan Mîndrescu said.

Last year, the Social Democratic-led Ministry of Transport blocked a key procedural step required for the listing of Bucharest Airports Company on the Stock Exchange (BVB), then valued at around EUR 1 billion. The ministry owns roughly 80% of the company’s stocks.

World.title: CoE Commissioner for Human Rights expresses concern over illegal care homes case in Romania
World.content:
The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, addressed an open letter to Romanian acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan on Tuesday, July 21, expressing concern over the issue of the unauthorized care homes operating in Bihor County, western Romania.

The letter follows a visit to Romania that O’Flaherty conducted in May of this year, during which he gained “deep insights into the human rights situation of older persons in residential care.” The CoE official noted that Romania achieved progress in reforming social services in recent years.

“I was encouraged by the commitment demonstrated by many of those working in care homes,” he said.

The visit also revealed problems. “Older people and others in care institutions continue to be regarded as beneficiaries of services rather than fully-fledged rights holders, a perspective that warrants reconsideration across the social care system. The ongoing shortage of care services makes access difficult, particularly as Romania’s population ages and care needs are growing,” the official noted in the letter.

Similarly, some of the most vulnerable, including those living in poverty or with disabilities or mental health issues, struggle to obtain proper care.

Bihor illegal care homes

The letter, however, centered on the issue of unlicensed care homes operating illegally in various forms in Romania, particularly the ones in Bihor County, where Ilie Bolojan served as mayor of Oradea and then County Council president.

“For many years, this institution operated unlawfully, reportedly hosting thousands of vulnerable people under abusive conditions, with over a thousand deaths recorded. I welcome the recent intervention of the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism and the transfer of residents to hospitals and licensed care facilities. However, I am concerned by how long this situation persisted, despite repeated alerts from civil society and journalists,” the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights said.

The CoE official argued it would be useful to review and adopt legal provisions to combat the operation of illegal care homes and to strengthen independent monitoring mechanisms. He said Romania should establish clear procedures for reporting and investigating deaths occurring in homes for elderly people.

Michael O'Flaherty also said that care home residents should have access to mechanisms through which they can report problems and request their resolution. At the same time, the role of non-governmental organizations in promoting respect for human rights and the dignity of residents should be recognized and supported.

Care homes owner’s response

The owner of the illegal care homes in Bihor, Viorel Paşca, responded to O’Flaherty’s letter, rejecting his criticism. Paşca disputed the CoE official’s information and said that his establishment, Dumbrava, never operated as a center or a care home.

“All the locations were actually residential homes where Romanian citizens lived and had their official residence. None of them lived there illegally, were held against their will, abused, or tortured, as was claimed in the media,” he said in a post on Facebook.

Finally, Viorel Paşca criticized O’Flaherty’s appreciation for DIICOT prosecutors and the way they acted in the Dumbrava case.

The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of last month, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023. Prosecutors claim that hundreds of elderly individuals, people with severe mental disabilities, and homeless people were turned into simple “sources of income” under the guise of charitable activity. According to DIICOT, over 2,200 vulnerable persons passed through centers controlled by the group in the last 6 years.

Unlike the 2023 case, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions.

(Photo source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights on Facebook)

World.title: German company DEHN starts production at first Romanian factory in Pitești
World.content:
German electrical technology company DEHN has started production at its first manufacturing facility in Romania, located in Pitești. The new plant will supply surge protection devices for European markets and is expected to employ up to 150 people.

The facility, which began operations in July, is part of DEHN's global manufacturing network and complements the company's existing production sites in Neumarkt and Mühlhausen, Germany. While the German factories focus on high-volume, highly automated production, the Romanian site specializes in smaller production runs that require a higher degree of manual assembly, the company said.

The 9,500 sqm built-to-suit factory was developed by industrial real estate company CTP at CTPark Pitești and marks DEHN's first manufacturing investment in Romania.

“We are proud to have partnered with DEHN on its first manufacturing investment in Romania and to contribute to strengthening the country’s position as a destination for high-value industrial production. This project also reflects the growing demand we see from international manufacturers looking for flexible, future-ready facilities in strategically located industrial parks,” said Tatiana Axinte, CTP Romania Business Developer.

According to the company, Romania was selected after evaluating several locations across Europe, with factors including transport infrastructure, access to skilled workers, and proximity to technical universities contributing to the decision.

In addition to manufacturing and logistics, the Pitești site will also host support functions such as human resources, IT, marketing, and other shared services.

The factory is part of DEHN's broader strategy to expand production capacity closer to key markets. The German family-owned company, which specializes in lightning protection, surge protection, and electrical safety equipment, also opened a manufacturing facility in Mooresville, North Carolina, last year to serve customers in the United States.

Located near the A1 motorway, CTPark Pitești now comprises around 80,000 sqm of industrial space and provides direct road connections to Bucharest, Western Europe, and the Port of Constanța.

World.title: Serbia Indicts Six for Drug Trafficking Linked to North Macedonia
World.content:
Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime filed an indictment on Tuesday accusing six alleged members of an organised crime group of producing and trafficking drugs within Serbia and North Macedonia during 2025 until January 29, 2026.

The prosecution on Wednesday said the indictment was filed against Aleksandar Mijajlovic as the organiser, Ivan Dragnic as the co-organiser, and Nebojsa Spasojevic, Rade Spasojevic, Uros Mladenovski and Robert Zivkovic as members of the same crime group.

“The evidence collected … indicates that the organisers devised the group’s operational structure, established its hierarchy, assigned roles among its members in advance, and secured the financial resources necessary to carry out the criminal plan,” the prosecution said in a press release.

The group is suspected of transporting nearly five tonnes of marijuana from North Macedonia to Serbia and storing it in residential and commercial premises used by Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic in the village of Konjuh, near Krusevac, central Serbia, where the drugs were repackaged and prepared for distribution to end-buyers.

Spasojevic was a local official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the time of the bust. Serbian Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, himself from Krusevac, denied the party was involved and repeated that it was clear that there are “no protected individuals” in Serbia because they had arrested Spasojevic.

The suspects are charged with using the company Alfapharm Group, based in Skopje, as a legitimate business entity to cover the narcotics production.

The company held permits issued by the authorities in North Macedonia to cultivate and produce cannabis extracts for medical purposes.

“The company was misused to conceal the organisation of the procurement, storage, repackaging, and transportation of large quantities of the narcotic drug marijuana,” the press release said.

According to the prosecution, in November 2025, the group organised the procurement of 8,832 kilograms of dried cannabis flower from the supplier CBD Med Plant from Strumica, North Macedonia.

The drugs were stored at the premises of Alfapharm Group, weighed, repackaged and prepared for transportation. The group used documentation relating to the export of textile goods for this during international transport.

The indictment added that Robert Zivkovic is charged with managing storage of the drugs, supervising the packaging process, organising their transportation, and overseeing their unloading and storage in Serbia. Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic are alleged to have been responsible for receiving, storing, repackaging, and arranging the further transport of the drugs.

Serbian police arrested Uros Mladenovski at the end of January in Belgrade, when he collected around a hundred kilograms of marijuana from Spasojevic’s premises and transported it to the capital.

During searches of the residential and business premises used by the Spasojevic family, police discovered various arms, such as automatic firearms, ammunition, and a “Zolja” hand-held anti-tank rocket launcher.

Dragnic, Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic and Mladenovski are in detention.

Zivkovic is a fugitive. A detention order has been issued for him, and both domestic and international arrest warrants have been sought.

Aleksandar Mihailovic was arrested in Austria on July 1 and a Serbian request for his extradition is pending.

The prosecution added that proceedings are being conducted before the North Macedonian authorities as well, and that both countries “continue to cooperate and exchange information within the framework of international legal assistance”.

Serbia’s authorities on January 29 seized five tons of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, which the Serbian prosecution then suggested may have originated from North Macedonia. A week later, North Macedonia police seized more than 40 tons of drugs.

The record-breaking seizures in both countries fuelled questions about whether North Macedonia’s legalisation of marijuana grown for medicinal purposes in 2016 has encouraged illegal production and smuggling.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Access-to-Information Agency Accused of Hindering Appeals
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information. Photo: BIRN.

Legal experts and transparency advocates have criticised North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information after it began requiring electronic signatures on email appeals, arguing that this unlawfully restricts access to public information.

The Agency is the only institution responsible for deciding appeals when public bodies refuse or fail to provide information requested under the country’s freedom of information law.

Until recently, appeals could be submitted by email without additional formalities. However, the Agency has started rejecting emailed appeals unless they are certified with an electronic signature, which costs 2,000 to 4,000 denars (30 to 65 euros) annually.

Critics say the changes create an unnecessary financial and administrative obstacle to exercising a constitutionally guaranteed right.

“I believe they obstruct free access to public information in this country,” German Filkov, one of the authors of the Law on Free Access to Public Information and president of the Centre for Civil Communications, an anti-corruption and transparency watchdog, told BIRN.

Instead of creating new barriers, Filkov said, the Agency should focus on the growing number of state institutions that fail to respond to freedom of information requests.

The Agency has defended the new requirement by citing the 2015 Law on General Administrative Procedure, which it says obliges anyone communicating electronically with state institutions to use an electronic signature.

However, the State Administrative Inspectorate, which the Agency initially cited as the source of the guidance, told BIRN it had issued no written decision or instruction requiring such a practice.

One of the authors of the Law on General Administrative Procedure, which the Agency cites as the legal basis for its new practice, Skopje university law professor Borce Davitkovski, also questioned the Agency’s interpretation.

“They are not allowed to reject an appeal because it lacks an electronic signature,” Davitkovski told BIRN, noting that the law was designed to protect citizens rather than burden them with unnecessary bureaucracy.

Konstantin Bitrakov, an assistant professor at Skopje’s State Faculty of Law, argued that the Agency was misapplying the legislation and “setting a negative example for public institutions that hold information, whose decisions it is supposed to review on appeal”.

He said the legal provisions on electronic signatures apply to officials issuing administrative decisions, not to citizens filing appeals.

Lawyers told BIRN that citizens and organisations whose appeals have been rejected for lacking an electronic signature should challenge the Agency before the Administrative Court within 30 days.

The dispute comes amid concerns over access to public information.

A BIRN analysis found that the number of appeals filed with the Agency over administrative silence or incomplete responses had doubled last year, from over 300 filed in 2024 to over 600 in 2025.

The European Commission’s latest Rule of Law Report warned that some public institutions continue to reject information requests on arbitrary grounds or with significant delays.

In April, the new head of the Agency, Petar Gajdov, told BIRN in an interview: “As institutions, we are service-oriented towards citizens.”

World.title: Who Really Benefits from ‘Strategic Investor’ Status in Albania?
World.content:
A company granted a stretch of Albania’s Adriatic coastline lists its official address as the 12th floor of the European Trade Centre in Tirana, where, according to a BIRN investigation, “there was no company sign, and building staff said they were unaware of any company by that name”.

A public asset belonging to all citizens is now registered under the name of a company that cannot even be found at its own listed address – because its ownership has been ‘constructed’ as a chain of corporate shells, one nested inside another, with the final shell empty. In that vacuum is where the problem begins.

Attempts to frame the public debate over luxury tourist developments in Zvernec, on the Albanian coast, and nearby Sazan island as a choice between environmental protection and economic development are, at best, unhelpful. At worst, they are misleading.

World.title: EU’s Failure to Address Balkan Disputes Undermines Its Credibility
World.content:
It also underlines the consequences of the EU’s failure to put forward an overall strategy to address the many bilateral disputes in the Western Balkans.

North Macedonia’s current centre-right government led by Hristijan Mickovski, elected in 2024, has insisted that before it amends the constitution, Bulgaria should guarantee it will make no new demands that could further block negotiations down the road.

The background to this request relates to the long list of obstacles placed on the country’s aspirations to join the European Union ever since it applied for membership in 2004, and successive governments’ efforts to address them with varying degrees of success.

In her response, however, Commissioner Kos underlined that “EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance. It is built on trust, commitments, dedication in fulfilling these commitments and hard work”.

A week later, she repeated the same call on the government to build trust with all the EU member states.

In doing so, she seemed to forget the number of times North Macedonia’s citizens were let down by promises made by the EU which were not kept. She should acknowledge that trust can only succeed if it exists on both sides and is based on solid foundations.

Under the so-called Prespa Agreement, signed with Greece in June 2018, the country agreed to replace its constitutional name with “Republic of North Macedonia”, to be applied erga omnes. The agreement also included recognition of the Macedonian language.

In return the EU assured the country that this agreement would open the door to EU and NATO membership, only to be confronted with a French government veto in 2019, calling for a pause on EU enlargement.

This was resolved the following year with the adoption of a revised methodology for accession negotiations, and the European Council recommendation that negotiations should start with both Albania and North Macedonia.

However, Bulgaria then decided to impose its own veto against the latter, which was transformed into an EU veto in 2022, with the adoption of the French proposal. Under this proposal, formal negotiations with both countries were launched in July 2022. But until parliament in North Macedonia adopts the constitutional amendment, its accession negotiations remain blocked.

Renewed momentum flawed by unanimity rule

World.title: ‘Nobody Mentions Us’: Silence Surrounds Wartime Rape of Kosovo’s Ethnic Minorities
World.content:
Those who fled and never returned often have no means of applying for recognition as survivors of wartime sexual violence.

That includes a fourth woman interviewed by BIRN, who was 29 years old when she was raped twice by uniformed men in the police headquarters in Gjakova/Djakovica in March and April 1999. A cleaner in the building, she fled when the war ended out of fear of being targeted for revenge as a former employee of the Serbian state.

The woman now lives in the Montenegrin capital, Podgorica, but does not possess Kosovo documents.

“Living in a refugee camp for a long time, we didn’t have food, let alone a psychologist,” she told BIRN. “Sometimes I bought sedatives when I had a few dinars.”

When the war ended, ethnic minorities were targeted for revenge by Kosovo Albanian guerrillas and civilians.

Speaking to BIRN, an Egyptian woman from a village near Peja/Pec recalled five armed men entering her house on July 27, 1999, one of them in a T-shirt featuring the symbol of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA. Her husband was beaten and she was dragged into the woods. “One of them raped me, and my husband was unable to help.”

The men later went next door, where they raped the woman’s neighbour.

Three days later, the family left Kosovo. Her case was documented in a 1999 report by the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Centre. In the report, she says: “When they came, they asked me to find two other women and go with them. I told them I could not find any and begged them to let me go because I was a mother with small children. One of them threatened to kill my husband if I did not comply. Crying, I went there. They left me there, crying and dishonoured.”

However, Kosovo’s Law on the Status and Rights of Martyrs, Invalids, Veterans, Civilian Victims, and Victims of Sexual Violence only provides for recognition of survivors of wartime sexual violence between February 1998 and June 20, 1999, i.e. roughly a week after Serbian forces pulled out of Kosovo and the war ended.

The woman said she doesn’t “need” recognition. “But I am frustrated that nobody mentions us,” she said. “Egyptian Roma women have also been raped here.”

Agushi, the Roma rights activist, said rape survivors from minority communities barely feature in public discourse surrounding the war and wartime sexual violence; those raped after the official cessation of hostilities are doubly discriminated against.

“They are even more marginalised, and those who were victims of sexual violence after June 20, 1999, are particularly discriminated against because they are not legally recognised and remain in the shadows.”

Campaign of terror

World.title: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH

This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN.

“I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said.

Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions.

For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1.

If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price.

The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”.

It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff.

Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill.

Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum.

The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems.

Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious.

“This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei.

“It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country.

“It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added.

Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures.

The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism.

According to media reports, ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity.

Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases.

Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed.

The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored.

At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine.

Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview.

Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards.

“It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said.

“That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

World.title: Tests Show Faeces Contaminated North Macedonia Town’s Water Supply
World.content:
The centre of Gostivar, North Macedonia. Photo: Fazlijah/Wikimedia Commons.

Lab tests have confirmed the presence of faecal contamination in the drinking water supplied to the western North Macedonian town of Gostivar, local prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

The findings, disclosed by the Gostivar Basic Prosecutor’s Office, appear to prove that the town’s water supply is linked to an epidemic of gastrointestinal illness that has overwhelmed local health services since last week.

On Monday, police detained the head of the local public water utility, Artana Asani, and two other managers over the outbreak that has made more than 3,000 people sick so far.

The Gostivar Prosecutor’s Office said three officials are suspected of committing “serious crimes against the environment and nature through the pollution of drinking water.

“The suspects, acting together in their official capacities … made the drinking water in the overflow chamber of the system supplying Gostivar municipality and several surrounding villages unusable by introducing a harmful substance into it,” the Prosecution said.

The probe suspects the water supply became contaminated when the water company, in a presumed attempt to increase the water supply last month, connected additional pumps to the existing system that drew in water from an unhealthy surface-level source.

According to the prosecution, laboratory tests conducted by the Institute of Public Health detected faecal contamination in the water supply, including extremely high concentrations of coliform bacteria and the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli), indicating contamination with human or animal faecal matter and rendering the water unsafe to drink.

Before her arrest, water utility head Asani last week insisted the outbreak of illness in the town was not caused by water but food poisoning. But authorities pinpointed drinking water as the most likely culprit, given the sheer scale of the outbreak.

The outbreak has sent more than 3,000 people to hospitals and clinics with symptoms including severe stomach pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and nausea, making it one of the largest recorded waterborne health incidents in North Macedonia in decades.

The Health Ministry has warned that the flow of new patients is not subsiding yet and is running at about 200 to 300 new patients per day.

Meanwhile, tap water in the town of roughly 80,000 people, some 65 kilometres west of the capital, Skopje, is unusable, and the municipal and state authorities have sent trucks with bottled water for residents’ use.

The Health Ministry on Monday said some of the contaminants found in the system are not easy to deal with, so the ban on drinking tap water will likely stay in place for some time.

The incident has triggered widespread public anger, with residents questioning how contamination on this scale could have gone undetected until thousands of people had already become ill.

Gostivar Mayor Valbon Limani on Monday denied any responsibility for the crisis himself, saying he had no role in the water company.

“I do not feel any moral responsibility because the public utility company Komunalec is a separate legal entity that manages and operates the water supply system. Otherwise, the citizens who know me are aware that, had the situation been different, I would certainly have been the first to resign,” Limani said.

World.title: Hungarian PM’s Presidential Gambit Fails as Polgar Declines Nomination
World.content:
“The responsibility is entirely mine,” Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar admitted on Monday night, after he had failed to convince the world’s greatest female chess player of all time, Judit Polgar, to accept the nomination to be the country’s next president.

“I don’t feel the strength to take on the historic responsibility, therefore I am unable to accept the invitation,” Polgar, 49, posted last night, ending a day of intense speculation in Hungary and abroad.

Nominating a grandmaster as Hungary’s next president was just the latest in a series of unconventional moves by the government headed by Magyar’s Tisza party. It was a hasty decision by a government that seems to be under constant time pressure to deliver on the numerous promises it made during the campaign for the April 12 election, which it won by a landslide.

“The selection of Hungary’s next president should not be rushed, Peter Magyar is acting as if there were no time for a meaningful public debate about the country’s next head of state,” the human rights watchdog Amnesty International said in a statement.

Tamas Sulyok was regarded as an ideological presidential appointee of former prime minister Viktor Orban. According to Sulyok’s critics, he stood by as the previous government weakened democratic institutions and undermined the rule of law. As a result, voters had lost confidence in him, Magyar argued during the campaign, and his removal would be an essential step in rebuilding democracy and the system of checks of balances in Hungary.

Sulyok refused to budge for weeks until a constitutional amendment was passed on July 13 by the Tisza-dominated parliament which, among other measures, term-limited MPs to 12 years, pensioned off constitutional court judges at 70 and, in a single sentence, terminated the president’s mandate with immediate effect. Sulyok announced on Saturday he would sign the constitutional amendment, “fulfilling my obligation under the Fundamental Law [Hungary’s constitution] after carefully weighing my legal options and my conscience”.

In a lengthy video posted on Facebook, the outgoing president lamented the “end of constitutionalism” and warned that the Tisza government posed a threat to Hungarian democracy. The president has a largely ceremonial role but can block some legislation and delay appointments.

Hungary’s parliament now has 30 days to elect a new head of state, who will be in office until a new constitution is drawn up and adopted, but no longer than five years.

Magyar had promised broad public consultation in choosing the next president, saying he wanted a person capable of uniting Hungary’s deeply polarised society and representing the country abroad. But on Sunday, only hours after Sulyok had stepped down, a group of Hungarian intellectuals, athletes and public figures – mainly critics of the former Fidesz government but also some more aligned with it – published an open letter on Facebook endorsing Polgar for the presidency.

Magyar replied in a Facebook post that he would discuss the matter on Monday with Polgar, who he saw as the most suitable candidate. Tisza’s parliamentary group leader Andrea Bujdoso also described Polgar as the party’s preferred candidate for the presidency.

Some sensed a stitch-up after evidence emerged showing Magyar meeting with Polgar two weeks earlier at the US embassy’s Fourth of July reception in Budapest, where she quickly defeated the prime minister in a chess match. It remains unclear whether they discussed a possible political role before or after the event.

Polgar and her two older sisters were born into a Hungarian Jewish family and educated by their father, Laszlo Polgar, who developed an unconventional method aimed at proving that geniuses are made rather than born. The sisters did not attend school in Communist Hungary but instead spent eight to ten hours a day playing chess. The family travelled extensively around the world at a time when few Hungarians enjoyed such opportunities.

Polgar won her first championship at the age of nine and became the world’s highest-ranked female player at just 12. Throughout her career she played in the men’s league, and defeated several world champions, including Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov. “They thought I was this little girl with a cute ponytail, but I wasn’t that cute when I played,” she once said in an interview.

At the age of 15, she became the youngest grandmaster in history at the time, breaking Bobby Fischer’s longstanding record. A documentary of her life, Queen of Chess, was released earlier this year and became an instant hit on Netflix. Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has focused on educational initiatives and promoting chess among children. She is married to a veterinarian, has two children, and lives in Budapest.

Her potential nomination prompted a variety of reactions. Critics argued that Polgar has never shown any interest in politics and was never publicly critical of Orban’s government. Supporters argued it is an advantage that she has never been affiliated with any political party or movement, but is admired across the political spectrum as one of Hungary’s most accomplished and internationally respected public figures.

But most criticism was focused on the speed with which Tisza tried to rush through the nomination process, arguing that there had been little genuine public consultation despite the lack of urgency.

Fidesz politicians maintain that whoever is elected under the current circumstances will lack democratic legitimacy because of the manner in which the previous president was removed.

World.title: Lebanon PM says Beirut working for ‘complete Israeli withdrawal’
World.content:
Zawtar al-Gharbiyah – Lebanon is working towards a “complete Israeli withdrawal” from areas it occupies, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday on a visit to a village where Lebanon’s army recently deployed.

“We will continue mobilising our political and diplomatic efforts to secure a complete Israeli withdrawal from the south,” he said in Zawtar al-Gharbiya.

Israeli forces were previously present on the outskirts of the village following the war with Iran-backed Hezbollah.

Salam visited the town a day after Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met with his US counterpart Donald Trump at the White House, where he “stressed the urgent need for a full Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory”.

Under a US-sponsored agreement signed last month, Lebanon’s army is meant to disarm Hezbollah and the Israeli military is to withdraw from “pilot zones” where Lebanese forces will subsequently deploy.

Hezbollah has repeatedly rejected the agreement and refuses to lay down its weapons.

The military said on Tuesday that Israeli forces “opened fire” near troops deploying at Zawtar al-Gharbiya.

The Israeli military said it had only fired “warning shots into the air” after Lebanese soldiers entered an area that was “not part of the pilot area”.

Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war by attacking Israel in support of Tehran on March 2, prompting major Israeli airstrikes and a ground invasion.

After planting a Lebanese flag in Zawtar al-Gharbiya on Wednesday, Salam said “in parallel with the army’s deployment, we will continue opening roads, removing rubble, and securing essential services, enabling our people to return safely and with dignity to their homes and villages”.

– ‘Heads held high’ –

The war caused widespread destruction, mainly in the south, though violence has declined since the signing of a framework agreement between the United States and Iran last month and the Lebanon-Israel deal.

According to the United Nations, more than 700,000 people have returned to their homes over the past few weeks.

In Zawtar al-Gharbiya, dozens of residents waited at the village’s entrance for permission to go check on their homes.

“We will enter the town with our heads held high, thanks to the presence of the Lebanese army,” Abbas Yaghi, 73, told AFP.

The military had told residents on Tuesday to avoid entering the village “until the security situation stabilises”.

The army is conducting a sweep of the town, which is geographically contiguous with its Israeli-occupied neighbour, Zawtar al-Shariqya.

Israeli troops still launch intermittent strikes in surrounding towns, the latest on Nabatieh al-Fawqa.

“We will follow the army if it gives us permission to enter,” Mostapha Ammar, a 60-year-old resident of Zawtar al-Sharqiya said, hoping that Israel would withdraw from other areas.

Wafaa Ismail, 64, also from Zawtar al-Sharqiya, was not granted permission to enter the neighbouring village as Salam visited.

She expressed frustration at seeing the prime minister enter on his own, escorted by the army, saying: “He should have brought the people in with him so he could claim victory.”

World.title: Ukraine’s new army chief: who is Mykhailo Drapaty?
World.content:
Kyiv – Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky has announced Mykhailo Drapaty as the country’s new commander-in-chief, following a political crisis triggered by Zelensky’s surprise ousting of a young modernising defence minister.

The 43-year-old Drapaty replaces Oleksandr Syrsky, 60, an accomplished military strategist but who was long criticised for Soviet-style practices and not caring about human losses.

Here is what we know about Drapaty.

– Fighting Russian separatists –

Drapaty is a career military officer trained exclusively inside Ukraine’s independent, post-Soviet system.

He began as a lieutenant and rose through the ranks, shooting to nationwide fame during the war with Russia-backed separatists in 2014.

In a video which went viral, he commanded an infantry vehicle as it smashed through a makeshift barricade set up by pro-Moscow forces in the southern city of Mariupol.

Recalling the incident in an interview with Ukrainian media, Drapaty said his driver asked: “Major, there are barricades ahead. What do we do?”

“I said, ‘Dima, step on the gas'”.

The vehicle, with the blue-and-yellow Ukrainian flag affixed to its top, then smashes through the tyre-and-barricade wall, leaping into the air and speeding on.

During the fight with Moscow-backed rebels, Drapaty is also credited with re-capturing several settlements from Russian control and then saving his unit from being encircled.

Drapaty has a wife and kids, Ukrainian media reported.

– Backing army ‘transformation’ –

Drapaty is seen as a consensus candidate and popular choice.

He enjoys a good reputation within the military, and protesters calling for his predecessor’s removal often chanted his name as their preferred replacement.

Despite being well-known, he has kept a low profile and only rarely given interviews — in contrast with many other Ukrainian commanders.

After a string of Russian attacks on Ukrainian training grounds, he resigned from his position as ground forces commander in June 2025 — a move that set him apart as commander willing to take responsibility for mistakes.

“If we fail to draw conclusions, to change our attitude toward service, to acknowledge our mistakes, we are doomed,” he said at the time.

“That episode illustrates his decisiveness and strong ethical standards,” political commentator Volodymyr Fesenko told AFP on Wednesday.

Drapaty was immediately moved to become head of Ukraine’s joint forces command, from where he pushed for reforms inside the system.

After the dismissal of moderniser Fedorov last week, he said the “transformation” of the army must continue.

“When the right decision has to be implemented in spite of the system, rather than because of it, it means that the system itself needs to change,” he said in a rare public intervention.

“The army needs new rules,” he added.

– Hailed as ‘fresh air’ –

His nomination was hailed by many inside and outside the army.

The appointment is “wonderful news”, said Sergiy Prytula, the head of one of Ukraine’s biggest charities supporting the military.

“This is a breath of fresh air and a new hope in the struggle of free people for freedom and justice,” the ousted defence minister Fedorov, an ally, said on social media.

In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the change would not impact the course of the war.

“I don’t think this will lead to any changes on the front lines,” he told reporters, adding that Moscow intends to continue pressing on with its almost four-and-a-half-year offensive.

– Facing a ‘very difficult time’ –

Despite Ukraine being in one of its best positions on the front line in months, Drapaty faces serious challenges.

The army has been blighted by several scandals — particularly over an unpopular mobilisation drive, the treatment of conscripts and reports of widespread absenteeism and equipment shortages in some units.

“The new Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine will have a very difficult time. Much harder than he imagines,” former army chief Valery Zaluzhny — removed in 2024 — said.

The public row over the last week has exposed hidden divisions within Ukraine’s military and political leadership.

His appointment, seen as an attempt to bridge the divide, carries heavy expectations.

“Appointments made against a backdrop of social turmoil always come with many pitfalls,” said Prytula, adding that Drapaty now faces “inflated expectations”.

World.title: Iraq signs $200 billion in deals with US energy companies
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair said on Tuesday that the deals struck with US energy corporations during Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States are estimated at $200 billion.

In a televised interview, Khudair explained that the new agreements will raise Iraq’s oil production capacity, create job opportunities, and help the country achieve self-sufficiency in gas by 2030, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The deals include agreements with HKN Energy, Chevron, and Halliburton to develop the oilfields of Hamrin, West Qurna-2, Nasiriyah, Balad, Bin Omar, and Sindbad, as well as an agreement with Syria to construct the Haditha-Baniyas oil pipeline.

Khudair noted that Iraq’s current oil production capacity is 4.8 million barrels per day, but the government is in serious discussions with the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to increase oil exports.

Just like most other oil producers, Iraq has to face the issue of how to attract investments and increase production under the restrictions imposed by OPEC.

Despite having some of the world’s greatest crude oil reserves, ongoing production constraints impede Iraq’s efforts to generate revenues needed to support its growing population.

World.title: Italian FA chief says in touch with Guardiola over coaching vacancy
World.content:
Rome – The head of Italy’s football federation has confirmed he held discussions with legendary coach Pep Guardiola over the vacancy at the Italian national side but added he was “not sure that this will come about”.

Giovanni Malago revealed the talks had taken place in an interview with the website Cronache di Spogliatoio (Dressing Room Chronicles) published on Wednesday.

Asked whether the budget for the coach’s salary could be increased in the case of Guardiola, he said: “Yes, and that is the exception for obvious reasons”.

“I won’t go into detail here but it’s not sure that this will come about.

“However, I still believe it was the right thing to do. It was important to open a dialogue and keep it alive,” he added.

Guardiola has first hand knowledge of Italian football having played for Brescia and AS Roma (2001-03).

Already at a low ebb, Italian football was sent into a tailspin in March after the men’s national team failed for a third consecutive time to qualify for the World Cup.

Italy has won four World Cups.

Guardiola, 55, stepped down at Manchester City at the end of last season after winning six Premier League titles and the Champions League in his glittering decade at the Etihad Stadium.

According to Italian media reports, former Italy internationals Andrea Pirlo and Roberto Mancini — who guided the Azzurri to the Euro 2020 title — are also being considered as candidates to coach the national team, which faces Belgium on September 25 in the Nations League.

World.title: Cooler inflation hands new UK PM Burnham an early boost
World.content:
London – Britain’s annual inflation rate fell more than expected in June, driven by lower fuel prices, official data showed Wednesday, in a boost to new Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s cost-of-living push.

The Consumer Prices Index rose by 2.6 percent in the 12 months to June, down from 2.8 percent in May, the Office for National Statistics said in a statement.

Analysts’ consensus forecast had been for a slowdown to 2.7 percent last month.

Much of the fall was a result of petrol and diesel prices easing as crude prices tumbled in the wake of a ceasefire between the United States and Iran.

However, analysts expect the inflation dip to be short-lived as fresh fighting in the Middle East this month led to the collapse of a preliminary peace deal, pushing oil prices back up.

Burnham, who became prime minister on Monday, has pledged to ease cost-of-living pressures, unveiling a tax cut on household electricity prices and a £2 ($2.70) cap on single bus fares in his first days in the job.

“Falling inflation is news families want to hear but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need,” said newly appointed finance minister John Healey.

“We have chosen to focus on the cost of living in our first week, signalling that concern for working people will be at the heart of everything we do,” he added.

– ‘Higher inflation still coming’ –

Burnham announced that value-added tax (VAT) would be taken off electricity bills from October in a policy costing the Labour government about £850 million in the current UK financial year.

The measure’s start date coincides with an expected rise in the UK energy regulator’s price cap on electricity and gas bills, a consequence of the ongoing US-Iran war that will likely spur inflation.

“Higher inflation is still coming,” said Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics.

“The lagged effect from high energy prices will probably lift inflation above 3.0 percent in September and to about 3.5 percent early next year,” he said.

Higher inflation meanwhile risks hikes to UK interest rates, analysts said.

The new PM has said he wishes to ease pressure also on small businesses, hit by the previous Labour administration’s tax hikes.

At the same time, Burnham has pledged to respect the strict fiscal discipline seen under his predecessor Keir Starmer, whereby the government balances tax receipts with day-to-day state spending.

Official data Tuesday showed UK government borrowing dropped more than expected in June, handing a boost Healey, who replaced Rachel Reeves as chancellor of the exchequer.

“While the general trend in the data is encouraging… the latest flare up in US-Iran tensions and the spike in oil prices means that it is unlikely to last, regardless of the cost-of-living measures deployed by the Burnham administration,” said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury.

Burnham’s long-term goal is a “reindustrialisation” of Britain and mass building of municipal housing.

World.title: Iraq Oil Minister: $200B U.S. energy deals to boost crude output and gas by 2030
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Minister of Oil, Basim Mohammed Khudair, announced on Tuesday that the federal government is advancing a clear strategic roadmap to comprehensively expand the nation’s energy infrastructure.

Speaking during an interview on the official Al-Iraqiya News channel, the Minister confirmed that the agreements finalized during Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi’s official visit to Washington will significantly boost total crude reserves, increase daily production, and generate extensive employment and technical training opportunities across the country.

Khudair revealed that the total estimated value of the energy contracts, strategic agreements, and memorandums of understanding executed during the U.S. summit reaches approximately $200 billion, emphasizing that the active presence of top American energy firms sends a strong message of market confidence to international investors.

Key Highlights from the Washington Energy Portfolio

HKN Energy Deal: Strategic development agreement signed to expand production at the Hamrin oil field.

Chevron Expansion: Operations and development agreements covering West Qurna 2, as well as the Nasiriya and Balad fields.

Halliburton Integrated Management: Comprehensive field management pacts secured for the Bin Umar and Sindibad fields.

Syrian Export Corridor: A major cross-border pipeline agreement signed with Syria to construct and reactivate the strategic Haditha–Baniyas pipeline.

The Minister underscored that Iraq’s total crude oil production capacity has now officially crossed 4.8 million barrels per day (bpd). In response to severe disruptions caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Baghdad is actively establishing alternative export bypasses through both the Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey and the Baniyas route through Syria.

OPEC Negotiations & Domestic Energy Security

World.title: Mideast conflict lifts Brent back above $94, stocks give up gains
World.content:
Tokyo – Oil prices rose sharply on Wednesday as fresh US strikes triggered air defences in Iran, while stocks in Asia gave up earlier gains and inched higher in Europe.

Brent crude was up more than three percent, briefly hitting northwards of $94 per barrel, as President Donald Trump said the United States was “not finished” attacking Iran.

The latest round of US attacks included targets such as “military logistics infrastructure”, according to the military, while Iranian state media reported strikes around the country, including Bushehr, which hosts a nuclear power plant.

Trump also said he would “take care of” Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels if they carried out threats to blockade Saudi Arabia’s ports, something which — if realised — could be a body blow to the global economy.

“Our view is that we’ll be… in this $80-to-$90 range, depending on the news flow,” Jay Hatfield at Infrastructure Capital Management said of the oil price.

“If we actually have a closed Red Sea, that’s a threat. We haven’t seen that yet. That could shoot us over $100,” Hatfield told Bloomberg News.

The Houthis have previously tried to cut off shipping through the Red Sea, leveraging the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint at its southern tip which vessels must navigate when travelling to or from the Suez Canal and the Mediterranean.

Mirroring overnight gains on the Nasdaq, Asia tech stocks rose for a second straight day, with Tokyo up almost two percent before closing slightly lower. Seoul also gave up gains to end the session almost a percent higher.

London, Paris and Frankfurt eked out early gains.

“During the early phase of the (AI stock) boom, companies were rewarded simply for announcing larger investment plans,” said Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management.

“A higher spending guide may still support chip demand, but it also raises questions about free cash flow, funding needs and how much of the future is already embedded in valuations,” he said.

Some clues may come later Wednesday with results from Tesla and Google parent Alphabet, followed by fellow tech bellwethers Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon next week.

On currency markets, the Japanese yen was under pressure again after falling below 163 against the dollar late Tuesday, its weakest since 1986, in part due to the oil price.

Comments from Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama that Japan was ready to take “appropriate and bold action at any time” did little to lift the currency.

World.title: Bezos holds talks with group interested in buying Liverpool stake: reports
World.content:
London – Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has held talks about joining the Amit Bhatia-fronted consortium that has expressed interest in buying a minority stake in Liverpool, according to reports on Wednesday.

Bezos, one of the world’s richest men, could become part of the group led by British-Indian businessman Bhatia, the son-in-law of billionaire steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal.

Sky News reported Bezos’ interest but said he is not certain to proceed with the potential plan.

The 62-year-old American is estimated by Forbes to be worth around £192 billion ($257 billion).

Liverpool’s owners Fenway Sports Group confirmed on Tuesday Bhatia’s consortium had approached them to discuss buying a minority stake in the 20-time English champions.

Bezos has reportedly explored previous bids for the NFL’s Seattle Seahawks and Washington Commanders, but decided against pursuing either deal.

Bhatia’s interest in the Premier League club came on the same day the 46-year-old stepped down from the board at QPR.

He ended an 18-year association with the English Championship team by transferring his stake to majority owner Ruben Gnanalingam.

In 2023, FSG sold a minority stake in Liverpool to investment firm Dynasty and any deal with Bhatia, should it proceed, is expected to be along similar lines.

According to the Financial Times, a deal with the consortium led by Bhatia would value Liverpool at more than $6 billion.

FSG, which also owns the Boston Red Sox baseball team, bought Liverpool in 2010 for £300 million.

World.title: '5,200 applications have been received' for CEO post: Ram Mandir Trust holds second meeting after donation row
World.content:
Ram Mandir Trust holds second meeting after donation row

NEW DELHI: The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday held its second meeting in Ayodhya since the alleged donation embezzlement case surfaced, reviewing administrative matters as the probe continues.The trust said it has received 5,200 applications for the post of CEO of the Ram Mandir, but has deferred the appointment by a month to allow the selection committee more time to scrutinise the applications. It also announced plans to set up a permanent institute to train and certify priests for the temple.Addressing a press conference after the meeting, trust treasurer Govind Dev Giri said the trust had decided to establish a permanent institute for training priests."We have decided to set up a permanent institute for training priests, who would be certified by the Ram temple trust," Giri said.He said the trust had received 5,200 applications for the CEO post."A total of 5,200 applications have been received for the Ram temple trust CEO post. Considering the volume of applications, the selection committee sought one month's additional time, which has been approved by the Trust," Giri said.He added that the trust would appoint a secretary on an interim basis to meet its growing administrative requirements until the CEO is selected.Interim general secretary Krishna Mohan said there was no discussion on appointing the CEO as the trust is still awaiting the report of the Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the alleged donation embezzlement case."There was no discussion on the appointment of the CEO as the SIT report has not been received yet," Krishna Mohan said.The trust also announced the formation of a permanent committee to oversee the religious affairs of the Ram temple.According to Giri, the committee will comprise nine saints, including five from Ayodhya and four from outside, to supervise the temple's religious activities.The meeting comes weeks after the trust accepted the resignations of its former general secretary Champat Rai and trustee Anil Mishra following the alleged donation embezzlement case. Krishna Mohan was appointed interim general secretary, while an SIT was constituted to investigate the allegations.

World.title: 'Unacceptable in a democratic society': SC bar bodies condemn police action against protesters, lawyers during CJP march
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Two Supreme Court bar bodies on Wednesday condemned the alleged police brutality against students and lawyers during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led July 20 march to Parliament, calling for an impartial inquiry into the "excessive use of force" and demanding accountability from those responsible.

The Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), headed by its president and senior advocate Vikas Singh, in a resolution, alleged that the police action left several students and members of the legal fraternity, including SCBA members, injured.

The resolution, issued by SCBA secretary Pragya Baghel, described the use of force against the protesters as "deeply disturbing and wholly unacceptable in a democratic society".

The bar body urged the authorities concerned to conduct an immediate, impartial and time-bound inquiry into the incident, identify those responsible for the alleged excessive use of force, and take appropriate action in accordance with the law.

It also called for proper medical treatment and assistance for all injured students and members of the legal fraternity, while urging authorities to take steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.





"The association stands in solidarity with all those injured and reiterates its commitment to protecting constitutional rights, human dignity and the rule of law," the resolution added.

In a separate statement, the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) expressed deep concern over "reports and visuals showing the use of force by Delhi Police against students and young protesters" who had gathered to peacefully raise concerns over the integrity of public examinations and the future of the country's youth.

SCAORA, in its resolution, maintained that peaceful dissent was not an act of defiance but an exercise of fundamental freedoms guaranteed under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. It added that while the State has the authority to maintain public order, any restriction on these freedoms must meet the constitutional requirements of legality, necessity and proportionality.

The association called for an independent and impartial examination of allegations of excessive force, immediate medical assistance for those injured, and a more restrained, dialogue-based approach while engaging with peaceful protesters.

"The strength of our Republic lies not in suppressing dissent but in protecting it within the framework of the Constitution. The true measure of constitutional governance is not how the State responds to agreement, but how it responds to peaceful disagreement," the resolution added.

On Monday, thousands of students demanding the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak issue and alleged irregularities in the examination system attempted to march to Parliament but were stopped by police using tear gas and batons.

World.title: 'Used to getting punched': Rahul Gandhi says he is 'ready to take many more' after detention during NEET protest
World.content:
'Used to getting punched': Rahul Gandhi says he is 'ready to take many more' after detention during NEET protest

NEW DELHI: Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday said he was âused to getting punchedâ and was ready to âtake many moreâ while standing with students protesting over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and demanding reforms in the education system.His remarks came a day after he, along with Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and other opposition leaders was detained by Delhi Police during a sit-in outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence over the issue.Addressing a press conference at the AICC headquarters, Gandhi said standing up for students, farmers and young people was part of his responsibility as the Leader of the Opposition.Responding to a question about his detention and the police action during Tuesday's protest, Gandhi said, "It's fine. I'm used to getting punched and all. It's no problem. My job is to express the will of India's people, whether it is the will of the students, whether it is the will of young people, whether it is the will of the farmers. This is the job that I am supposed to do as leader of opposition."He added, "I am supposed to become an expression of the voice of India's people.I am supposed to bring attention to where pain is being felt. These are very small costs. These are not big costs. It's a huge honour for me to do this, to be able to stand with the wishes of my people. So couple of punches and all. This is not a problem at all. I'm happy to take many more."Replying to another question about what happened outside the Prime Minister's residence, Gandhi said, "My job is to express the will of India's people. Whether it is the will of the students, the young people, or the farmers, this is the job I am supposed to do as the Leader of the Opposition. I am supposed to become an expression of the voice of India's people. I am supposed to bring attention to where pain is being felt. These are very small costs, not big ones. It is a huge honour for me to do this, to be able to stand with the wishes of my people. So a couple of punches and all, that is not a problem at all. I am happy to take many more."During the press conference, Gandhi reiterated his criticism of the Centre over the alleged examination irregularities, accusing the government of destroying India's education system and expressing full support for the protesting students.He said students were demanding a fair education system and backed their demand for the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Gandhi also demanded that those responsible for the alleged police action against students be held accountable and said Prime Minister Narendra Modi should apologise to them.He claimed that 152 paper leaks had taken place over the past decade with 'zero convictions', alleged that 7.5 crore students and their families had been affected, and said the country's education system had become "rigged" and unaffordable.Rahul Gandhi's remarks came a day after he, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Akhilesh Yadav and several opposition leaders staged a sit-in outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence, demanding a discussion on the alleged NEET paper leak, the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and action over the police crackdown on students.Delhi Police later removed and detained the leaders after the protest entered the high-security zone. Rahul Gandhi was taken to Chhatrasal Stadium before being released a few hours later, while Priyanka Gandhi and some Congress MPs were taken to Mandir Marg police station and later released.The Congress also released videos and photographs showing Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi being removed by police during the protest.One video showed Rahul Gandhi lying on the road as police personnel attempted to carry him away, while another appeared to show him being dragged during the detention. The party also shared a photograph that appeared to show him with a nosebleed following the police action.The Congress has accused the government of suppressing protests over the alleged examination irregularities, while the Centre has said it was willing to discuss the issue in Parliament and criticised the opposition's protest outside the PM Modi's residence.

World.title: Politics of silence: Is NCP(SP) chief Sharad Pawar keeping options open on Delimitation Bill?
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Will

âs NCP(SP) support BJPâs Delimitation Bill if the

government decides to bring it again in the monsoon session of Parliament? While speculations do the rounds, the Maratha strongman remains conspicuously silent and lets his actions keep everyone guessing.

So, while on Tuesday Sharad Pawar joined forces with the opposition at Jantar Mantar where students are protesting against NEET paper leak and seeking education minister Dharmendra Pradhanâs resignation, on Wednesday he was meeting Prime Minister

along with his daughter MP

Supriya Sule

.

In June, there were several reports to suggest that Sharad Pawarâs NCP(SP) could be considering a merger with the

Congress

to prevent any possible poaching of his legislators. A month later in July, there are strong speculations that Sharad Pawar is leaning towards the NDA to secure the future of his party in the twilight years of his politics.

Does this come as a surprise? Well, definitely not. When it comes to politics of ambiguity, no one can beat Sharad Pawar - who is known to keep his cards close to his chest. And that perhaps explains why there is suspense around the line his party could possibly take on the Delimitation Bill.

His daughter Supriya Sule, who is MP from Baramati, has rejected all speculations on backing or joining the NDA and has maintained that the party is yet to take any stand on the Delimitation Bill.





But her remark last week: âif the proposed Delimitation Bill- a key legislative agenda of the NDA government- is based on a uniform 50 per cent increase in seats across all states, there would be little reason to oppose it," has already set tongues wagging.

Pressure to keep his flock together

Sharad Pawar has at present 8 members in Lok Sabha and 10 MLAs in Maharashtra assembly. With the NDA government working aggressively behind the scenes to reach the magic figure of two-thirds majority in Lok Sabha for the Delimitation Bill, Sharad Pawar knows that his MPs are vulnerable. He has just seen

Uddhav Thackeray

helplessly lose his 6 MPs to

Eknath Shinde

âs Shiv Sena. Both Uddhav Thackeray and Sharad Pawar have suffered coups that split their parties vertically.

While Shinde revolted against Uddhav and took control of the Shiv Sena, in NCP the revolt was led by the late Ajit Pawar, who rebelled against his uncle Sharad in 2023 and wrested control of the party.

After a dismal show in the 2024 assembly elections, Pawar knows that his politics and influence is on the wane and his legislators could be lured with promises of greener pastures. Seen in this context, Sharad Pawarâs silence and his mixed signals could be a weapon to keep his legislators hopeful and guessing about his next moves.

The balancing act

Those who have followed Sharad Pawarâs politics, will recount many such instances when he used his power of silence to convey mixed signals to opposing camps. One such example was in 2019 when Sharad Pawar was trying to stitch anti-BJP front in Maharashtra with Uddhav Thackerayâs Shiv Sena and the Congress, while on the other hand, at the same time, his nephew Ajit Pawar was negotiating with the BJP. The two-track politics eventually resulted in a pre-dawn swearing-in of Devendra Fadnavis as chief minister and Ajit Pawar as deputy chief minister.

However, the government was short-lived as Sharad Pawar was forced to dump Ajit Pawar then. But questions were raised even then if Sharad knew about Ajitâs moves and had allowed both the channels to progress simultaneously. Years later, Sharad Pawar dropped enough hints to suggest that he actually knew about the Track 2 manoeuvres by his nephew then.

So while Sharad Pawar remains silent, letâs analyze some of the developments in the recent past to understand his politics of ambiguity.

On July 7, Maharashtra chief minister and senior BJP leader Devendra Fadnavis announced that no new party will be joining the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) or the state's Mahayuti alliance at present.

On July 8, Sharad Pawar paid a courtesy visit to Maharashtra deputy chief minister Eknath Shinde at the Vidhan Bhavan complex. Pawar also met his party MLAs at Shindeâs office.

On July 12, NCP (SP) leader Eknath Khadse, currently a member of the legislative council (MLC), acknowledged that he had travelled to Delhi and had met BJP general secretary Vinod Tawde. Khadse claimed that Amit Shah had called him and asked him to join the BJP.

On July 15, NCP(SP) leader Jayant Patil met Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis to discuss the disqualification of the mayor of Urun-Ishwarpur in his constituency. Interestingly on the same night ruling NCP leaders Praful Patel and Sunil Tatkare also met Fadnavis.

These developments triggered speculations around NCP(SP)'s possible support to Delimitation Bill or the possible merger of the two NCP factions (one led by Sharad Pawar and the other led by Sunetra Pawar, wife of late Ajit Pawar) at the behest of the BJP. As expected, Sule denied both. "Neither the BJP nor the Congress nor any NDA ally has contacted us. When there is no proposal, the question of merger or joining any alliance does not arise," the Baramati MP said.

She also denied any political planning behind these developments and labelled them as âcourtesy visitâ, âunexpected meetingâ and âcoincidenceâ. Sule claimed that the NCP(SP) chiefâs meeting with Shinde was "purely a coincidence". On NCP (SP) leader Jayant Patil's meeting with Fadnavis, she said Patil had officially sought an appointment to raise the issue of action taken against a municipal council president belonging to the Sharad Pawar-led party.

Sule has also dismissed reports that party MPs and MLAs were under pressure to join the ruling alliance and claimed that all eight NCP (SP) MPs firmly rally behind party chief Sharad Pawar. "We meet regularly. None of our MPs or MLAs has told me that they want to take a different political stand. Everyone is happy where they are," she said.

When Sharad Pawar differed with allies

Sharad Pawar is known for breaking ranks with allies and taking independent stand.

When all regional parties were determined to isolate Congress and make a third front excluding both BJP and Congress, it was Sharad Pawar who said that any opposition alliance without Congress would not be effective. Similarly, it was Sharad Pawar who once advocated that regional parties that were born out of Congress should consider âghar wapsiâ.

Just as Pawar broke ranks to back Congress on some occasions, he did the same to back Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the NDA government on other occasions.

Often, Pawarâs praise for PM Modi and his policies have generated political buzz. While all opposition parties, including the Congress, were targeting PM Modi over his many foreign trips, Sharad Pawar had a different take. In May this year he praised the Prime Minister for working to uphold India's prestige on the global stage.

"Political differences should not come in the way when it comes to protecting India's prestige, and PM Modi is working to uphold the country's honour abroad," Pawar stated.

'If you are being discussed ... '

While it may not be easy to comprehend what guides Sharad Pawarâs politics of silence, this one remark from his daughter Supriya Sule perhaps gives some insight into his thought processes. Responding to constant media scrutiny, the Baramati MP recently invoked a lesson from her father and said: "Sharad Pawar always says that if you are being discussed -- whether for good or bad reasons -- it means your political currency is still strong and sound.

"

That explains why it has always been difficult to predict the politics of Sharad Pawar. His politics of silence and his art of conveying mixed signals to friends and foes are perhaps his weapons to keep all possibilities open - for we all know there are no permanent friends or permanent enemies in politics.

World.title: 'Dharmendra Pradhan should be shown the door': Rahul Gandhi backs students - top quotes
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday launched a fresh attack on the Centre over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, accusing the government of failing students and demanding the removal of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Addressing a press conference, Gandhi alleged that India's education system had become a ârigged systemâ, claimed there had been â152 paper leaksâ over the past decade with âzero convictionsâ and criticised the police action against students protesting over the examination controversy. He also reiterated his demand that Pradhan resign.

His remarks came after police used tear gas and lathi-charged protesters during the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) march towards Parliament over the alleged paper leak.

Here are the top quotes from Rahul Gandhiâs press conference:

On education system and paper leaks

"The thing that is very clear to everybody is that our education system, which was known to be one of the best education systems in the world, is today a rigged system."

"In the last 10 years, 152 paper leaks have taken place and there have been zero convictions. Zero. So somebody, or a group of people, has destroyed our education system, India's most valuable asset, destroying the lives of our students. And what does the government do? Zero convictions."

"What we do know is that 152 paper leaks have taken place over the last decade. So, approximately one a month. Every month, lakhs of students are told that all the stress they went through, they're going to have to go through again."



"We are 100% in agreement with what every single student is feeling and what every single student is doing. There must be consequences to what has been done some days ago."

On students and police action

"The question is, why is this happening to our students? What exactly have our students done? Thousands and thousands of students... To have security forces aiming weapons at them, to be beaten up, to be thrashed, to be humiliated. What have they done wrong? They're protesting peacefully."

"They're simply asking, 'Listen, as students in this country, we deserve an education system that works. We deserve an education system that is fair,' and we don't have it."

"Children have committed suicide. Our students go through immense stress. And then, at the last minute, they are told that the paper has leaked. So there is a legitimate problem. And it is now a very deep problem in this country."

On students and their families

"7.5 crore students and their families are affected by this. These are middle-class and poor families. They put their hard-earned money into this... And the best part of this is zero convictions."



"They (students) have some demands. The first demand, a completely legitimate demand, is that Dharmendra Pradhan, who has failed as an education minister and is known to be corrupt, should be relieved of his duties. It is a 100% legitimate demand. There is nothing wrong with it. He has shown India and the world that he is incapable of running this system. Exam leaks are happening one after the other."

"The second demand is that every single person who raised a finger on our students â it doesn't matter who ordered it or who executed it â should be made accountable."

The first demand, a completely legitimate demand, is that Dharmendra Pradhan, who has failed as an education minister and is known to be corrupt, should be relieved of his duties. It is a 100% legitimate demand. There is nothing wrong with it. He has shown India and the world that he is incapable of running this system. Exam leaks are happening one after the other." "The second demand is that every single person who raised a finger on our students â it doesn't matter who ordered it or who executed it â should be made accountable." "The third thing is that the man who is running this entire system, the man who is finally accountable for all this, should have the decency to apologise to the students for what has happened."

On education minister Dharmendra Pradhan

"Dharmendra Pradhan should be shown the door, he is incapable of holding the post."

"This gentleman, Dharmendra Pradhan, has literally destroyed India's biggest asset... Our education system has been wiped out and so we fully support these demands and we fully support every single student who's on the streets."

"The government wants to push this under the carpet, but we want that Pradhan goes, the Prime Minister apologises and the education system changes."
